What happened in failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?

title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
excerpt:
Watch: Why are students staging protests at schools in France?

Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school fund...
body_text:
Watch: Why are students staging protests at schools in France?

Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.

Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance of a school in the northern city of Rouen.

Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.

The interior ministry said 1,949 people had been arrested on Thursday, with 305 police officers injured. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest.

The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".

Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.

In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.

While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.

The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.

So far, 1,027 lycees have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.

At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.

On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.

Aftermath of the fire at the Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes

Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks.

He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets.

"The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.

While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.

The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.

Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.

LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.

Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."

The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.

Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city.

While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.

Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

Protesters set e-scooters on fire near Saint-Charles high school in Marseille

Dozens hurt and hundreds arrested in wave of French school protests

title: World Cup darling Freddy is back stateside, almost makes fatal mistake touring notorious southern city
excerpt:
'Outnumbered' co-host Kayleigh McEnany shares the story of Freddy, a now-famous German soccer fan whose U.S. trip continues for three weeks after his team's World Cup elimination.

The World Cup guest...
body_text:
'Outnumbered' co-host Kayleigh McEnany shares the story of Freddy, a now-famous German soccer fan whose U.S. trip continues for three weeks after his team's World Cup elimination.

The World Cup guest from Germany stole the hearts of soccer fans all across America for his love of the host country, documenting his trip through the United States on social media and giving glowing reviews along the way.

German soccer fan Freddy's summer to remember concludes with a visit to the White House on Tuesday. In June, Freddy and his friends had the pleasure of meeting country star Ella Langley after a show in Oklahoma City. (FreddyLA7 / Getty Images)

Well, Freddy is back in the Lower 48, this time spending his days in the American South and enjoying the actual greatest sport on earth: college football.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Fredster has been to Auburn and LSU to see a couple of SEC games, and this week he finds himself in the Magnolia State en route to Alabama for an Oktoberfest event over the weekend.

And what do you do when you find yourself in Mississippi for a couple of days? Go hang out in Jackson, of course!

Jackson, MS skyline including the State Capitol Building (iStock)

Wait, that can't be right. What, was Memphis already booked up for the week?

Yes, our dear Freddy has decided to make a stop in the capital city for a little RnR, and made the cardinal sin of thinking he was going for a stroll in gay old Paree instead of the deadliest city, per capita, in the contiguous U.S.

"Hey guys, Freddy here! Just thinking about maybe hitting up Buffalo Wild Wings for a quick bite to eat then walking through a literal warzone to take in the sights and sounds of the place."

Did this guy read the travel itinerary or what?

FIFA EYES WORLD CUP FORMAT EXPANSION FROM 48 TO 64 TEAMS: SHOULD THE US BE THE PERMANENT HOST?

This isn't the first time Freddy made a classic tourist mistake, as he has a well-documented ride on the MARTA in Atlanta from his days as a World Cup visitor.

The best part is that pretty much everyone on social media was trying to warn our lieber freunde about the dangers of Jackson, Mississippi.

While his followers were whipped up into a frenzy wondering if their dude from Deutschland was okay, Freddy apparently enjoyed a nice meal at the great American eatery known as Chili's and then returned safely to his hotel bed.

Chili's retro "Margarita Bar" celebrates one of the chain's signature drinks. (Chili's)

Maybe Freddy can try the lottery or head to Las Vegas next, since he likes playing the odds so much.

I don't know if it's ignorance or testicular fortitude, but our guy spent a night on the streets of Jackson and lived to tell about it.

Now, don't ever pull a stunt like that again.

title: 'Yellowstone' star Neal McDonough refuses to watch hit series for ‘painful’ reason
excerpt:
The actor explained that his wife gave him an ultimatum when it came to his drinking, which ultimately got him to stop.

Neal McDonough may be known as one of the most ruthless villains in the "Yellow...
body_text:
The actor explained that his wife gave him an ultimatum when it came to his drinking, which ultimately got him to stop.

Neal McDonough may be known as one of the most ruthless villains in the "Yellowstone" universe, but there's one thing the actor himself has never done: watched the show.

McDonough, 60, portrayed ruthless businessman Malcolm Beck on the hit Taylor Sheridan series, appearing in six episodes during Season 2.

But reliving the performance is something McDonough admitted he avoids.

JEFF BRIDGES NEARLY PLAYED JOHN DUTTON BEFORE KEVIN COSTNER LANDED 'YELLOWSTONE' ROLE

Neal McDonough said he has never watched his performance on "Yellowstone." (Jesse Grant/Getty Images for A+E Networks )

"I've never seen it. You know, I don't watch any of my stuff," McDonough said on the "Arroyo Grande" podcast.

He went on to explain why he refuses to watch himself on screen.

"As a method actor, I can tell you if I look at a frame – that's why I don't watch any of my stuff. If I look at a frame of a show from 20 years ago, I know exactly the thought I was thinking. I know the song I was thinking about. I know where I was going. So going back to me sometimes can be really kind of traumatic and painful," he shared.

Even attending his own movie premieres doesn't necessarily mean he'll watch the finished product.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Neal McDonough attends "The Last Rodeo" red carpet premiere on May 12, 2025, in Fort Worth, Texas. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)

"I'll go to premieres of our films, and I'll do the red carpet. [His wife] Ruvé and I will walk in, out the exit, grab a nice dinner someplace, go to the party after. ‘How'd you like the movie?' 'It was great. It was awesome. I loved it.’ I just don't like to watch myself," he said.

And McDonough isn't losing sleep over whether he delivered in a particular scene.

"I was there on the day," he said. I know I did a great job because God gave me a talent. I'm terrible at pounding nails. I'm not very good at telling jokes. But as Ruvé said, ‘Man, you can act.’ And so I don't need to look to see if it was good or not. They keep on hiring me, right? If they keep on hiring, I must be doing something right."

'WIZARDS OF WAVERLY PLACE' STAR DAVID HENRIE SAYS HIS FAITH COST HIM AGENTS, MONEY AND FRIENDS IN HOLLYWOOD

His decision to avoid watching "Yellowstone" comes years after a painful chapter in McDonough's life that left him questioning whether his Hollywood career was over.

McDonough portrayed ruthless businessman Malcolm Beck on "Yellowstone," but admitted he has never watched the hit Taylor Sheridan series. (Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)

McDonough has claimed that he was fired from ABC's "Scoundrels" in 2010 after refusing to perform intimate scenes with a female co-star, saying the decision effectively derailed his career and left him struggling financially and personally.

"What time is the bar open? That was generally my thought process back then," he explained to Fox News Digital in May. "It was, you know, fired from a show because I wouldn't kiss a woman. No one would hire me because they thought I was this religious nut bag, which is that I love my wife so much. And no one can understand it, no one could understand it."

McDonough has also spoken openly about his struggles with alcohol during that period.

He said he "was always a drinker," but "it became a bad problem" after he said Hollywood had blackballed him.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Neal McDonough has long credited his wife, Ruvé McDonough, with helping him navigate the emotional highs and lows of a decades-long Hollywood career. (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images)

"I lost the house, lost the cars, lost everything," he said.

"She grabbed me and says, it's us or the bottle, you choose," McDonough recalled. "And I never looked back."

The ultimatum changed everything for the longtime actor.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

McDonough and Ruvé have been married for nearly 23 years. They share five children and have also built a professional partnership, producing projects together including "Boon," "The Warrant: Breaker's Law," "Homestead" and "The Last Rodeo."

The couple met while McDonough was filming "Band of Brothers" in 2000 and married on Dec. 1, 2003.

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Marine turned homeschool mom sues Oregon district over denied reimbursement for Christian curriculum
excerpt:
Tessa Bulzan says Hillsboro School District approved her Christian curriculum academically, then denied reimbursement because of the authors’ biblical worldview. ADF is suing on her behalf.

A Marine ...
body_text:
Tessa Bulzan says Hillsboro School District approved her Christian curriculum academically, then denied reimbursement because of the authors’ biblical worldview. ADF is suing on her behalf.

A Marine veteran and mother of five is suing an Oregon school district, alleging officials denied reimbursement for academic curriculum solely because the books reflected a Christian worldview.

Tessa Bulzan, who left a six-figure job after an incident at her children’s school conflicted with her moral and biblical beliefs, joined Hillsboro School District’s homeschool partnership program in July 2025. She says the district initially approved her Christian curriculum as academically valid before denying reimbursement months later.

"There was an incident where a teacher said something against our moral and biblical beliefs, and it was so convicting and, after a lot of prayer, my husband and I decided that I would quit my six-figure job and I would become a stay-at-home mother and start homeschooling our children," Bulzan told Fox News Digital on Wednesday. "And so far, it's been the best decision we've ever made."

CALIFORNIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SUED OVER FIELD TRIP TO MOSQUE WHERE STUDENTS ALLEGEDLY DONNED MUSLIM GARB

Tessa Bulzan with her family. (Alliance Defending Freedom)

Bulzan said joining Hillsboro’s homeschool partnership program felt like an answer to prayer, particularly because homeschooling was expensive, and her husband was earning less than $50,000 in his new job.

She said the family was encouraged to learn that the Christian curriculum they were already using, including Abeka and Classical Conversations, met the district’s academic requirements.

"Then in January, when we went to go reimburse or seek reimbursement for that curriculum, we were denied solely on its author's biblical world beliefs," Bulzan said.

Bulzan said she was shocked and devastated when her reimbursement request was denied because the family had planned to use the money for extracurricular activities and additional curriculum.

WISCONSIN STUDENT ALLEGES SCHOOL BARRED HER FROM USING BIBLE VERSE AT GRADUATION

A child clasps their hands in prayer over a Bible outdoors. (iStock)

She said she questioned an administrator about why the district would reject academically rigorous core materials, including a cursive book used to help her daughter, who has dyslexia. According to Bulzan, the administrator acknowledged that there was no comparable alternative at the same academic level but said the materials could not be funded because of the author’s biblical worldview, references to God and incidental Scripture.

"One-hundred percent, it was discrimination," Bulzan said. "When I first started the program, I was told that all of my curriculum not only met the standards of the school board and the state of Oregon, but it excelled and went past most of their standards for all of their core."

"So, math, arithmetic, writing, grammar, all of these books that I was using to satisfy their academic requirements were all being accepted and there was no argument, there was no denial of that," she continued. "When I was denied, I wanted to understand, is it just because it's the Bible or and my Christian beliefs, or is it because they just are trying to be neutral? They're trying to make sure that everybody has a fair play in the reimbursement process."

SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT

A stock image shows students reading books in a school setting. (Ryan McVay/iStock)

Bulzan said that after some investigation on her part, she felt as if she was being singled out.

"What I quickly realized is that that's not true, that they were singling me out as a Christian because I bought two different books with very, very secular and very opposing worldviews that I, in my opinion, should not be taught or be within the school district," she said.

"One of them is of Indian or ancestral nature where they're worshiping water spirits, and they believe that as you drink water, these spirits become part of you," Bulzan added. "And so they're allowing other forms of worship for reimbursement, but they won't allow my grammar book because it references God."

VERMONT PAYS $566K IN DAMAGES, LEGAL FEES TO CHRISTIAN SCHOOL IT BANNED FROM ALL SPORTS COMPETITIONS FOR YEARS

A gavel, legal books, and a statue of Themis are displayed on a judge's desk. (iStock)

In September, ADF attorneys filed suit against the Hillsboro School District in federal court.

"We just filed this case in federal court in Oregon, so it's very early stages, but the case is really clear here," ADF attorney Kate Anderson told Fox News Digital.

"This is religious discrimination, and it's discrimination that the Supreme Court and the Constitution does not stand for," she added. "Over the last decade, the Supreme Court has over and over again said that when a government sets out a public benefit program like this funding that can go to any person, it cannot exclude religious conduct, religious content."

"In this case, it's religious curriculum," Anderson added. "Religious families need to be treated on equal footing with secular families and the same with their curriculum. And so this violates the Constitution very clearly, and we're very hopeful that the court will step in quickly."

JUDGE ORDERS WASHINGTON SCHOOL DISTRICT TO LOOSEN LIMITS ON OFF-CAMPUS BIBLE CLUB FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL STUDENTS

Police stand outside the U.S. Supreme Court. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Hillsboro School District said the district cannot comment on pending litigation.

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

title: After Red Sea losses, Yemen’s government forces hold the line
excerpt: Yemen’s Houthi rebels conducted intense attacks across frontlines in Taiz governorate on Thursday, as the Iran-allied group attempts to build on its lighting offensive that captured the country’s Red ...
body_text:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels conducted intense attacks across frontlines in Taiz governorate on Thursday, as the Iran-allied group attempts to build on its lighting offensive that captured the country’s Red Sea coast last month.

Thus far, Yemeni government forces have been able to hold their positions on the frontlines and even claimed to have inflicted heavy losses against the Houthis.

Still, there are few signs that the Saudi-backed government intends to begin a serious counteroffensive against the Houthis in the near future, despite the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi calling for a general mobilisation against the rebels on September 25.

The government instead seems to be pursuing a more gradual process, building up its military forces and attempting to make them more cohesive.

Abdul Basir al-Bahr, a senior official with the internationally recognised government army’s Taiz Military Axis, told Al Jazeera that the general mobilisation call was part of that effort.

Al-Bahr said plans include bringing reserve personnel back into the military’s ranks and retraining them, alongside local anti-Houthi fighters and civilian volunteers.

He stressed that the measures were at an early stage and their battlefield impact could not be judged yet.

In Taiz, Al Jazeera’s field monitoring has found that fighting has continued since early September without any major shifts that can be directly attributed to the general mobilisation.

The picture is similar on other fronts, including the Kahboub Mountains overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and in Lahj, south of Taiz.

Yemeni government field commanders told Al Jazeera the general mobilisation had not yet led to frontline reinforcements.

But that does not mean that military activity has not intensified. On Monday, Colonel Majid al-Nazili, spokesman for the government’s military forces, said the forces had carried out more than 400 strikes over a 24-hour period against the Houthis, causing losses in personnel and equipment.

The ability of the Yemeni government’s military to halt further Houthi advances since the Red Sea reversal appears to reflect a combination of more favourable defensive terrain in the Taiz mountains and Lahj, as well as increased firepower.

The loss of the coastline was aided by weak coordination among anti-Houthi forces, who – despite officially being under one military chain of command – appeared divided and unable to respond quickly to the Houthi advance.

In both Taiz and Lahj – as well as Marib in Yemen’s north – anti-Houthi forces have shown more unity and have years of experience preventing Houthi military advances. Government-aligned forces have also had time to reinforce areas where the Houthis are attempting to advance.

The use of air power is also growing, with government forces reporting hundreds of air, drone, artillery and other strikes targeting Houthi positions and reinforcements in the past few days.

After having seized stretches of the Red Sea coast, the Houthis now need control of the mountainous high ground overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and the roads leading inland to consolidate those gains. Their attempts to take that high ground have so far failed, while the expanded territory has increased the manpower and logistical burden of defending their new positions.

The result, so far, is increasingly a battle over roads and supply lines, with neither side so far able to reproduce the kind of rapid breakthrough seen on the Red Sea coast.

title: Saudi-led coalition says power station attacked in Medina, blames Houthis
excerpt: The Saudi-led alliance fighting Yemen’s Houthis has accused the Iran-aligned group of attacking an electricity facility in the Muslim holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia this week, a claim the Houthis...
body_text:
The Saudi-led alliance fighting Yemen’s Houthis has accused the Iran-aligned group of attacking an electricity facility in the Muslim holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia this week, a claim the Houthis deny.

Meanwhile in Yemen on Thursday, Saudi-backed government forces said they were repelling a large-scale Houthi attack in the Taiz governorate and inflicting heavy losses on its fighters.

The Saudi-led coalition said that a power distribution station in Medina, which supplies electricity to the Masjid an-Nabawi (the Prophet’s Mosque), was attacked on Tuesday, putting one transformer out of service but without affecting ⁠the electricity network.

It said an investigation and examination of drone wreckage confirmed Houthi involvement in planning and carrying out the attack.

A Houthi military source, quoted by the Houthi-run Saba news agency, denied the accusation, calling it a “lie” and saying it was intended to cover up ‌what he described as Saudi Arabia’s failure to substantiate its earlier accusation that the Houthis targeted the Muslim holy city of Mecca.

The coalition claimed the Medina attack was part of what it described as repeated Houthi attempts to target the two holy mosques – the Masjid al-Haram (the Grand Mosque) in Mecca and Masjid an-Nabawi – and “provoke” ⁠Muslims worldwide. It said it would continue taking measures to protect the holy sites and pilgrims.

Separately, the ⁠coalition said that on Thursday it intercepted ⁠and destroyed four drones ⁠launched by the Houthis over the southern Saudi city of ‌Khamis Mushait and two ballistic missiles over Khamis Mushait and Jazan, also in the south.

The latest escalation in Saudi Arabia comes as the armed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government claimed that they killed dozens of Houthi fighters as intense clashes spread across several fronts in Taiz province in southwestern Yemen.

Yemen’s army said in a statement on X that the Houthis had opened heavy fire on Wednesday evening in Jabal Habashi and Maqbanah districts, west of Taiz, and on the al-Aqrud front in al-Masrakh district to the southeast.

Citing a military source, the Saudi-backed forces reported killing at least 30 Houthi fighters on the al-Aqrud front alone, in addition to wounding dozens.

Six air strikes also inflicted heavy losses southeast of Taiz, and on the Humayr front in the Maqbanah directorate to the west, the statement added.

As the number of people internally displaced in Yemen rises, the majority are being resettled in Taiz, according to government figures. The management unit for Yemen’s internally displaced people camps said 197,906 individuals had been officially registered as of Wednesday, comprising 29,519 families.

More than 97,000 people are being housed in Taiz province, followed by Lahij, with more than 50,000.

Amid the intense fighting, Saudi Arabia on Thursday announced it approved 224 million Saudi riyals ($59.7m) in budget funding for Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

The funds will help “enhance the regularity of government financial flows, support the efficiency of fiscal policy, and contribute to strengthening the purchasing power of the Yemeni citizen”, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jabir, said on X.

Last month, Houthi fighters expanded control over the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important trade routes, by seizing the Red Sea city of Mocha.

Known as the Gate of Tears, Bab al-Mandeb is a critical artery for crude oil and fuel travelling from the Gulf to the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, as well as for Asian commodities and Russian oil.

Government forces then pledged not to let the Houthis advance further, with field commanders in Taiz and on the western coast saying they would attempt to retake Mocha.

title: California issues investigative subpoena to OpenAI over rogue agents’ hacking
excerpt:
State attorney general issues subpoena to OpenAI as ​part of broader inquiry into potential security vulnerabilities

California’s attorney general has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI, star...
body_text:
State attorney general issues subpoena to OpenAI as ​part of broader inquiry into potential security vulnerabilities

California’s attorney general has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI, starting an investigation into the startup ⁠as ​part of a broader inquiry into potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents related ⁠to its AI models, his office said on Thursday.

Last month, Rob Bonta announced that ⁠the Department of Justice was conducting a formal ​investigation into the “Hugging ‌Face incident”, amid increasing ‌scrutiny of the AI industry. AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked Hugging Face in July, gaining access to parts of the open-source platform’s infrastructure.

“My office is ​asking ​OpenAI additional questions ​regarding cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the ​company and ‌its AI models,” ​Bonta said ​in a statement.

OpenAI did not ‌immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Federal Trade Commission is ‌conducting an industry-wide investigation into Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI labs to uncover ​the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers. The investigation is the first official US enforcement action ⁠that delves into rogue AI agents.

Bonta warned that developers failing to uphold this responsibility could face legal accountability.

title: Canada to fast track oil pipeline meant to diversify economy away from US
excerpt: Canada will fast track the approval process for a new proposed crude oil export pipeline to its west coast that could generate billions in revenue and boost economic growth, Prime Minister Mark Carney...
body_text:
Canada will fast track the approval process for a new proposed crude oil export pipeline to its west coast that could generate billions in revenue and boost economic growth, Prime Minister Mark Carney has said.

Carney made the announcement on Thursday to fast-track the pipeline, which is a crucial part of his bid to diversify the economy away from the United States and help lessen the effect of US President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Carney said Ottawa is officially listing the Pacific Link pipeline, which had been announced in July, as a project of national interest. That will ensure it proceeds through a single federal regulatory review process. He said Ottawa aimed to complete the process by September 1, 2027.

“A pipeline to the west coast is part of our mission to transform our economy, to double our non-US exports over the next decade … [and] to unlock our full potential as a global energy superpower,” he told reporters in Fort McMurray, hub of Alberta’s tar sands industry.

Ottawa says the 1 million barrel a day project would create 140,000 jobs and generate more than 20 billion Canadian dollars ($14bn) in gross domestic product (GDP) per year and 100 billion Canadian dollars ($70bn) in government revenue by 2060.

Canada currently has just one east-west oil export pipeline in Canada, the 890,000-barrel-per-day Trans Mountain pipeline. An expansion of that pipeline was completed in 2024, but it is already running at capacity.

For years, Canada has sent more than 90 percent of its crude oil exports to the US via pipeline. A new oil export pipeline could make Canada a major global energy supplier, as Asia’s top importers seek oil from outside the Middle East in the wake of the Iran conflict.

Filling the pipeline, however, would require new tar sands expansions of the type no company has undertaken in more than a decade.

The pipeline will be built by government-owned Trans Mountain Corp in coordination with Pembina Pipeline Corp. Alberta estimates it could cost between 35.2 billion Canadian dollars and 43.7 billion Canadian dollars ($24.7bn – $30.7bn).

The majority owners will be the federal government and the government of Alberta. Indigenous communities will be offered a minimum of 10 percent ownership interest.

Previous oil pipeline projects in Canada have faced strong opposition from environmentalists and Indigenous groups, resulting in the cancellation of some projects and leading to cost overruns and construction delays with others.

Carney made the announcement alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith in Fort McMurray in the heart of Canada’s tar sands, a move meant to mend relations with oil-rich Alberta as separatists push for a referendum on leaving Canada.

Alberta is holding a public vote on October 19 on whether to hold a referendum on leaving Canada. Smith has long complained that Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, hindered Alberta’s energy industry and fuelled separatist sentiment.

Smith said she would vote to keep Alberta in Canada and called the roughly 22 percent support for separation in a recent poll “still too high for my liking”.

“I don’t like the fact that many of our fellow citizens have given up on Canada,” Smith said, adding that the pipeline was an example of how “cooperative federalism can work in action”.

Asked what message Albertans considering separation should take from the announcement, Carney said it demonstrated that “Canada is working” and showed what the country could achieve by acting together.

title: How success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in power
excerpt:
Critics argue PM’s praise of Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester ignores public cost of city’s transformation

In July 2016, the Manchester City player Yaya Touré ambled into a s...
body_text:
Critics argue PM’s praise of Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester ignores public cost of city’s transformation

In July 2016, the Manchester City player Yaya Touré ambled into a small bar near Beijing’s Workers’ Stadium and offered a bemused smile as dozens of Chinese fans rushed towards him.

Manchester City had just won their sixth trophy under the big-spending ownership of Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group and the blues were international megastars. They were also magnets for investment.

On a trade mission led by Sir Howard Bernstein, the architect of modern Manchester, civic leaders rolled out club legends such as Mike Summerbee and Sun Jihai in a charm offensive to football-mad Chinese businessmen who saw that the club and the city were on the rise.

A decade on, Manchester is transformed. Estate agents advertise £15,000-a-month penthouses in a city-region growing faster economically than any other in Britain, while the success of “Manchesterism” has powered its mayor, Andy Burnham, to Downing Street.

Yet the city’s close ties with Abu Dhabi United Group are now facing fresh scrutiny, after Manchester City’s owners were found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules.

In a surprising intervention on Wednesday, Burnham praised Abu Dhabi United Group as “such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester” and that he would be “really concerned” to lose them as the club’s owners.

The prime minister went on to say that he would not get involved in the Premier League’s disciplinary process, but appeared to express some sympathy for City’s plight by referring to a similar investigation into Everton, the club he supports.

“I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled,” he said.

Burnham’s comments raised eyebrows given the continuing disciplinary process – the Premier League is considering a range of sanctions – and because it turned the spotlight on to Abu Dhabi United Group’s wider investments in Greater Manchester, where he was mayor from 2017 until June this year.

One Burnham ally said it was “absolutely mad” for the prime minister to comment and risk being seen to be influencing a disciplinary process, describing it as his “biggest mistake so far”.

In an attempt to clarify the prime minister’s remarks on Thursday, a No 10 spokesperson said: “As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgment is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process.

“It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected. Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.”

When Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi group took over Manchester City in 2008, the grounds for success had already been laid.

The club had a gleaming new stadium, built with taxpayers’ money for the Commonwealth games just four years earlier, and council bosses were eager for a reliable long-term investor in a city battling the financial crash.

In 2014, Manchester city council announced a “£1bn deal” with City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour, one of the world’s richest men, to transform a large stretch of land between the stadium and the edge of the city centre. Richard Leese, then the council leader, promised it to be “a world-class exemplar of regeneration”.

The partnership between the council and Manchester City’s owner, which was called Manchester Life, included more than 1,000 private rented apartments and 395 built-for-sale homes – but not one social or affordable home.

In a sharply critical assessment of the Manchester Life partnership published in 2024, researchers at the University of Sheffield said it appeared that the council had leased the land to Abu Dhabi at a much cheaper rate than many comparable developments – they had “sold the family silver too cheaply”, the academics said – and did not appear to be receiving any rental income or revenue from the property sales.

All of the property, with an estimated worth of £350m, is controlled by Jersey-domiciled subsidiaries and ultimately owned by Abu Dhabi interests, the researchers found.

They described it as a “transfer of public wealth to private hands that is difficult to justify as prudent”.

Dr Richard Goulding, who co-authored the University of Sheffield research, said on Thursday that the Manchester Life development raised “questions about what type of Britain we’re trying to build and who the type of Manchester that we’ve built works for”.

He added: “On the one hand, [the Abu Dhabi deal] was bringing money in. On the other hand, a lot of that money was flowing into flats whose rents, according to our research, are being taken offshore.”

In July, Manchester city council published a review of its deals with private developers. It found that while these agreements had delivered “significant benefits”, there were “weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance”, particularly around the profit-sharing nature of these deals.

A Manchester city council spokesperson said: “We do not recognise the criticisms linked to the disposal of public land and the idea that there is no financial benefit to the council through this partnership.

“The tired claim that working in partnership with Manchester City FC’s owners has not been a good deal for the council or the city has been debunked repeatedly. It is a one-sided perspective that fails to take into account the positive impact of investment in Ancoats and New Islington as well as the wider east Manchester area.”

The council added: “Claims that some land was sold too cheaply to Manchester Life ignore the fact that there was zero market interest at the time of the sale, that the land is worth more now precisely because of Manchester Life’s investment and the significant financial return the council is receiving through profit-sharing arrangements.”

Gleaming skyscrapers have transformed Manchester’s skyline over the past decade, when the city’s population has grown by nearly 100,000 people and become one of Europe’s most attractive destinations for foreign money.

Yet born-and-bred Mancunians have felt increasingly pushed out. A report published earlier this year by Greater Manchester Combined Authority, which Burnham led until June, revealed that of the 10,974 homes built across the region in the nine years to 2024, only 679 (6%) were classed as affordable.

Hayley Flynn, an anti-gentrification campaigner who leads tours of Manchester, said development of luxury flats in Ancoats, the home of Abu Dhabi’s Manchester Life project, had not benefited the area’s existing community.

“What provisions have we got for them? They’re not going to spend £7 on a loaf of bread in Pollen [a trendy bakery], but that’s their nearest bakery,” she said. “All these apartments for influencers – it’s quite a forceful erosion that’s just pushing the community out.”

Tim Heatley, a co-founder of the Manchester developer Capital & Centric, said the city had benefited from Abu Dhabi’s riches and that the success of City had “put Manchester on the map internationally”.

Under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups, seven League Cups and one Champions League, becoming one of the world’s elite clubs.

The club, which continues to deny any wrongdoing, won eight trophies, including three Premier League titles between 2009 and 2018, the period under investigation.

Heatley said Abu Dhabi had “a major impact on that particular area of the city” between the Etihad Stadium and Manchester city centre, but that he believed the region’s economic upturn would have happened without the football investment.

title: Netanyahu says Flydubai attacker had 'Islamist radical indoctrination'
excerpt: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoct...
body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".

The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.

Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".

The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.

UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.

Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".

Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes

"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."

However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.

Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.

He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again."

Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel, unlike the UAE.

The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".

Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack

Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?

Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".

India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".

The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"

Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.

The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.

Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.

Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.

At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at  Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.

Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.

Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.

Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.

The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

title: Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes
excerpt:
Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment

Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benef...
body_text:
Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment

Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned.

Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work.

The move could be fraught with political danger after last year’s dramatic welfare rebellion by Labour MPs. But ministers have spent weeks trying to persuade them the plans are about reform, and feel confident opposition has waned.

The plans are still awaiting the conclusions of reviews by Alan Milburn, who is looking at young people’s employment, and the Timms panel, which is examining the personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested benefit that helps sick and disabled people with support costs.

However, a central option under consideration for young people is removing the health element of universal credit for claimants under 25, which has already been almost halved to £217 a month, and offering intensive support for people to get into work. The possibility of removing it for existing claimants – not just new ones – is being looked at.

The extra support will include subsidised jobs for younger people, more targeted “back to work” schemes and support with mental health, as part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.

As part of the same package, officials are looking at a new system to replace the Pip, which is claimed by four million people, after attempts to change existing eligibility criteria were rejected by MPs last year.

One possible plan is for a separate regime to apply to the under-25 agegroup, with reduced or withdrawn entitlements – although those with the most severe and debilitating disabilities would not lose any money.

More broadly, officials are working up plans under the replacement system for a new set of eligibility criteria and assessments for the extra costs of disability, and looking at whether this would apply to all claimants of working age, or those below a cut-off point such as 50 or 60. Again, those with the most severe conditions would not lose money or be reassessed.

Officials have also been returning to the idea of cuts to the Motability scheme at a future budget, after axing tax breaks worth £300m. The scheme allows disabled people to use their Pip benefit to lease new cars for three years.

One Whitehall source said removing or further cutting the health element of universal credit for those older than 25 had been considered, but government sources said this was not on the table.

Officials have looked at systems in other countries, such as Denmark, which restricts access to its “disability pension” for under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they have no ability permanently to work.

A government source said: “We will be bringing forward a comprehensive package of support and reform to tackle the scandal of a million young people not in education, employment or training. The details are yet to be decided, but we are committed to enabling work and opportunity, while always protecting those unable to work.”

The significant changes would need legislation, with ministers and officials looking at a bill encompassing the replacement for Pip and changes to the under-25 system to be presented in the next session of parliament next year.

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, used his conference speech this week to describe changing the welfare system as a “moral crusade”, saying too many younger people were stuck claiming benefits for too long.

However, the scale of the plans could reignite concerns among Labour MPs about the impact on the cost of living for disabled people, particularly when Pip is a non-means-tested benefit that is unrelated to a person’s employment status.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has gone further by saying she would ban young people from signing straight on to the benefits system if her party won the next election, as part of a plan to cut £23bn from the welfare bill. Under-25s with less than six months of continuous employment would no longer be able to claim universal credit and would instead have to undergo intensive job coaching.

Reform UK plans to cut the overall welfare bill by £50bn, with Pip replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the “gravely ill and severely challenged”, while “lower level conditions” would get support overseen by local authorities.

Polling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe that tackling the root causes of joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. Burnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts”, and used his party conference speech to signal an overhaul of the welfare system to pay for an expansion of youth jobs and training support.

UK welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55% of the budget, and young people including Neets – but not children – about 2.5%. Milburn said it was “shameful” the government spent 25 times as much on benefits for them than it did on supporting them into work.

More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities warned ministers earlier this year against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people.

In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.

The disability charity Scope has estimated about half of households with an under-22 receiving the universal credit health element are already in poverty, which it said could rise to more than nine in 10 if support was removed.

Campaigners warned that any move to cut benefits or increase conditionality rules was likely to drive many youngsters further away from the jobs market.

Lucy Schonegevel, the director of impact at Action for Children, said: “We are deeply concerned by reports that disability benefits for under-25s could be cut. If confirmed, that would be at odds with the prime minister’s recent warning against ‘crude cuts’ … Serious investment in high quality, tailored employment support is vital, but employment support alone cannot overcome a lack of jobs.”

A DWP spokesperson said: “The Milburn and Timms reviews, due in the autumn, will lay the foundation for sustainable reform, and we will not pre-empt their findings.
 “We are already changing the system through the youth guarantee, narrowing the gap between universal credit standard and health rates, restoring face-to-face assessments, and investing a record £3.5bn in employment support for disabled people and those with long-term conditions. We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.”

Milburn has said that too few young people who moved on to disability benefits received help into work. Many became “trapped” on benefits, with evidence showing half were not in work 15 years later, an outcome he called a “catastrophic failure”.

He appeared to hint at the potential political risks of cuts to benefits at a Labour party conference fringe meeting on youth employment on Monday, saying “when it comes to benefit cuts it will be tricky” – but added that not acting would be financially unsustainable and worse for young people.

About 184,000 young people in the UK aged 16-24 receive the universal credit health element. The government has already cut this benefit, having previously announced a 50% reduction to £217 a month for most new claimants from next April.

title: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed
excerpt:
Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls

Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions ...
body_text:
Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls

Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after a Guardian report revealed how the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court.

Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added.

Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused of trying to influence – where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls.

According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story.

Last year, the Trump administration used a campaign of sanctions and tariffs in a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.

In recent months, the Trump administration has again been accused of meddling in Brazilian affairs by using tariffs and the designation of two Brazilian organised crime groups as foreign terrorist organisations to boost Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign and weaken Lula.

Writing on Thursday, Messias said: “Disagreements between governments are inherent to international relations. What cannot be tolerated is for foreign political interests to seek to interfere in the functioning of Brazilian institutions or to influence, directly or indirectly, choices that belong exclusively to the Brazilian people.”

Messias added: “It is the right of each generation of Brazilians to freely decide their destiny, protect their institutions, and hand over to their children a country that does not accept decisions about Brazil being made outside of Brazil. Our democracy belongs to Brazilians. And so it must remain.”

The attorney general’s comments came in response to a report that the Trump administration was pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa and the campaign against Brazil’s supreme court.

A $1m award titled “Countering lawfare and censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court.

Bolsonaro’s far-right movement considers the supreme court – and in particular justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s trial – its greatest foe.

Moraes is widely seen to have played a key role in thwarting Jair Bolsonaro’s authoritarian plot, which culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, despite concerns about the judge overstepping his constitutional authority in his crusade to protect democracy.

During the rightwing riots, hardcore Bolsonaro supporters trashed the presidential palace, congress and supreme court. The court sustained the most severe damage.

Bolsonaro supporters continue to claim their leader’s imprisonment is unjust and that he is the victim of a politically motivated sham driven by a corrupt “judicial dictatorship”.

Their criticism of Moraes and the supreme court has been bolstered by a recent scandal linking several judges, including him, to Daniel Vorcaro, the playboy banker at the centre of Brazil’s biggest banking scandal. Vorcaro has also been linked to the Bolsonaro family.

The banker reportedly gave the family more than £9m, supposedly to produce a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro starring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s film The Passion of the Christ. On the eve of Vorcaro’s arrest last November, Flávio Bolsonaro messaged him to say: “Brother, I’ll always be with you.”

Vorcaro is being held in federal police custody in Brasília. His legal team has consistently denied wrongdoing. On Wednesday, his lawyers said he was not involved in “any kind of illicit activity or criminal practice”.

title: Labour figures uneasy about Healey’s ‘underpowered’ approach to budget
excerpt:
Chancellor faces global volatility and soaring energy costs as some insiders worry lack of clarity could trigger fresh market shock

Senior Labour figures are privately voicing unease about John Heale...
body_text:
Chancellor faces global volatility and soaring energy costs as some insiders worry lack of clarity could trigger fresh market shock

Senior Labour figures are privately voicing unease about John Healey’s approach to his crucial first budget this month, against the backdrop of volatile global markets and soaring energy costs.

The chancellor’s work has been made significantly harder by the global bond sell-off, which continues to raise the cost of government borrowing, and ever increasing energy prices as Donald Trump continues the US war with Iran.

The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds hit 6% on Thursday for the first time since 1998. Barclays raised some of its mortgage rates for the second time in a week, underlining the impact of these market moves on UK borrowers.

The chancellor’s party conference speech, which centred on the theme of reindustrialisation, was warmly received by Labour members in Liverpool. But government insiders and other Labour figures cast doubt over the lack of detail about policy on investment and growth or any pitch-rolling for possible tax rises.

One senior Labour politician said: “I missed any real sense of growth and investment, which Rachel [Reeves, the former chancellor] often emphasised, despite her faults – when business leaders speak to me, that’s what they were waiting to hear, and we got nothing.”

A Labour MP lamented the fact that on tax and spending Healey had gone little further than reiterating the fiscal rules. “It was Rachel’s speech delivered by John,” they said.

One senior Labour insider said they believed the chancellor was risking a fresh market shock on 28 October if he was not willing to be clearer about his approach to taxation, headroom and spending.

Market moves since the spring are expected to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn “headroom”, or buffer, Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules.

Healey is believed to be minded to accept a slimmer margin, but he gave no indication of his likely approach in his speech, aside from repeatedly stressing the need for discipline. Rebuilding the headroom in full could require significant tax increases or spending cuts.

Prof Arun Advani, the director of the centre for the analysis of taxation at the University of Warwick, said: “The chancellor didn’t give us a sense of how he’s thinking about these issues. It was a speech where at the end of it we didn’t come away understanding more about the direction of policy, or what he wants to do with the Treasury.”

There are concerns, too, about how Healey will tough out demands to say when the UK will spend 3% of GDP on defence – having resigned as defence secretary three months ago over the issue.

Treasury sources stressed that Healey was intimately involved in some of Andy Burnham’s significant conference announcements, with 40 officials working at the department through the weekend on the details of the triple lock pension changes.

They also pointed out that the chancellor opened the door to a renewed attempt to overhaul welfare for the young unemployed – a fraught issue for Labour – and stressed his determination to present an optimistic picture of the UK economy.

Healey’s team are committed to avoiding the rollercoaster of leaks that happened in the run-up to Reeves’s budgets, particularly last year.

The Treasury team have initiated military-style “black boxes” – learned from Healey’s time in the Ministry of Defence – for different teams to work within to avoid accidental leaks.

They also remain committed to what one called a “tightly focused” budget, though they concede that offering voters more “breathing space” on energy costs had become more urgent.

The narrow focus of the statement is expected to rule out radical changes to property and capital gains taxes previously mooted by Burnham supporters including the first secretary, Louise Haigh; though reports that Healey is calling in bank bosses next week has reignited speculation of a windfall tax on the sector.

Labour MPs fear that failing to take more drastic action, particularly on surging energy prices, could leave voters nonplussed. One MP said: “The budget is only a few weeks away. He may want it to be low key but it will send a massive signal of our intent.”

Others are concerned that Burnham’s focus on long-term issues such as social care and public ownership of utilities will suck up political airtime without helping with the immediate crisis.

Alfie Stirling, the director of policy and insight at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “The focus on ‘room to breathe’ now, alongside the focus on taking greater control over the costs of essentials over the longer term, is the right strategy for government. But families are currently facing the worst parliament on modern record for real incomes and they simply cannot wait three years for government to grip this in the here and now.”

Several Labour figures pointed to Burnham’s last-minute decision to appoint Healey as one factor making the chancellor’s job harder, giving him little time to build up an effective team before the budget.

Rav Athwal, an economist and the author of Labour’s 2024 manifesto, has only just joined Healey as a senior special adviser. Reeves’s chief economic adviser, Neil Amin-Smith, was poached by No 10.

One Treasury insider said: “He’s slow to get through his boxes and it’s hard to get meetings in the diary because he needs time to prepare before each one. It all feels a bit underpowered.”

But another Labour figure defended him: “John got virtually no notice he was getting this job. He’s not an economist. He didn’t have two years in opposition to prepare. It’s early days and the Treasury is there to support him. He’s very capable – just give him time.”

title: Reporter's Notebook: Congress dodged a fall shutdown, but the real fight looms
excerpt:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Senate Democrats blocking data center legislation and a bill barring members from stock trading on ‘Special Report.’

"And all at onc...
body_text:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Senate Democrats blocking data center legislation and a bill barring members from stock trading on ‘Special Report.’

"And all at once, summer collapsed into fall…" – Oscar Wilde

Congress certainly collapsed into fall this year. It lacked the usual mayhem of an imminent government shutdown for the first time in years. The government is usually only funded through September 30, the end of the federal fiscal year. Lawmakers solved that fiscal riddle early.

So the beginning of fall in Congress is usually anything but enjoyable. Others are devouring cobbler, enjoying spiced pumpkin lattes and viewing leaves of amber. When a government shutdown looms, the infernality of summer continues to stew on Capitol Hill. Imagine simmering political temperatures mixed with boiling urban concrete and a soupçon of petrichor. That epitomizes the customary fall tension in the halls of Congress when lawmakers are on the precipice of a shutdown.

TRUMP SIGNS GOVERNMENT FUNDING BILL, AVOIDING A SHUTDOWN AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

The US Capitol past traffic on North Capitol street in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Dec. 23, 2025. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

No shutdown. That’s a good thing, considering last year’s 43-day shutdown odyssey which crawled from October 1 into mid November. Everything is funded through December 11. So at least members and journalists can enjoy some of those autumnal fall trappings and dash to the pumpkin patch. That’s because we don’t know what’s going to await everyone for the next spending round in mid-December.

Lawmakers are recovering from the battle scars of last fall. So with the midterms approaching, no one wanted to return to the 2025 contretemps. The sides are willing to tussle over spending. But only after the midterms.

Does that mean a shutdown in December? Unclear.

If Democrats seize control of the House or Senate — or both — that could compel House and Senate Republicans to fund the government the way they want through the fall of 2027 right away. They won’t want an interim spending bill which punts things into early next year when Democrats may have power.

That said, if Democrats capture either the House or Senate, they will argue that the voters have spoken and it’s incumbent on them to decide how to spend taxpayer money next year. Under those scenarios, Democrats will push for a stopgap bill, hoping to tangle with President Trump in the early days of 2027.

The only thing which is known is that President Trump will in fact still be in office come January. This scenario could spark a shut down next year – if not December.

The reason? You still need 60 votes to clear a filibuster (and probably two) in the U.S. Senate. That means Republicans just can’t ram through whatever spending package they want. That may work in the House. And the GOP could even test the willingness of Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., to buck their party and assist passing a GOP-favored spending measure in the lame duck.

FETTERMAN STRONGLY SUPPORTS THE FILIBUSTER AS TRUMP URGES SENATE REPUBLICANS TO SCRAP IT

Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, attends a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center in Washington, July 17, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

But in the Senate, Republicans will certainly need the cooperation of at least seven Democrats to help them hit the 60 vote threshold. Those Democrats won’t be anxious to assist unless they won the majority and think they can apply their stamp on federal spending in the first quarter of next year.

This is the same problem which vexed the Senate during the shutdown of 2025.

The House passed a partisan spending bill to re-up all current funding on an interim basis. But Senate Republicans could never break a filibuster to lug that spending package across the finish line. The same circumstances may be true in December.

So could the 120th Congress begin in January with a shutdown?

It’s happened before. In fact, under very similar circumstances.

Democrats flipped control of the House during the 2018 midterms – two years into President Trump’s first term. But the President and outgoing House Speaker Paul Ryan, R-Wis., balked at a bipartisan spending package the Senate cleared just before Christmas that year. So the government closed. There was no way to resuscitate the Senate-approved package. So the 116th Congress began with a shutdown. It ran a then-record 35 days.

A possible government shutdown over spending disputes frankly serves as a symptom for what could be ahead if voters flip either or both bodies of Congress. Democrats will convulse at spending plans made by Republicans and the President. Plus, House Democrats likely add several progressives and Democratic Socialists to their ranks in November in solidly blue districts. Granted, those left-wing politicians won’t take office until January. But House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., must court the support of candidates Melat Kiros in Colorado along with Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York to win the Speaker’s gavel. Any missteps by the Democratic brain trust in the lame duck could ignite an internecine firestorm – before Democrats potentially seize the majority in January.

Republicans could face their own issues, too.

SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS

Democratic congressional candidate Melat Kiros speaks after winning the Democratic nomination during a primary election night watch party at The Broadway, Tuesday, June 30, 2026, in Denver. (Rebecca Slezak/AP Photo)

Some rank-and-file Republicans are ready to move on from House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA). Granted, it is said that Johnson is Speaker as long as President Trump wants him in the job. But what’s not clear is what happens if Republicans lose control of the House. Will the President and others support Johnson for Minority Leader? Does Johnson want that job? What happens to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-LA) and House Minority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn.?

There are signals that House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, is interested in moving into leadership. Especially if the GOP loses the majority. Jordan is tight with President Trump. He lost a bid to become Speaker three years ago after Republicans unceremoniously ousted former Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif.

If Republicans lose the majority, it’s not clear that some Republicans will back Johnson for the top GOP job in the House – regardless of what President Trump says. Some House Republicans will blame the President if the party loses the House. Especially since they believe he’s responsible for the toxic political climate they face right now. It’s unknown if a Republican party out of power might begin pushing back against President Trump, frustrated by the economy, tariffs, the price of gasoline and the war in Iran. Most GOPers have shown a reluctance to break with the President so far. But that could change if voters hand Congressional Republicans their head in the midterms.

We haven’t even raised the question about the future of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. – although the New York Democrat insists he isn’t going anywhere. But questions would emerge if Democrats don’t flip the Senate, considering that progressives and younger activists want to move on from the 75-year-old Schumer.

The same with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. President Trump and Thune have never been close. If Republicans lose the Senate, would the President use that as a reason to call for the removal of the South Dakota Republican?

All of this will color those question about spending bills, maybe renewing FISA – or even getting the House to sync up with the Senate on the college sports bill during the lame duck Congress.

Summer collapsed into fall. Capitol Hill was bereft of the usual autumnal mayhem.

So go pick out some pumpkins. Sip a cinnamon spice latte. Prepare for trick or treating. Fall is here.

But that autumn Congressional bedlam is only delayed. It will hit Capitol Hill after the election.

Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
excerpt:
A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attempt to seize control of the flight.

A Flydubai pla...
body_text:
A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attempt to seize control of the flight.

A Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes around two hours into its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered him and retook control to land safely.

Adam Polovincik told BBC Newshour that he hugged his six-year-old son and three-year-old daughter "really hard" and tried to stay calm for them as the attack unfolded.

He praised the pilot who was stabbed and passengers who fought off and subdued the attacker, saying they were "true heroes".

The stabbed pilot is in a stable condition in hospital, while the alleged attacker has been arrested.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to say whether Iran was involved in the attack, but that the alleged attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".

Polovincik, who was sitting in aisle 13, was flying home with his wife and children after an "amazing" holiday in Singapore and Thailand.

He said there had been a "huge degree of panic" on the plane as there was a "very, very, very sharp decrease in height".

What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel

He thought at first that this was simply because of an air pocket, but "it took a lot of time, almost a minute".

Everyone who had not been seated fell to the floor, the 40-year-old said.

"After a couple of seconds, we started to hear screams. 'There is blood, there is stabbing, we need help'," Polovincik said.

"At the end of the day, you understand very, very quickly that literally there is nothing that you can do at this point in time," he said.

Polovincik, a performance marketing analyst, said he tried to "be cool" for his children.

"You just tell them, yeah, everything's going to be all right. It's just a malfunction in the aeroplane, there is a crew under control, the passengers are helping them, [you] hug them really hard and try to keep your face so it doesn't look very panicked, try to keep your tone of voice."

But he said there was naturally a "high degree of panic" on the flight.

There were lots of families with children on the plane because the flight took place towards the end of a Jewish holiday period.

After about 10 to 15 minutes, he said a passenger in the cockpit told them the incident was "under control" and other staff were flying the plane.

In a video released by Netanyahu's office, passenger Yaniv Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out of the cockpit before other passengers helped pin him down.

Two other pilots who were onboard the flight then took over the controls and safely landed the plane, which had been carrying more than 150 passengers.

Polovincik said: "After they told us that the situation is, again, 'under control', then it was a bit harder to tell the kids that it's malfunctioned because people start to walk around the aeroplane covered with blood."

Polovincik was praised Indian pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, who fought off his attacker and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing passengers to step in.

"Without him opening the door, we're probably not speaking here right now," he said, adding that he "can't even start saying our gratitude for this human being".

Polovincik said that, although he was not religious, he could not escape "the feeling that it was the hand of God yesterday" that had put "the pieces on the board in the way that they did".

After the situation onboard was brought under control, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where Polovincik stressed the passengers, who were almost all Israeli, were treated well.

"They brought us water and food and coffee and even sweets for the kids - even though we don't have any diplomatic relationship between Israel and Saudi Arabia," he said.

The alleged attacker, who was arrested in Saudi Arabia, is expected to be transferred to the United Arab Emirates, from where the plane departed, Netanyahu told Fox News.

The passengers were taken to Tel Aviv on another flight later on Wednesday and were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.

Polovincik said it had been "such a terrible ending" to an amazing family trip and that it would take some time for his family to come to terms with what had occurred.

title: Russia ‘poses rapidly increasing threat’ to Nato, warns Dutch prime minister – Europe live
excerpt:
Rob Jetten says that European countries are working closer together on intelligence ‘to an unprecedented level’ to combat threats

He says the message of deterrence is “more vital than ever”, as Russi...
body_text:
Rob Jetten says that European countries are working closer together on intelligence ‘to an unprecedented level’ to combat threats

He says the message of deterrence is “more vital than ever”, as Russia “poses a rapidly increasingly threat to the Nato alliance,” whether in the Baltics or in Germany, as he points to a recent drone incident in Leipzig.

“Europe needs to show what it’s made of, show that we are prepared to do whatever it takes to protect our security,” he says.

He says Europeans are “ramping up our intelligence cooperation to an unprecedented level so we can combat hybrid threats,” and “reaffirming and stepping up our support for Ukraine.”

He says the Netherlands is increasing its defence spending, too.

Ukrainian troops have regained ground in a counteroffensive in the Donetsk region, according to an AFP analysis of data from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).

Operation “Vivaldi” was launched in September with the aim of pushing Russian forces back from the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

The Ukrainian military has retaken small patches of territory from Russia, for total gains in the Donetsk region of 172 square kilometres (66 square miles), an area more than 1.5 times the size of Paris.

Elsewhere, Ukraine retake small areas in the regions of Kharkiv in the north (seven square km) and the eastern regions of Dnipropetrovsk (12 square km) and Luhansk (13 square km).

By contrast, Russian offensives in Zaporizhzhia (south) and Sumy (north) enabled Kremlin forces to seize 104.5 square km and 20 square km respectively.

Overall, Ukraine made a net territorial gain of 80 square km in September, according to the data.

The European Commision and Ukraine have said in a joint statement they had “identified the means” to cover Kyiv’s budget and defence needs for this year. It read:

Today through coordinated joint efforts, we have identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defence needs for 2026. We have also reconfirmed the steps needed to ensure their timely release.
