title: US judge rules Wisconsin mosque leader Salah Sarsour can be deported
excerpt: A United States immigration judge has ruled the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque can be deported under a controversial law that United States President Donald Trump’s administration has used again...
body_text:
A United States immigration judge has ruled the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque can be deported under a controversial law that United States President Donald Trump’s administration has used against non-citizens advocating for Palestinian rights.

Judge Jayme Salinardi ruled on Wednesday that Palestinian-born Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, can be removed from the US based in part on a memo by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that “his actions undermine US foreign policy to combat antisemitism around the world”, according to his lawyers.

Sarsour, who has lived in the US for more than three decades, called the ruling “deeply disappointing”.

“I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” he told The Associated Press news agency.

His lawyer, Patrick Taurel, strongly rejected the decision.

“I wish the world could see the evidence that we presented and hear the testimony that the court heard because the case we presented compels only one conclusion, which is that Salah is not deportable,” Taurel told reporters on Wednesday.

“He’s done nothing wrong. He should be given back his green card, frankly, with an apology for what’s being done to him.”

The ruling does not mean Sarsour will be immediately deported.

His lawyers have 60 days to argue that sending Sarsour back would put him at risk of torture, which could protect him from deportation under the Convention Against Torture. If they lose, they plan to appeal. Taurel said he can’t be deported while that appeal is pending and will remain in the US for the “foreseeable future”.

Sarsour was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Milwaukee in March, nine months after Rubio issued a memo declaring him deportable on foreign policy grounds.

The June 2025 memo invoked a rarely-used US law that allows the Secretary of State to seek the deportation of non-citizens whose presence could have “potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.” The administration has used the same provision against pro-Palestinian activists Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi.

Sarsour’s lawyers criticised the “extreme deference” Salinardi gave to Rubio’s memo. But Taurel said the judge believed his hands were tied by an earlier ruling in Khalil’s case, which found that a letter from the Secretary of State could be enough to make someone deportable on foreign policy grounds.

That meant Salinardi could not look behind Rubio’s decision to examine the evidence supporting it, Taurel said.

“If the Secretary of State says the person is deportable, it is game over,” he told reporters Wednesday.

The government did not win on all of its arguments.

Salinardi rejected its allegation that Sarsour had lied on his green card application. Taurel said the judge also rejected an allegation that Sarsour had falsely claimed to be a US citizen in order to vote.

Al Jazeera reached out to the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security but did not receive responses by the time of publication.

Sarsour is separately fighting the Trump administration in federal court over his detention while his deportation case is ongoing.

A federal judge ordered his release from ICE custody in June after 81 days, questioning why decades-old convictions that US authorities had long known about suddenly justified detaining him. The judge found there was a “substantial” case that the government was retaliating against him for speaking out about Palestinian rights.

The Trump administration has appealed his release, arguing that Sarsour’s convictions in Israel make him a security threat. He was imprisoned in 1988 after confessing to throwing stones and a Molotov cocktail at Israeli military personnel, and was convicted again in 1995 over an attempt to hold weapons.

Sarsour denies the offences, and his lawyers say the confessions were forced through torture. His former lawyer, Jawad Boulos, testified in August that Sarsour was coerced into signing confessions and was not convicted of an offence tying him to a “terrorist” organisation.

Taurel criticised Salinardi for giving what he called “extreme deference” to Israeli government records submitted by ICE, which Sarsour’s lawyers argue were incomplete and relied on confessions obtained through torture.

“A great deal of evidence we presented was ignored,” Taurel said.

The evidence challenged Israel’s military court system, where he said secret evidence can be used and Palestinians can be denied access to lawyers for extended periods.

Luna Droubi, an attorney representing Sarsour, said the case raises broader questions about whether immigrants can speak freely on political issues without fear of being targeted by the government.

“Why raise these arrests now?” she said. “Do I have the right to speak out about issues that matter to me? What if I draw a political cartoon? Am I going to be arrested and detained because of that?”

Sarsour said being deported to the occupied West Bank “means the end of my life”.

His lawyers argue his prior treatment in Israeli custody shows he could face torture if sent back. Taurel said Sarsour’s former lawyer testified that his case stood out because Sarsour told him that Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, had taken him to hospital while in custody.

The judge also named Jordan as a possible destination. Sarsour travelled to the US on a Jordanian-issued document, but his lawyers say he is not a Jordanian citizen and has no right to live there. They believe he could ultimately be returned to the West Bank and Israeli custody if sent to Jordan.

title: Caitlin Clark puking her brains out at halftime appears to be key to Indiana Fever victories
excerpt: Cal and Jody hear from a caller wanting to talk about the Chicago Bears. That’s as normal as sports radio gets, until it starts to seem like this listener could be phoning in from across time and spac...
body_text:
Cal and Jody hear from a caller wanting to talk about the Chicago Bears. That’s as normal as sports radio gets, until it starts to seem like this listener could be phoning in from across time and space.

All of the focus after Game 2 between the Indiana Fever and the Las Vegas Aces was on A'ja Wilson getting into it with a fan. That's a shame because it overshadowed a gutsy — in every sense — postseason performance from Caitlin Clark.

The Fever kept the best-of-three series alive with a 99-88 win, and in it Clark posted 27 points, 15 assists and seven rebounds.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

And she did it all despite going all Old Faithful in the team's locker room at halftime.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

The Indiana Fever are officially undefeated in games where Caitlin Clark pukes at halftime. (Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

"To be honest, I threw up everything in my stomach at halftime," Clark said after the game. "I was just out there so tired. It wasn’t because I didn’t feel good or anything. I just was that gassed."

Way to power through it. For some reason, puking is exhausting. Most of us puke and then cancel plans; Clark went out there and continued to ball.

But what's wild is that this has happened to Clark before.

And, even wilder, the Fever are 2-0 if she gets an encore presentation from her pregame meal.

Caitlin Clark #22 of the Indiana Fever dribbles while defended by Jackie Young #0 of the Las Vegas Aces during Game 2 of the first round of the WNBA Playoffs at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on Sept. 29, 2026. (Getty Images)

PRIME VIDEO WNBA BROADCAST CREW EMBARRASSES ITSELF WITH COVERAGE OF A'JA WILSON FAN INCIDENT

In June, Clark vomited at halftime during a game against the Atlanta Dream, which the Fever went on to win.

So, with the season on the line, the team might need to make sure she takes a beeline to a prayer session with the porcelain god next game.

If I were head coach Stephanie White, I’d say, "All right, ladies, pregame meal at the raw bar down the street. The team nutritionist will make recommendations, but Caitlin, I’ve already entered you in the three-dozen oyster challenge. Finish them and you get a T-shirt. That's team building!"

Then after she housed thirty-six mollusks and earned herself a very thin, XL shirt, we'd hit Baskin-Robbins for samples of as many of their 31 flavors as possible before heading back to Gainbridge Fieldhouse.

If the Fever want to move on to the next round, the statistics indicate that they'll need Clark to vomit at some point, preferably at halftime. (Photo by Jeff Haynes/NBAE via Getty Images))

There, I'd tell Clark to relax in the steam room for a bit, and when she's done — what do you know? — it'd be time for a pregame warm-up jog.

That should create a maelstrom in the ol' tummy, but if not, I'd have some pimple-popping videos cued up on a TV in the locker room at the half just as a fail-safe measure.

That seems a bit much, but you can't argue with statistics: Clark puking means a win.

And that's what the Fever need when they head to Vegas for Game 3 on Thursday night.

title: Good news in US inflation report boosts chances Fed won’t hike rates
excerpt:
Traders see an about 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from ​about 45% following White House pressure

Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes on Wednesday, as a softer-than-antic...
body_text:
Traders see an about 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from ​about 45% following White House pressure

Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes on Wednesday, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading buoyed hopes that the Federal Reserve might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month.

A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) ​price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters.

Separately, second-quarter GDP data – the broadest measure of the economy’s health – showed that the US economy grew at a solid clip, driven ⁠by robust consumer spending and business investment related to the buildout of AI infrastructure.

“The market had been tracing out a bullish formation, meaning the price pattern suggested that any positive catalyst could trigger a move higher and that’s exactly ⁠what happened,” said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research.

Traders now see a roughly 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from about ​a 45% chance seen before the data, according to data ‌compiled by LSEG. The Federal Reserve is under pressure to cut rates from the White House after raising them earlier this month for the first time since 2023.

Inflation has emerged as the top issue for voters in the run-up to the midterm elections with Donald Trump receiving poor marks for his handling of the economy.

At 09.55am ET, the Dow Jones industrial average rose 50.58 points, or 0.10%, to 51,400.50, the S+P 500 gained 33.17 points, or 0.43%, to 7,704.01 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 193.57 points, or 0.72%, to 26,991.11.

Five of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were trading higher, with information technology and energy leading gains.

Despite weakness in September, driven by bond market volatility and elevated oil prices amid the US-Iran conflict, the benchmark S&P 500 and the ‌Nasdaq were on pace for a second straight quarterly advance, if gains hold.

On ​Wednesday, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond held steady at 5.246%, a day after hitting its highest since June 2007. Crude oil prices rose on the day, with the December contract for Brent crude futures moving higher.

There was also positive news from the jobs market. ADP, the US’s largest payroll supplier, said private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, higher than expected and up from 36,000 in August.

On Friday, the labor department will release its latest monthly jobs tally, which is expected to show a gain of 84,000 for September, down from 162,000 in the prior month.

title: Netanyahu says pilot arrested after stabbing fellow pilot and apparently trying to crash Israel-bound plane – latest
excerpt:
Israeli PM issues statement on flydubai incident, which saw plane plummet mid-air before emergency landing in Saudi Arabia

Full report: Pilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried...
body_text:
Israeli PM issues statement on flydubai incident, which saw plane plummet mid-air before emergency landing in Saudi Arabia

Full report: Pilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried to crash it, says Netanyahu

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, after an apparent brawl between its pilots prompted distress signals that briefly raised fears of an attempted hijacking. The flydubai flight was over Jordan when it diverted to Saudi Arabia, transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated a possible unlawful interference.

The plane dipped dramatically during the reported fight, descending about 16,000ft in just two minutes. Israeli officials scrambled fighter jets, fearful of a possible hijacking attempt on a plane containing dozens of Israelis, and the plane landed at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one of the flydubai pilots stabbed his fellow pilot and intended to crash the plane. He added that one of the passengers on the flight managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members, and together they “neutralised” the attacking pilot.

Netanyahu described it as “an extremely severe security incident”. Other officials, including defence minister Israel Katz, have called it an attempted terrorist attack. Netanyahu thanked the passengers and crew who helped to stop the attack, saying they “showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage”.

An Israeli official has identified the attacker as an Omani national, Reuters is reporting. The co-pilot of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv is believed to have stabbed the captain in a possible attempted “terror attack”.

The Boeing 737 plane, which Israeli officials said had between 160 and 180 passengers on board, transmitted a general emergency signal about two and a half hours after departing from Dubai, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.

Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was “pretty much out of control” when the alleged stabbing took place over Jordan on the flight’s path from Dubai to Tel Aviv. “The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.

The plane again transmitted the initial general emergency signal before later landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport. Tabuk airport said the plane landed at 9.45am local time and that both pilots were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries.

A second flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv landed safely at its destination after the tracking data website Flightradar24 initially showed the plane diverting back towards the UAE. Flight FZ1081 was later shown to be on its way to Israel, where it landed in Tel Aviv this afternoon.

A plane carrying passengers from an earlier diverted flydubai flight has landed at Tel Aviv airport on Wednesday, AFP TV images show.

The second aircraft, also operated by flydubai, landed on the tarmac of Ben Gurion airport at 3.34pm GMT, after the passengers’ earlier flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia due to an altercation between the pilots.

⁠Israeli prime minister ⁠Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠has ​ordered authorities ⁠to “ramp up” ⁠security ​on ‌both on ‌Israeli carriers ‌and non-Israeli carriers on ‌Wednesday.

The order was confirmed by a spokesperson for ​the prime ⁠minister’s office ​after ​the flydubai ​flight ‌incident.

The flydubai aircraft plummeted a little over two hours into the flight, dropped from nearly 34,000ft.

Between 5.21am GMT and 5.22am GMT, the plane dropped to less than 17,000ft, according to data from the Flightradar24 website.

Saudi Arabia turned down a request ⁠by Israel to allow its planes to bring back ⁠Israeli passengers from a ⁠FlyDubai ​flight that made an emergency landing in the kingdom, ⁠two security sources told Reuters.

The request was made to allow ⁠Israeli military planes to bring back ​Israelis from Saudi ‌Arabia, which ‌has no diplomatic relations with Israel, the ‌sources said.

The mother of a passenger onboard a flight from Dubai to Israel said her daughter told her the plane lost control before other pilots took over and the aircraft landed in Saudi Arabia.

Yasmin Abukasis, whose daughter Miriam was on the flight, said she told her she heard screaming and saw a man pull out a knife and force the pilot to the floor.

A key piece of information from the FlyDubai flight is that someone in the cockpit transmitted emergency codes.

“It was really on the way to crashing and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him,” she said.

“There was also a doctor who gave first aid and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do.”

Israeli media have reported dramatic testimonies and video from people on board, with some describing passengers storming the cockpit to subdue the attacker and one of the pilots being seriously injured.

The Israeli national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, said the incident highlighted the need for Israel to escalate its military campaigns across the region.

“Thank God and the heroic passengers, but Israel’s security doctrine must be taken to the next level,” he wrote on X, adding that the country “must continue until achieving total victory” in Iran, Lebanon, Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

“The naive notion that our enemies value life and deserve our pity was given yet another stark reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to blow up a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board.”

Local media reported the military had scrambled fighter jets after fears of a possible hijacking, which the prime minister’s office had ruled out shortly after the incident came to light.

title: Execution of US murderer Christa Pike halted shortly before it was due to happen
excerpt:
If the execution proceeds, Christa Pike would be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years

The execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike has been halted just over an hour be...
body_text:
If the execution proceeds, Christa Pike would be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years

The execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike has been halted just over an hour before it was due to happen.

Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.

In their ruling on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court said they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case. It is unclear how long the pause will last.

This latest ruling comes after the Supreme Court denied a reprieve and the Tennessee governor declined to grant Pike's request for clemency earlier this week.

Her lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that Pike had lied about being sexually abused as a child.

But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the State said it does not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape.

Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected.

The appeal that led to Wednesday's stay is different from that made to the Supreme Court, which refused to hear Pike's appeal.

It came from her challenge to Tennessee's lethal injection method, which Pike's lawyers said could cause suffering beyond what is needed to carry out the death sentence - something the Constitution does not allow. The lawyers argued that Tennessee's procedures had denied Pike a fair chance to prove this.

"We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue," Tennessee's Attorney General said in a statement.

"It is common in capital cases for the defence to raise last minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the Supreme Court of the United States to lift the stay."

Colleen Slemmer was 19 when she was murdered in 1995

She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself.

She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.

A year later, Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.

Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence.

At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.

title: ‘He persuaded us’: Labour ministers moved by Andy Burnham’s emotional conference speech
excerpt:
Prime minister’s pure political argument marks new era for party as he sets out his plans and priorities

The hottest ticket at Labour conference – after Andy Burnham’s speech – was an afterparty in L...
body_text:
Prime minister’s pure political argument marks new era for party as he sets out his plans and priorities

The hottest ticket at Labour conference – after Andy Burnham’s speech – was an afterparty in Liverpool’s Baltic Triangle, headlined with a set by the noughties girlband Sugababes. As Labour activists and ministers belted out the lyrics under pink spotlights, it was hard not to draw some parallels with the party’s recent history.

There have been painful lineup changes and a lot of internal division, but this week onstage in Liverpool the originals are back together and they only played the hits. The fans can’t get enough.

Burnham’s own show on the main stage had the conference hall in raptures not because of Brexit or social care but because of the display of raw emotion after the tightly choreographed repression of the last six years. He may as well have walked across the stage with his feet crunching over the debris of shattered Ming vases.

The speech combined plans that had been forming inside Burnham’s head for the last decade as well as seat-of-his-pants political instinct. On the morning of the conference, the prime minister took off early for a morning jog and then returned to make final amendments. Even moments before he went on stage, he was still rewriting, aides said. About a quarter of the speech was entirely ad-libbed.

When Burnham was rehearsing the speech, aides said, he knew he was going to cry when he got to the paragraph about his late father – he never managed to get through any of the practice runs without tears.

But the long pause as he composed himself was the most emotional he had been. Several ministers said they themselves had been moved to tears, including Ed Miliband, who had recently lost his mother, as well as Louise Haigh and Anneliese Midgley, who are Burnham’s closest friends in government and the architects of his ascendancy.

After his speech, Burnham gathered all his ministers for a private pep talk. He said he knew they would not agree with everything, but – with the aura of a general sending his troops into battle – he told them to “get out there” and fight for it. He said he would not send them out with “a pea-shooter” – they needed proper weapons for the fight ahead and he promised he would provide them.

In the hallway outside the conference hall, minister after minister spoke with voices quivering with emotion. “This is all I have ever wanted,” one said.

The bar for speeches from political leaders has been low for the past decade or more. It is rare for clips to be anything more than a soundbite for social media and then a long shopping list of statistics and achievements. Burnham’s was the first time many MPs can recall a speech that was pure political argument.

And there was much in the speech that in normal times would have been a recipe for rebellion: Brexit, the triple lock, electoral reform and the lingering question marks over growth and defence.

“I found parts of the speech challenging, if I’m honest,” one cabinet minister admitted. “It contained things I had always thought we should never touch or an argument about public control which I would previously have said was too backward-looking. But in the room I agreed with every word because he persuaded us, he made an argument and made me question myself. It was a quite extraordinary thing.”

Even within the cabinet, there are those who grimace at the idea of electoral reform. “But you know, he believes in it, and I’m going to swallow it,” said one.

Burnham called his cabinet ministers in for a last-minute meeting just before the speech, where he laid out his private arguments and took their comments and feedback. “I feel almost embarrassed admitting this, but that has never happened before with any other leader,” one said.

On the sidelines of the conference, when cabinet ministers are at their most candid, they sometimes talk as if they have been through a kind of collective trauma – and the Burnham ascendancy has given them the release they need to confess how hard they have found the last two years. There are close new friendships and alliances forged in the coup, which defy previous factional lines.

“There’s the management-speak slogan: ‘Culture eats strategy for breakfast.’ Well, this is proof positive,” one cabinet minister said. “The past two years were utterly miserable, almost every single thing we achieved was poisoned by petty fighting. Every meeting was a choreographed exercise in pointlessness. Now we are discussing ideas and politics among colleagues who respect and like each other. I look back and I am so overwhelmed with relief that we did this.”

Another cabinet minister said: “I wasted so much of my own bandwidth fighting over the most puerile things, or defending my own staff who were being made miserable. Keir [Starmer] never dared to take it on.”

Even veterans of the Starmer years said they found themselves persuaded despite themselves. “Feels like there’s something quite psychologically profound about daring to take on the triple lock and finding that the planes don’t fall from the skies,” Starmer’s former strategy director Paul Ovenden posted.

Darren Jones, the ousted chief secretary who has made himself the face of the awkward squad, was also quick to lavish praise. “[The speech] told the story of his politics and the type of Britain he wants to build,” he said. “He told us we’d be in no doubt what his priorities are for the country, and he was right.”

Burnham will not welcome the comparison, but the closest recent one is how it felt at the Conservative party conference in the pre-disgrace Boris Johnson years: an electric electoral prospect who can genuinely reach across the political spectrum, hypnotising his doubters by the sheer force of his personality.

But this prime minister has no hint of the sleaze or incompetence that was always in the shadows for Johnson. If it comes, Burnham’s downfall will probably be his own voracious appetite for political risk – but that could also be the making of his premiership.

title: What happened on diverted Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv?
excerpt:

The Flydubai flight FZ1073 was...
body_text:
A flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel was diverted to Saudi Arabia after issuing a distress signal, in what appeared to be a hijacking attempt, on Wednesday.

The Flydubai flight FZ1073 was diverted as it flew from Dubai to Tel Aviv through Jordanian airspace, prompting Israel to deploy warplanes, the Reuters news agency reported.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one of the pilots had stabbed the other and then tried to crash the plane. He added that Israel was preparing for other “potential threats” after the incident.

There has been no official confirmation of a hijacking attempt, however.

Flydubai said an altercation had occurred on the flight deck and that all passengers were safe and accounted for. The plane was secured by on-duty crew travelling onboard, it added.

At Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport, where the plane landed, officials said both the plane’s captain and the first officer had been hospitalised after sustaining injuries. Both were taken to the hospital, according to a statement from the Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk carried by the Saudi state-run Alekhbariya television.

The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalised ties in 2020. Here’s what we know about what happened.

Footage taken onboard the plane appears to show the captain of the aircraft lying on the ground with several stab wounds, and a passenger with a bloody wound to the head.

In another video, passengers weep and cry out in distress as the aircraft shakes.

Yasmin Abukasis, the mother of one of the passengers onboard, said her daughter Miriam thought she was going to die. “The plane started to lose control,” she told journalists at Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport, before other pilots onboard took control of the aircraft.

Flight tracking data indicated the plane descended over 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds around two and a half hours after leaving Dubai. Flightradar24 said on X that an initial general emergency signal designated by code 7700 was issued at around 05:31 UTC and was later changed to another emergency signal with code 7500 declaring “unlawful interference”.

Passenger Dalia Shpigel told Israeli newspaper Haaretz that some people seated towards the front of the plane broke into the cockpit after the plane began to descend and they realised something was wrong.

“An hour before landing, we felt that there was no control over the plane, that it was starting to jump,” she said. “The guys saw that the plane had begun to dive and broke into the cockpit.”

Netanyahu said he later spoke to one of the Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit and overpowered one of the pilots who was reportedly trying to sabotage the aircraft’s systems.

“I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage,” Netanyahu said in a statement. “They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster.”

03:05 – Flight FZ1073 takes off from Dubai05:21 – Altitude fluctuations begin05:22 – Aircraft drops more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds05:31 – Signal from aircraft changes to 7700 (general emergency)05:38 – Signal changes to 7500 (unlawful interference)06:45 – Aircraft lands at Tabuk Regional Airport

The motive of the apparent attack was not immediately clear. Netanyahu said Saudi authorities were interrogating the pilot who had committed the attack.

Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz said preliminary information indicated the attacker intended to crash the plane, killing everyone onboard, calling the incident an “attempted jihadist terror attack”.

An Israeli official who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity identified the attacker as an Omani national.

Israel does not have formal diplomatic relations with Saudi or Oman, maintaining a policy of occasional dialogue through informal channels. Muscat has chosen not to join other countries in the region in normalising ties with Israel over Palestinian rights. Saudi Arabia has made normalisation of Israeli ties conditional on Israel’s acceptance of a Palestinian state.

Israel is days away from marking the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, in which around 1,200 people were killed and which sparked Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 75,000 Palestinians – mostly women and children – including around 1,400 since a US-brokered ceasefire supposedly took effect in October 2025.

No. A second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, FZ1081, was erroneously reported in Hebrew media to have turned around, according to The Times of Israel.

The news outlet added that the mistake appeared to have been due to a glitch on flight-tracking sites.

The plane did not issue any emergency signal and it was reported to be on its course to Tel Aviv without disruptions.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid claimed Netanyahu’s political allies had attempted to pass off the incident as the fulfilment of warnings a day earlier about a possible attack on Israel ahead of its legislative election scheduled on October 27.

“The warning about activity abroad is specific, has been in place for more than two years, and has nothing to do with planes or anything resembling what happened this morning,” Lapid wrote on X.

Speaking of Netanyahu, Lapid said: “He’s trying to hitch a pathetic ride on heroic Israelis who prevented a disaster that he (once again) wasn’t prepared for.”

title: Tennessee halts plan to execute woman for first time in 200 years
excerpt:
State governor and supreme court earlier refused calls for clemency for Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder

Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in 200 years was halted by a court on Wednesda...
body_text:
State governor and supreme court earlier refused calls for clemency for Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder

Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in 200 years was halted by a court on Wednesday morning an hour before it was set to take place.

The state governor and the supreme court had earlier refused calls for clemency in the case of Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder 30 years ago.

She was set to die by lethal injection at 11am ET on Wednesday but the execution has been halted by a federal appeals court.

In a 2-1 majority, the court said: “The interests of justice and the finality of Pike’s impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits.”

The office of Jonathan Skrmetti, the state attorney general, issued a statement reacting to the news on Wednesday, saying: “We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue. It is common in capital cases for the defense to raise last-minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the supreme court of the United States to lift the stay.”

The Guardian has reached out to the office of Bill Lee, Tennessee’s Republican governor.

Pike, who is now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995.

The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of everyone involved, as well as a satanic symbol that was carved into Slemmer’s chest.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

title: Photos: Kashmir’s 600-year-old Wazwan wedding feast adapts to modern life
excerpt: As autumn approaches, the rhythmic thud of wooden mallets pounding lamb echoes across courtyards and back lanes in Kashmir, where cooks prepare Wazwan – a lavish, multi-course mutton feast that remain...
body_text:
As autumn approaches, the rhythmic thud of wooden mallets pounding lamb echoes across courtyards and back lanes in Kashmir, where cooks prepare Wazwan – a lavish, multi-course mutton feast that remains central to traditional wedding celebrations.

Wazwan arrived in the valley from Central Asia in the 14th century, when rulers brought skilled chefs along with the carpet and shawl weavers that later defined the region’s craft heritage.

Today, the feast is both a marker of social status and a powerful symbol of Kashmiri identity.

Among its guardians is 74-year-old Ghulam Nabi Baba, a veteran Wazwan chef who traces his lineage to those early migrants. His forefathers settled in Srinagar’s old city as part of a community of cooks known as Wazpora.

“There were only seven mutton dishes at that time. Over the centuries we added more, and now there are around 20,” Baba said.

He explained how the number of dishes and the amount of meat often reflect a family’s wealth.

“Forty years ago in Delina [a village in north Kashmir] I cooked 4,500kg (9,920 pounds) of meat. That was a very big wedding. Normally, at an average marriage we cook 200kg (440 pounds),” he added.

Despite the expanding menu, the core techniques have changed little. Lightly spiced meat is still pounded by hand before being simmered slowly over wood fires – a labour-intensive process Baba has followed since joining his father as a cook at 15.

But the pressures of modern life are reshaping the tradition. Baba’s son has chosen to open a restaurant rather than work weddings, saying the round-the-clock demands are too exhausting.

He believes he is still carrying forward the family’s centuries-old culinary legacy – just in a different setting, as Wazwan adapts to contemporary tastes and lifestyles.

title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
excerpt:
Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage

The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid g...
body_text:
Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage

The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage.

Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant”. Meanwhile, it was becoming harder for the public to have proper oversight of powerful AI models that were “functioning within a self-reinforcing loop”.

That is putting financial stability at risk, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”, he said. The governor warned it could threaten daily card payments, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets.

The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) said the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks.

The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in.

In an opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind, the answer is unequivocally yes.”

But Bailey said authorities needed to figure out why they might be forced to step in. He said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new AI models to understand how they behave and identify “credible points” where authorities could intervene.

“In time, that understanding could be codified into a set of standards which will help to ensure consistency in approach across the financial system, and perhaps more broadly across the economy,” he said.

However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown, saying it was “not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.”

A growing number of lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence in recent weeks. However, hopes for international cooperation faded after Donald Trump broadly rejected calls for more regulation of AI technology – most of which is being developed in the US – warning it could hurt efforts to compete with China and threaten economic growth.

But Bailey said a set of standards could help safeguard the financial system from harmful AI, which may end up operating outside well-established “shared norms, obligations and responsibilities”.

“Central banks have a responsibility to safeguard the stability of the system as a whole,” Bailey said. “We cannot stand aside and assume that technological progress will resolve these questions on its own. The public interest requires that we engage with them now, before the risks become more difficult to contain.”

Warning of the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector had taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026.

That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to the fortunes of AI companies at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit.

“The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said.

“The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”

body_text:
Dan Dakich thinks the lights are a little too bright for A'ja Wilson.

Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson only received a technical foul on Tuesday night when she stepped across the baseline and went a few rows deep to address an Indiana Fever fan.

The incident occurred in the fourth quarter of the Aces’ Game 2 loss to the Fever at the Gainbridge Fieldhouse. Wilson drew a blocking foul after Sophie Cunningham stepped in front of her and fell to the court. Cunningham was upset with the call, meanwhile, Wilson was seen yelling and pointing at a fan a few rows from courtside.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Las Vegas Aces center A'ja Wilson talks to teammates after going into the stands to confront a fan during Game 2 of the first round of the 2026 WNBA Playoffs against the Indiana Fever at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on Sept. 29, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

The broadcast showed Wilson taking a few steps into the stands. Crew chief Randy Richardson was asked by a pool reporter about the incident.

"So, at that point, A’ja Wilson was assessed a technical foul for unsportsmanlike conduct," Richardson told the reporter when asked what happened with the incident.

When asked, "Why did A’ja Wilson receive a tech for her interaction with the fan on the baseline," Richardson responded, "For unsportsmanlike conduct."

Wilson finished the game, but it appeared the incident may have warranted an ejection.

The league considers the stands the first row of seats. Wilson didn’t climb over anyone to get to the fan she had an issue with, but, on the baseline, she didn’t need to.

"Any coach, player, or trainer who deliberately enters the spectator stands during the game will be automatically ejected and the incident reported via e-mail to the Commissioner," the rulebook states.

OutKick asked the WNBA and National Basketball Referees Association for comment on why Wilson’s action didn’t warrant an ejection. OutKick also asked the WNBA if it would review the incident further.

The Fever released a statement on the incident.

"Following a report of a comment directed toward a player, arena security spoke with the fan involved and witnesses," the team said. "Security determined there was no violation of the Fan Code of Conduct, the fan was not removed from the arena. We consider the matter closed."

Las Vegas Aces center A'ja Wilson talks to a referee after going into the stands to confront a fan during Game 2 of the first round of the 2026 WNBA Playoffs against the Indiana Fever at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on Sept. 29, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wilson addressed the confrontation after the game.

"If I see a man, come at me, taking steps toward me and point at me, I don’t give a damn what you said, I don’t give a damn how you said it, the tone, that is unacceptable," she said. "You don’t step toward me and point at me. I’m not for that s--- at all.

"That’s unacceptable and how he gets back in the game because they said he didn’t know anything, of course he didn’t, and that’s fine. And I apologized to my team because I got us a tech and I didn’t … but there’s certain things I’m just not gonna allow anymore because it’s just unacceptable. You don’t know me at all to come and step toward me and point at me and say anything."

A fan sitting next to the man in question later told OutKick that the man only said the foul was on Wilson and pointed at her.

As the WNBA has grown more popular, the scrutiny over officiating in the league has come under the microscope and this season was no different.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert said last summer the league was going to evolve terms of its officiating. The league formed an offseason officiating task force that included an effort to clean up some of the WNBA’s issues regarding physicality and officiating.

Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve, who blasted officials during last year’s WNBA Finals, said in the beginning of the 2026 season that coaches weren’t looking for referees to call marginal fouls.

New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart and Dallas Wings rookie Azzi Fudd also talked about the fouls. Stewart was annoyed that a game against the Washington Mystics earlier in the year took nearly three hours to complete. Fudd was dismayed about being unable to be physical with opponents.

Fever star Caitlin Clark went as far as to call for full-time WNBA referees as she racked up technical fouls this season that nearly cost her a game.

Las Vegas Aces center A'ja Wilson holds the ball while Indiana Fever center Aliyah Boston defends during Game 2 of the first round of the 2026 WNBA Playoffs at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on Sept. 29, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

"It's kind of been a discussion for three years now, and I think we really need to do a better job protecting the people in this league," she said in July. "I've been involved in a few of those plays, but there's been plenty of others across the league that haven't been called. You go back postgame or whatever it is, teams submit clips and nothing changes. I think overall the league has to do better."

"Overall, the league just has to do better and we have to invest in those areas," she added. "The technology can get better. We can treat the referees a little bit better. Pay them like they're full-time employees."
