title: Mamdani deflects Kimmel's anti-Trump bait when pressed repeatedly on relationship with the president
excerpt:
Jimmy Kimmel appeared fascinated by Mayor Zohran Mamdani's relationship with President Trump on Monday, as the late-night host pressed the mayor on their interactions.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamd...
body_text:
Jimmy Kimmel appeared fascinated by Mayor Zohran Mamdani's relationship with President Trump on Monday, as the late-night host pressed the mayor on their interactions.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani seemed to deflect late-night host Jimmy Kimmel's questions about his relationship with President Donald Trump, as the mayor avoided bashing him and rejected the late-night host's request to send him a selfie.

"Did you guys hit it off immediately or is it something that you really went into thinking, like, ‘Okay, I need to have a relationship with the President of the United States and I think the best way to do it is to charm him?' How did you do that and can you help me?" Kimmel asked Mamdani, calling his relationship with Trump "unexpected."

The mayor told Kimmel he and the president had many disagreements, but agreed on how much they both love New York City.

MAMDANI DESCRIBES TRUMP RELATIONSHIP AS 'HONEST' AND 'DIRECT' AMID RECENT BLOWOUT

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and late-night host Jimmy Kimmel during "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" on September 28, 2026. (ABC/JimmyKimmelLive)

"And so, from that first meeting in November of last year, I was just thinking of, ‘How can we make this meeting not about us, but about New Yorkers? How can we spend that time talking about the things that could make life in the city that little bit easier?’ And that's what it's been whether we've met at the White House or at Gracie Mansion," he said.

Mamdani and the president met earlier this month at the mayor's residence, Gracie Mansion, despite the major policy differences the two have.

"The number one thing that we've been speaking about recently has been Sunnyside Yard, which is this idea for decades of building a platform over a rail yard and then building 12,000 homes. And so, in that moment, you know, that you zoomed in on, I'm just thinking about 12,000 homes, 30,000 jobs, largest housing development since the early 1970s," Mamdani told Kimmel.

TRUMP'S HOUSING CHIEF PAINTS A GRIM PICTURE FOR HOMEOWNERSHIP IN ONE MAJOR AMERICAN CITY

President Donald Trump and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani walk out following their meeting at Gracie Mansion on Sept. 21, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

Kimmel asked, "When you text him about Sunnyside, are you sure he doesn't think you're texting him about eggs?"

Mamdani said he was "pretty sure" and noted that the texts were pretty normal and didn't resemble the president's Truth Social posts.

"Wow. You really have broken through with him," Kimmel said. "I mean listen, you seem to be doing a great job in New York, we might need you to move to Washington just hang out at the Oval Office all day. Like if you texted him a selfie of us right now."

"I love you, but I love housing more," Mamdani responded.

Kimmel went on to ask if Mamdani would come be the mayor of Los Angeles at the end of the discussion.

MAMDANI, LETITIA JAMES SUE TO BLOCK TRUMP ADMIN FROM REFUSING IMMIGRANTS OVER WELFARE STATUS

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani meets with President Trump at the White House on Feb. 26, 2026. (Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani via X)

The White House did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Trump first met with the socialist mayor last November and said Mamdani could "surprise some conservative people" and declared, "The better he does, the happier I am."

Their last meeting, on Feb. 26 at the Oval Office, was notably cordial, with Mamdani seeking Trump’s support for an ambitious New York housing proposal despite their political differences.

"The new communist mayor of New York City, I think he’s a nice guy, actually," Trump said in his State of the Union address in February. "I speak to him a lot. Bad policy, but nice guy."

Fox News' Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

title: ‘We will not be intimidated,’ says Estonian PM after attributing recent arson attack to Russia - Europe live
excerpt:
Kristen Michal says attack ‘against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services’, after Kremlin denies involvement

Estonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal does not seem to be convinced by...
body_text:
Kristen Michal says attack ‘against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services’, after Kremlin denies involvement

Estonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal does not seem to be convinced by Russia’s denials.

Minutes after we got a response from the Kremlin, he posted on X:

“The arson attack against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services.

This is part of Russia’s broader campaign across Europe to intimidate us and weaken our support for Ukraine. It will not work.

Our response will be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia.

The Estonian government also published a handy summary of the case so far:

“The criminal investigation into the exact circumstances of the incident is continuing, but the preliminary information gathered so far in the criminal proceedings also indicates that the attack was commissioned. The suspects believed to have directly carried out the arson attack have been apprehended and taken into custody and no longer pose a threat.

On the night of 15 August, a fire broke out in a building used by defence industry company Milrem Robotics on Betooni Street in Tallinn’s Lasnamäe district. Emergency services responded immediately and the fire was quickly brought under control. No lives were in danger.

On 17 August, two Latvian citizens suspected of carrying out the arson attack were detained in Latvia. A third suspect was detained on 18 August. Searches of locations associated with the suspects in Latvia resulted in the seizure of numerous data storage devices and items that may have been used to set fire to the building.

On 17–18 September, Latvia handed over all three suspects to Estonia.”

In his speech Burnham also talked about his plans to look at Britain’s future relationship with the EU again.

“We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long term relationship with what is still our largest market.

I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good.

We need to restore a higher level of growth and prosperity for Britain.

So I will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long term relationship with our European partners.

And there are different options, and I will see if we can find consensus around one.”

Over in the UK, prime minister Andy Burnham is addressing the Labour party conference this afternoon, setting his plans for the country.

In a brief passage on security and defence, he says:

“A country [reformed] like that will be much more resilient to the shocks we will undoubtedly face in the rest of this century and more able to meet its Nato obligations on defence …

I will be steadfast in my support for Ukraine, and stand up to threats whenever they come from: Russia, Iran, or anywhere.”

If you’re interested in details, my colleague Andrew Sparrow has all of it over on the UK blog:

We have got some more pictures for you from protests in Madrid.

Wielding a broom and dustpan, Marta García, 60, darted past the edges of tents, sweeping up bits of litter as she passed a poster that read: “What kind of times are these, when we need to defend the obvious?”

On Saturday, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Madrid to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, the retired schoolteacher was among a small group who had sought to take the protest one step further.

“At first we were 10 tents,” she said, gesturing to the sprawling encampment set up in the central Puerta del Sol plaza behind her. “Now, we’re more than 300 tents, and it keeps growing.”

Days earlier, many across Spain had watched in shock as news channels showed Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman with a disability, being evicted from the home where she had lived for seven decades.

The shock soon gave way to anger as the octogenarian was shown being brought out of her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police officers on the other.

Housing campaigners seized on the moment. “The whole country has seen that housing speculation has no mercy on anyone,” said Alicia del Río of the Madrid Tenants’ Union. “We’re not sad, we’re angry. And we’re not going to stop until we change things.”

Two ministers in Viktor Orbán’s former far-right government suspected separately of misusing millions of euros of public funds and taking millions more in bribes have been detained, hours after Hungarian MPs voted to lift their immunity.

Prosecutors said on Tuesday that Balázs Hankó, Orbán’s culture minister and still an MP in the former prime minister’s nationalist Fidesz party, was ​taken into custody late on Monday. Hankó is suspected of misappropriation of funds. He has denied any wrongdoing.

Miklós Seszták, an MP from Fidesz ally KDNP who served as minister for national development between 2014 and 2018, was also detained on Monday as part of an ⁠investigation into alleged bribery. He too has denied wrongdoing.

In more US-Russia relationship news, Interfax reports that Russian ⁠economy minister ⁠Maxim Reshetnikov ⁠will take ​part in ⁠a G20 ⁠trade ​ministers’ ‌meeting ‌in the US which is scheduled to start tomorrow.

Russian ⁠president ⁠Vladimir Putin’s envoy ​Kirill ⁠Dmitriev had ⁠meetings ​with ‌representatives of ‌US ‌departments of Treasury and Energy ‌during his ​visit to Washington, ⁠sources ​have told ​Reuters.

It is a further sign of the Trump administration normalising relations with Russia despite the ongoing attacks on Ukraine and concerns over Russia’s action from Nato allies. Last week US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US had invited Putin to attend a G20 summit scheduled for Miami in December.

And the UK has now also offered its support for Estonia after its government’s decision to attribute a recent arson attack to Russia.

“The UK stands with Estonia in confronting these unacceptable attacks. They will not weaken our resolve or our support for Ukraine.”

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha condemned Russia’s “terror against Ukraine” which he says is “intensifying by the day,” after another night of attacks on Kyiv and Odesa region.

“This is Russia’s deliberate escalation instead of accepting Ukraine’s offers to cease fire, negotiate, and end the war. Putin’s rejection of peace must have consequences for Russia,” Sybiha said.

“We are grateful to all partners who are strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and providing the systems and interceptors that are saving lives right now. Every successful interception proves that this support works.

At the same time, Russia must face growing pressure for every new wave of terror. Stronger sanctions, fewer resources for its war machine, and fewer opportunities to circumvent existing restrictions.

Moscow should not be allowed to turn another winter into a weapon. Every Russian escalation must bring the opposite of what the Kremlin expects – stronger protection for Ukraine, greater pressure on Russia, and a higher price for continuing this war.”

France’s Emmanuel Macron is the latest European leader to respond to Estonia’s decision to attribute a recent arson attack to Russia.

“I express our full solidarity with Estonia, which has just attributed to Russia the responsibility for a fire targeting a defence sector company.

A few weeks ago, Germany did the same for a very serious incident at Leipzig airport.

The proliferation of these hostile acts reflects a dangerous escalation on the part of Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end.

Russia must know that it will not prevail over either our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine.”

Estonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal does not seem to be convinced by Russia’s denials.

Minutes after we got a response from the Kremlin, he posted on X:

“The arson attack against Milrem Robotics was ordered by Russian special services.

This is part of Russia’s broader campaign across Europe to intimidate us and weaken our support for Ukraine. It will not work.

Our response will be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia.

The Estonian government also published a handy summary of the case so far:

“The criminal investigation into the exact circumstances of the incident is continuing, but the preliminary information gathered so far in the criminal proceedings also indicates that the attack was commissioned. The suspects believed to have directly carried out the arson attack have been apprehended and taken into custody and no longer pose a threat.

On the night of 15 August, a fire broke out in a building used by defence industry company Milrem Robotics on Betooni Street in Tallinn’s Lasnamäe district. Emergency services responded immediately and the fire was quickly brought under control. No lives were in danger.

On 17 August, two Latvian citizens suspected of carrying out the arson attack were detained in Latvia. A third suspect was detained on 18 August. Searches of locations associated with the suspects in Latvia resulted in the seizure of numerous data storage devices and items that may have been used to set fire to the building.

On 17–18 September, Latvia handed over all three suspects to Estonia.”

Meanwhile, the Kremlin rejected what it called Estonia’s “baseless” accusation that Russia ordered an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in August (10:10).

“Such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning. Consequently, we cannot and will not take such statements seriously,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters in response to an AFP question.

How could anyone ever think that Russia could do this, right? Right?

Rutte’s comments there are (perhaps not surprisingly) very much aligned with what Nato’s top commander Alexus Grynkewich told EU lawmakers last night.

In a rare appearance at the European parliament, Grynkewich warned that “the goal of the Russian activity right now is primarily to break our will to continue supporting Ukraine.”

“The logic of this is if we make the security situation seem dire enough, populations will want nations to withhold from Ukraine for their own protection. …

If there is a hybrid attack on your country, reinforcing the will to support Ukraine will show the Russians that their strategy isn’t working, and maybe have them back off that strategy.”

Top Nato figures appear to be focused on very publicly calling Russia’s tactics out in a bid to stop Moscow from succeeding and having any impact on social attitudes towards helping Ukraine – particularly ahead of 2027, with big elections coming up in France, Italy, Poland and Spain.

Nato secretary general Mark Rutte has urged allies to keep calm and carry on supporting Ukraine, saying Russia is “failing to undermine” the alliance’s support for Kyiv despite growing number of sabotage, drone incidents against Nato (11:07).

Rutte warned that Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies,” trying to “weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine” (10:57).

His comments came at a press conference with Lithuania’s prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius who warned that Russia’s actions are “becoming increasingly hostile and less restrained” (10:59).

But Sinkevičius pushed back against recent warnings from Denmark, Poland and Germany about a potential imminent threat, saying there is no evidence of Russia “getting ready” (11:10).

Pushed a bit further on hybrid attacks, Rutte acknowledges they “are having an impact,” but repeats his point that Nato has “all the response options: sometimes visible, sometimes not.”

He also says it’s important to, whenever possible on the basis of available evidence, publicly attribute these incidents to Russia, as Estonia did today.

He says Nato is acting “in the spirit of staying calm, carrying on.”

Lithuania’s Sinkevičius says Russia “seeks to spread fear, to bring division … but it will not succeed.”

“We are not shaking [with fear]; we are doing what is meant to be done,” he says.

He says countries also do a lot of work in the background that is not publicly seen.

He says it’s important to be open about the challenges posed by Russia, but pushes back against “exaggerations” that something could happen within “upcoming months of weeks.”

“Is there any proof, real proof, that our intelligence services are providing … that Russia is getting ready or something? There is actually none,” he says, stressing “the risk remains,” but it’s not deemed to be escalating at the moment.

He adds “we have to … calmly do our work and we are doing that.”

Rutte gets asked about various recent sabotage actions against Nato allies, including the UK, Germany, and Lithuania.

Should we stop calling them hybrid threats and call them what they are, he is asked. And does he agree with warnings coming from several countries about “decisive weeks and months” ahead?

Rutte says he agrees with the criticism of the phrase “hybrid threat,” as “it sounds a bit cuddly,” and does not reflect the severity of the threat.

But he says the key thing is that Nato “has all the response options we need,” even if “you will not always see them publicly.”

He says allies do a lot to counter the Russian threat.

“I would urge some calm, because we are investing in our defence [and] Russia is not in a good place,” he says.

He adds allies should “carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going, because the best response to any action in this grey zone of what Russia is doing is more support for Ukraine.”

Rutte says “we should not be naive about Russia,” but adds “they know we are stronger and we have to make sure by carrying on with our investments that we are also stronger in two, three, five years from now.”

Sinkevičius is up next, as he thanks Rutte for today’s talks.

He warns that “the security [situation] in Europe is challenging,” as Russia’s actions are becoming increasingly hostile and less restrained.”

“We see the hybrid attacks: in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now; it’s a question of Russia’s actions.”

He says Lithuania leads the way in Nato as one of the top defence spenders, above 5% of GDP, and invites Rutte to a formal ceremony marking the permanent deployment of a German brigade to Lithuania in 2027.

Rutte continues saying that “Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies.”

“[Russia] is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on a battlefield in Ukraine, and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine.

Our message to Moscow is clear: we will do even more for Ukraine and not less.”

title: FIFA could disburse millions to members as Infantino seeks re-election
excerpt: FIFA president Gianni Infantino is willing ‌‌‌‌to discuss the disbursement of millions of dollars to ⁠⁠⁠⁠the member associations of football’s global governing body as the Swiss chief seeks re-electio...
body_text:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino is willing ‌‌‌‌to discuss the disbursement of millions of dollars to ⁠⁠⁠⁠the member associations of football’s global governing body as the Swiss chief seeks re-election to the post he has held for 10 years amid growing opposition.

The ⁠⁠⁠⁠amount of the distributions to individual nations will be on the agenda of the FIFA Council’s October 15 meeting, according to a ⁠⁠⁠⁠letter Infantino sent to the heads of the six regional confederations, as reported by media in the United States on Monday.

“I will not prejudge the amount,” Infantino wrote, according ⁠⁠⁠⁠to one report. “I will support the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered through FIFA’s proper governance process, applied fairly and supported by transparent and auditable arrangements. The ambition is welcome. The financial evidence, governance and implementation must now support ‌‌‌‌it.”

“A single figure can begin the discussion, but it cannot complete a global policy. I have therefore instructed the Secretary General to consolidate all submissions into one integrated assessment for consideration by the FIFA Council.”

The move is seen as Infantino’s latest attempt to placate regional football bodies, as well as their chiefs, in a bid to hold on to his position as the most powerful man in football.

Earlier this month, the 56-year-old confirmed his bid amid widespread criticism of his leadership and the growing threat of legal proceedings.

Infantino has faced stiff opposition since the fallout from his proposed plan to sell approximately 20 percent of a proposed new entity, FIFA ⁠⁠⁠⁠Forward Enterprise (FFE), focused on the commercial and operational facets of the World Cup and other FIFA tournaments.

The Swiss-Italian has been the most powerful man in world football over the past 10 years, but has increasingly lost support from regional football confederations and national associations. Last month, he appeared to be pulling out all the stops in a bid to retain his position, despite growing calls for his ousting and wide-ranging disapproval of his plans.

On Friday, the English Premier League and three other top European leagues called for governance reform of FIFA.

A joint statement with leagues from Spain, Italy and Germany accused Infantino of actively promoting “exploitative ideas rather than safeguarding against them”.

He is seen as a divisive figure in international football, with his close ties to some of the most powerful global leaders and plans for maximising revenue from football viewed as a threat to the game.

With fewer than six months until the next round of elections for FIFA’s presidency, Infantino appears to be losing ground among his usual backers.

FIFA presidents are limited to three terms, each lasting four years.

However, in 2022, Infantino successfully argued that his first spell in charge, which began when he was elected at an extraordinary FIFA Congress in 2016 following Sepp Blatter’s resignation, should not count towards that limit because it completed an interrupted mandate.

His plans to run for a fourth term have been questioned by critics and rights groups, who have asked FIFA’s Governance, Audit and Compliance Committee (GACC) to block the re-election bid.

The financial discussion comes in the wake of UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC calling for Infantino to resign over the plan.

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin and CONCACAF’s Victor Montagliani recently wrote a letter to FIFA, seeking payments such as the one Infantino addressed in his letter. Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, head ⁠⁠⁠⁠of the Asian Football Confederation, made a similar request, per the reports.

Among the investors ⁠⁠⁠⁠in FFE was to be Joshua Kushner, the ⁠⁠⁠⁠brother of President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. Trump is a close ally of Infantino.

Infantino subsequently abandoned the private equity plan, but he has refused to resign, and he plans to run for re-election ‌‌‌‌in March. With seven weeks remaining for candidates to announce their intention to oppose Infantino, no challenger has stepped forward.

Had Infantino’s FFE plan gone through, each ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌member ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌nation would have received at least $20m. The letter from UEFA and CONCACAF asks for every member association to receive a minimum of $10m from FIFA’s reserves, according to the reports.

title: Asian Games: South Korea volleyball team latest to be taken to wrong venue
excerpt:
South Koreans were victims of another Asian Games transport mix-up in Japan when the bus carrying their men’s volleyball team went to a venue an hour away from where they were supposed to go.

South K...
body_text:
South Koreans were victims of another Asian Games transport mix-up in Japan when the bus carrying their men’s volleyball team went to a venue an hour away from where they were supposed to go.

South Korea’s volleyball players were forced to cancel their training on Monday morning before the group game against Taiwan later in the day following the latest logistical issue.

“An organiser-provided shuttle bus took our team to Okazaki instead of its training venue in Inuyama yesterday morning,” an official from the Korea Volleyball Association told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.

“With too much time lost to turn back, the training was cancelled. We lodged a formal complaint to the organisers through the KSOC,” the official added, referring to South Korea’s Olympic committee.

The volleyball team went on to beat Taiwan 3-1.

Repeated organisational failures at the games in Aichi-Nagoya have left athletes frustrated, with accommodation and transport for more than 17,000 athletes and officials among the main issues.

South Korea’s men’s basketball team were forced to miss training ahead of their final against Japan last week when their bus failed to turn up. The gaffe did not affect their results as they went on to win the title.

Also on Monday, Pakistan’s men’s volleyball players were bussed to the wrong arena for their match against Uzbekistan, delaying it by 45 minutes.

“This is another mismanagement by Japan at the ongoing Asian Games,” Pakistan captain Murad Jehan said from the bus in an Instagram video.

A spokesperson for the local organising committee said the Pakistani and South Korean teams had departed from the same accommodation and there was “an error in matching teams to vehicles”.

“Each boarded a bus heading to the wrong destination. We sincerely apologise to both teams for the inconvenience,” she said.

“We caused great inconvenience, and the organising committee takes this seriously,” the spokesperson added.

“It is basic, but we will again make sure boarding teams and vehicle destinations are properly checked and displayed, and work to prevent a recurrence.”

title: ‘Jaw-dropping’ play based on Pelicot rape trial comes to London for one night
excerpt:
Four-hour production featuring star-studded cast will be performed at London County Hall

A play based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot will come to London for one night on...
body_text:
Four-hour production featuring star-studded cast will be performed at London County Hall

A play based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot will come to London for one night only this November – and promises to feature a star-studded cast.

The four-hour production of The Pelicot Trial: Tribute to Gisèle Pelicot has been performed around the world, including in New York City and Avignon, the city in France where the trial took place. This autumn, it is coming to London County Hall, the home of Agatha Christie’s Witness for the Prosecution.

“I saw it in French originally – all four hours of it. It was jaw-dropping, harrowing, really emotional,” said Nadia Fall, artistic director and co-chief executive of the Young Vic, which is putting on the performance. “It was the act of witnessing that really got me: it is long-form and testimonial in form.”

Fall expects the show to sell out immediately. “Because it’s one night only, what we are able to do is ring our best actors, people you will know ‘off the telly’ as well,” Fall said. The full cast will be announced before tickets go on sale in the coming weeks.

Fall added: “The ensemble rehearses together just once. That allows you to call up the best of people who are available for a short commitment. I really can’t wait to announce the company. It is, I think, 27 actors all in all.”

The play was created by Milo Rau and Servane Dècle. The Swiss director and playwright Rau is known for adapting court cases for the stage, including the Moscow trial of the Russian punks Pussy Riot and the trial of the Romanian despot Nicolae Ceaușescu.

Pelicot became internationally recognised after she waived her right to anonymity to ensure a public trial of her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, who, for almost a decade from 2011, drugged her unconscious and invited dozens of men from an internet forum to rape her. Her husband was sentenced to 20 years in prison in December 2024 and guilty verdicts were returned for all 51 accused men. She wanted the story to be public, saying “shame must change sides”.

“We do it one time only in each city,” said Rau. “It is more of a political act really, than a play.”

“It is a harsh watch,” said Dècle, “but people stay for the whole time. We let them come in and out if they want, but very few do. Even Gisèle Pelicot herself came to watch in New York. That was amazing. She said, ‘The actress was doing better than I did on trial.’”

Journalists covering the trial gave Rau and Dècle thousands of pages of their notebooks, and the play is based on what was said in court.

“Everyone wanted to share with us,” said Rau. “It became a trial of our society, of the patriarchy. And we have toured it in at least 15 different countries, in different languages, some I barely understand myself, and the audience still understands the play. Sadly it is a universal experience. It would be better for humanity if this was just a French experience.”

“It isn’t scenes and costumes in a set like a traditional piece of theatre. It is the facts. It just floors you,” said Fall.

The large majority of the audience has been female, Dècle said. “I wish more men would see it. The very interesting thing about this whole affair is you can really dive into who these male perpetrators were.”

Fall said: “Pelicot represents so much for everybody, especially women; resilience and courage and a radical joy for me that she triumphed and lives on. She’s in love and lives her life. That is two fingers up to the patriarchy and I think that is really empowering for us women. This piece and her story is not just about the specifics about her story and sexual assault.”

She agreed to the play, the writers said, because she wanted to keep the conversation that was started by her trial going. “We always say she opened the door, and we just keep it open,” said Rau.

title: At least 40 rescued, 2 dead as boat capsizes after machete fight near Puerto Rico
excerpt:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations detected a vessel carrying 40 migrants near Desecheo Island, leading to a U.S. Coast Guard interception and apprehensions.

At least 40 peo...
body_text:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations detected a vessel carrying 40 migrants near Desecheo Island, leading to a U.S. Coast Guard interception and apprehensions.

At least 40 people were rescued in open waters by the U.S. Coast Guard and two people died after their boat capsized several miles from a tiny, uninhabited island west of Puerto Rico following a fight that involved a machete, officials said on Monday.

Survivors said there was an estimated 60 people aboard, according to the Coast Guard.

The Coast Guard said the makeshift boat capsized late Sunday after a fight in which some people were severely injured by a machete, forcing the group to jump into the water despite not wearing life vests.

Survivors had spent more than 12 hours in the water when someone on a boat passing near Mona Island noticed them at around noon on Monday.

CBP, COAST GUARD INTERCEPT MIGRANT VESSEL HEADING FOR PUERTO RICO; 40 APPREHENDED INCLUDING UZBEK NATIONAL

People sitting on and gathered in the water besides a capsized vessel off Mona Island, Puerto Rico, on September 28, 2026. (U.S. Coast Guard Sector San Juan/Handout via REUTERS)

The person alerted authorities and helped rescue four people at that moment.

Rescue efforts were still ongoing as of Monday evening.

The Coast Guard said it was not immediately known where the people who were on the capsized boat were from.

Migrants fleeing poverty and violence have long traveled from Hispaniola, the island shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic, to Puerto Rico and other islands, moving through the Mona Passage.

The U.S. Coast Guard and other agencies responding to the capsized vessel off Mona Island, Puerto Rico, on September 28, 2026. (U.S. Coast Guard Sector San Juan/Handout via REUTERS)

Many of these migrants navigate the passage on makeshift boats that can capsize in treacherous waters.

This incident marked only the latest deadly voyage.

In June 2022, 11 Haitian women and girls were buried in Puerto Rico after their grossly overloaded boat capsized in open waters northwest of the U.S. territory.

COAST GUARD OPENS FIRE ON BOAT SMUGGLING 25 CHINESE NATIONALS NEAR FLORIDA AFTER IT REFUSED TO STOP

Survivors said there was an estimated 60 people aboard. (iStock)

Last week, police in the Turks and Caicos Islands detained a makeshift vessel carrying 60 Haitian migrants.

In June, 240 Haitian migrants were detained near the the Turks and Caicos Islands.

Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,000 people were reportedly killed between January and June, according to U.N. data.

Armed men control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and portions of land in Haiti’s central region and beyond.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Rubio says foreign actor was ‘clearly’ behind suspected RAF Fairford bomb plot
excerpt:
The US secretary of state offered no evidence for his claims, and also said many people were ‘disturbed’ that the five suspects had been released on bail

A counter-terrorism operation near RAF Fairfo...
body_text:
The US secretary of state offered no evidence for his claims, and also said many people were ‘disturbed’ that the five suspects had been released on bail

A counter-terrorism operation near RAF Fairford in the UK was mired in confusion on Tuesday after police released five suspects on bail prompting concern and surprise from the US president and secretary of state.

Five British nationals from London were detained on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism after three suspicious vans were reported to police in the early hours of Sunday, outside the base in the village of Whelford, Gloucestershire.

A rapid and significant security response was triggered with the village locked down, residents evacuated for 36 hours and bomb disposal robots dispatched to the scene.

However, on Tuesday, the head of counter-terrorism policing in the UK announced all five men had been released on bail. Their release suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said.

Donald Trump later told reporters at the White House that he would not have released the suspects on bail. “We know everything about them. We would not have released them.”

Asked whether the case was linked to Iran, Trump said: “It might be.”

Pressed to give details, Trump said: “I’d rather not. I mean I know the answer, I could be very specific, but I’d rather not say. I would not have released them.”

Likewise, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said a lot of people were “disturbed that some of these people [being investigated] have been released on bail”.

“What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a ‌very serious situation,” Rubio said in an interview with Fox News on Monday evening, adding that it “clearly involves the hands ‌of a foreign actor”.

Rubio provided no evidence for his claims.

Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the last few days.

Adding to the sense of confusion on Sunday, Trump suggested the plot was known to the US authorities, but British sources were suggesting the specific activities of the men were unknown.

MPs and councillors representing the local area said the messaging was inconsistent. Tristan Wilkinson, a councillor representing the ward, said: “It seems insane that this appears to have been a tipoff from a member of the public, and the security services are claiming that there was a level of intelligence involved as well. I don’t see how those two things can both come through at the same time.”

The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.

He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.

“… But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”

An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release it emerged that no explosive material had been found.

Iran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy.

title: From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on women
excerpt:
As outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogs

As an Indian woman, I...
body_text:
As outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogs

As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.

Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.

I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women. We are the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.

Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that women might not be safe even inside their own homes.)

Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whose latest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”

In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.

Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.

“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.

Women, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University have come out on the streets demanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”

The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. A recently published survey of more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.

Another 2024 study from India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.

Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting on the molestation video said: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an “isolated” incident”.

Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.

Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations, and was acquitted by a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According to an analysis of 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.

For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”

Golden girls | Indian women’s cricket team beat Sri Lanka by 147 runs to win gold at the Asian Games last week. Smriti Mandhana’s smashing 79 off 45 deliveries helped India reach a formidable 216 in 20 overs. Deepti Sharma’s three-wicket haul helped India end Sri Lanka’s hopes with just 69 runs on board. Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.

Moma | A solo exhibition by one of south Asia’s most distinguished artists, Nilima Sheikh, opened at New York’s Museum of Modern Art at the weekend. Fractured Skies, presented in collaboration with the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi, will run until next June.

EC under fire | An explosive Indian Express investigation has revealed how two of the top three election officials objected at least 14 times over a period of 10 months to changes made by the Election Commission over its controversial exercise that has struck 130 million people from the voter rolls.

An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cash being removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.

According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.

Tony Klor’s city vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.

It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.

“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

title: Australia raises interest rates to 15-year high
excerpt:
Australia’s central bank has raised interest rates to a 15-year high, spelling higher mortgage payments for millions of Australian households.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) on Tuesday lifted th...
body_text:
Australia’s central bank has raised interest rates to a 15-year high, spelling higher mortgage payments for millions of Australian households.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) on Tuesday lifted the benchmark rate by 0.25 percent to 4.6 percent, its highest since 2011.

The RBA said inflation remained elevated and that previously flagged “upside risks” had materialised, including higher energy prices due to the United States-Israel war on Iran and an AI-driven surge in tech costs.

“There continue to be heightened uncertainties about the outlook for domestic economic activity and inflation,” the bank’s monetary board said in a statement.

“The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast,” it said.

“Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation. A period of prolonged uncertainty may also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia.”

Australia’s annual rate of inflation stood at 3.5 percent in July, well above the central bank’s 2–3 percent target.

Central banks typically raise their benchmark interest rate when policymakers believe prices are rising too fast.

Higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing, including mortgages, cooling consumer demand and bringing down inflation.

The latest hike is set to heap further strain on Australian households already grappling with three previous increases this year.

In a research report earlier this month, Roy Morgan said nearly one-third of Australian mortgage holders, or nearly 1.8 million people, were at risk of “mortgage stress” – where households spend 25-45 percent of after-tax income on payments – as of July.

Australia’s Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who is not responsible for setting interest rates, acknowledged that the hike would mean greater hardship for many Australians.

“We know a lot of Australians are under pressure and this will make things harder,” Chalmers said in a post on X.

“Inflation and interest rates are going up around the world but we know that doesn’t take the sting out of today’s decision.”

Chalmers said the government would take responsibility for “our part of the fight against inflation”.

“That means continuing to manage the budget responsibly, rolling out tax cuts and cost of living help, and addressing the longer term challenges in our economy in an uncertain global environment,” he said.

title: AFCON qualifiers: Wissa guides DR Congo to win, Tunisia held by Botswana
excerpt:
Yoane Wissa scored the first goal and created the second as the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) spoiled a Zimbabwe homecoming by winning a 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifier 2-1 in Harare.

T...
body_text:
Yoane Wissa scored the first goal and created the second as the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) spoiled a Zimbabwe homecoming by winning a 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifier 2-1 in Harare.

The 30-year-old Newcastle United striker struck in the 30th minute, poking a loose ball into the net after goalkeeper Elvis Chipezeze allowed a cross to slip from his grasp in the qualifying match on Monday.

DRC, who secured a historic last-32 finish at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, went further ahead in first-half added time when a Wissa pass sent Samuel Moutoussamy through to score.

After being outplayed in the opening half by a team 89 places higher in the FIFA world rankings, Zimbabwe improved after half-time, with Marshall Munetsi scoring a 93rd-minute consolation goal.

Zimbabwe last played at home in November 2021 before the Harare venue was deemed unsuitable for international fixtures, leading to lengthy renovations.

DRC, whose second of two AFCON titles came 52 years ago, top Group E with a maximum six points after launching their campaign with a 2-0 home victory over Equatorial Guinea.

Zimbabwe and Equatorial Guinea, who meet twice in November, have three points each, and Sierra Leone are pointless.

A first-minute goal from Loren Zuniga earned Equatorial Guinea a 1-0 win over Sierra Leone in Cameroon’s capital, Yaounde.

Equatorial Guinea are among the 11 of the 48 qualifiers for the AFCON group stage who must host matches at neutral venues as they lack an international-standard stadium.

Central African Republic are another “homeless” nation. They fell 1-0 to Burkina Faso in Group F in the Moroccan commercial hub of Casablanca. Aboubacar Camara netted the second-half winner.

Struggling Tunisia were held at home for the second time in four days, drawing 2-2 with Botswana in Rades near Tunis.

Tunisia looked set for a first competitive win this year when Hazem Mastouri scored either side of half-time after Botswana had taken the lead.

But the minnows from Southern Africa – 90 places below Tunisia in the world rankings – equalised on the hour through a delicate lob from substitute Lebogang Ditsele.

It was the second successive 2-2 draw for Botswana after sharing the points in Libya last week, and they remain top of Group H on goals scored ahead of Tunisia.

title: Hospitals in England hit by shortages of common drugs such as paracetamol
excerpt:
NHS trusts also report disruption to supplies last winter of co-codamol and blood pressure medication ramipril

Hospitals are being hit by shortages of key drugs used to provide pain relief, prevent b...
body_text:
NHS trusts also report disruption to supplies last winter of co-codamol and blood pressure medication ramipril

Hospitals are being hit by shortages of key drugs used to provide pain relief, prevent blood clots and tackle high blood pressure.

Dozens of NHS trusts in England have encountered scarcities of aspirin, the painkiller co-codamol – a combination of paracetamol and codeine – and ramipril, a blood pressure tablet.

Nine trusts have had problems getting enough supplies of two of those three common medications, while one – Kent community health NHS trust – ran short of all three.

The shortages underline how precarious the health service’s supply chains for basic medicines have become in recent years as a result of trade disputes, global conflict and manufacturing problems.

Pharmacists have said supply problems have become a “national crisis” and in some cases have left patients unable to access their usual medications for weeks at a time.

Hospitals’ drug supply problems have emerged in freedom of information requests by Dr Rodolfo Catena, an expert in global health supplies at University College London, about stock levels of the three drugs. Sixty of the 184 trusts from which he sought figures responded.

The most widespread shortage involved aspirin, which is used to reduce pain and the risk of blood clots. Twenty-six (62%) of the 42 trusts that responded about it had experienced disruption to their supplies between last December and March this year.

Thirteen (31%) of the 42 trusts that replied on co-codamol had run short of that drug, which helps relieve muscle pain, period pain and toothache. York and Scarborough NHS trust’s supplies had been disrupted since May 2025, and Royal Wolverhampton NHS trust had trouble getting enough co-codamol for the 10 months between October 2025 and August this year.

Seven (16%) of the 43 trusts that answered Catena’s question about ramipril had been unable to get as much of it as they needed. More than a third of adults in England are thought to have dangerously high blood pressure, which heightens the risk of a heart attack or stroke, but 59% are unaware they have it, research showed last week.

Frimley Health NHS trust, which cares for people in Surrey, Berkshire and Buckinghamshire, resorted to paying higher prices for ramipril to ensure uninterrupted supply of it, rather than risk supply problems that would affect patients, Catena found.

His findings tally with National Pharmacy Association analysis. It has found that although shortages in recent years have mainly been of specialist drugs, for example to treat ADHD and epilepsy, supply problems now often involve generic medicines, which are much cheaper to produce.

Catena, an associate professor in operations and supply chain management in UCL’s Global Business School for Health, believes the shortages he found show that NHS England is wrong to classify drug scarcities in its operational risk register as only a “medium” risk to the provision of care.

NHS England has given drug shortages a score of 16 out of 25 on its risk assessment scale. But the widespread nature of shortages makes it unlikely that it will be able to fulfil its ambition to reduce that score to nine by next month, Catena added.

Improving supply chain resilience is also a key priority for the Department of Health and Social Care. Catena called on it to change the current system whereby only drug companies are obliged to warn it about any impending shortages. He said NHS trusts should be put under the same obligation so that service bosses were more aware of disruption to drug supplies and could act to minimise them.

Almost all (92%) of the trusts that responded said they had no contingency plan to tackle supply problems and 82% said they had not reported the scarcities they were facing to NHS England.

A spokesperson for the Society for Acute Medicine, which represents hospital doctors, said: “Medicine shortages can disrupt treatment and create additional pressure for clinical and pharmacy teams. The key is ensuring resilient supply chains, timely communication and access to suitable alternatives so patient care is not delayed.”

A health department spokesperson said: “We regularly speak to NHS trusts and national clinical leads about medicine availability and are aware that ramipril is in limited supply, which is why we issued serious shortage protocols so patients in the UK can still get the medication they need. We are working closely with relevant suppliers to resolve this and issues with co-codamol and aspirin to ensure continuity of supply.

“The vast majority of the UK’s licensed medicines are in good supply, and we have robust measures in place to mitigate disruption for patients. This government is investing in the UK medicine manufacturing industry to manage supply disruptions where they occur.”

title: Tuesday briefing: Inside the suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford
excerpt:
In today’s newsletter: New details suggest there is a counter-narrative to how events unfolded at the airbase used by the US

Good morning. Vehicles suspected of carrying explosives zipping across Bri...
body_text:
In today’s newsletter: New details suggest there is a counter-narrative to how events unfolded at the airbase used by the US

Good morning. Vehicles suspected of carrying explosives zipping across Britain, entirely unbeknownst to authorities, is a disconcerting prospect.

Initially, it seemed precisely this had occurred in Gloucestershire early on Sunday. A major attack on RAF Fairford appeared to have been scuppered by “pure luck”, a local farmer said, after she noticed suspicious vans and masked men on an otherwise deserted country lane. Had she not tipped off police, the vigilant villager believes the five men arrested on terror offences would not have been apprehended. That account prompted questions about whether police and security services had been caught off guard.

Bu new details emerging suggest there are competing, if not conflicting, versions of how events unfolded in the Cotswolds this weekend. So what exactly happened in the early hours of Sunday morning? In today’s First Edition, we’ll explore this, and some other unanswered questions, with the help of Guardian international security correspondent Jason Burke. Before that, this morning’s headlines.

Energy | Andy Burnham will take his first major step to putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when, at the Labour conference, he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.

Immigration | Home secretary Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering watering down her plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK, amid growing demands for a U-turn from cabinet colleagues and unions.

AI | Two of the “godfathers” of modern AI and senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic have warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”, which they say could be the most consequential technological development in history.

Petrol | The price of diesel on UK forecourts has hit an all-time high average of 199.18p a litre, as the conflict in the Middle East continues to drive the cost of fuel to record levels.

Ebola | A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.

In the early hours of Sunday, a farmer from the village of Whelford was travelling home from a party along quiet rural roads. She was about to drop off a friend, while her husband dozed in the passenger seat. Around 1am, however, she encountered three vans “parked in a really weird fan shape” blocking the path to her farm, close to RAF Fairford, an airbase operated by the US air force.

Forced to turn around, she then described seeing “a large group of hooded and masked men” at a nearby junction, who quickly dispersed.

After a failed attempt to contact the Ministry of Defence, she phoned the police at 1.36am and posted in the local residents’ WhatsApp group. Roughly 10 minutes later, armed officers were on the scene. Five men were arrested 300 metres from the base’s perimeter, first under the Explosives Act, and subsequently also on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. All five – UK nationals from London aged between 23 and 25 – were released on bail yesterday. 
 In interviews, the farmer, who has remained anonymous, reiterated her belief that her tip off “foiled whatever plans” were unfolding. “I am absolutely staggered that it was left to me, as a member of the public, to see and report this,” she said.

That the high-security site was so exposed, and that the vans suspected of carrying explosives in its vicinity went totally unnoticed, has since raised questions. While thanking the farmer for her efforts, defence secretary Wes Streeting was quick to cast doubt on her assertions, hinting that UK security services were aware and that her account only offered “a partial picture”.

Donald Trump has claimed the US and UK agencies worked together and had the five men “under view for a long time”, adding the suspects “were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great”.

The farmer acknowledged there had been “activity” by what she “assumed were plain-clothed police officers” in the area in recent days. Another local told the BBC that while walking their dog early on Saturday evening they were stopped by armed police and told to return home.

Gloucestershire constabulary said they were first alerted to the suspicious vans at 12.45am on Sunday – almost an hour before the farmer’s 999 call. Counter-terror police have confirmed the three vehicles had been travelling overnight and been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts. It is now understood that the material found inside them was not viable explosives, but police have said the investigation is continuing.

And then there’s the expeditious nature of the response: the speed with which armed officers and police helicopters arrived at a rural location in the middle of the night appears improbable.

Police are still working to establish motive. Yesterday afternoon, the head of UK National Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, confirmed it may have been the work of proxies, or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state.

On Monday night, US secretary of state Marco Rubio told Fox News that a foreign actor was involved in the suspected plot, but provided no evidence for his claims.

Iran is the centre of speculation, having explicitly stated it considers RAF Fairford “a legitimate target”. Yesterday, the Iranian embassy said it “categorically rejects” any involvement.

Used by the US military for decades, RAF Fairford’s two-mile long runway was specially constructed by the Americans to allow long-range bombers to take off and land. Fairford has played a significant role in Trump’s war on Iran; since former prime minister Keir Starmer allowed the US to use UK bases in its assaults, bomb-laden American B-52 and B-1 planes have regularly been spotted taking off. The airbase is one of only two available to the US in Europe that can facilitate these operations, after Spain, France, Italy and Switzerland rejected similar American requests.

“Most observers and analysts would place Iran at the top of the list of potential suspects here,” Jason Burke, the Guardian’s international security correspondent, tells me, “though we have very little in the way of information to work on, so it’s entirely possible an altogether different scenario is at play.”

As for the five suspects, their being British nationals is likely of little help when determining who may be behind the plot. “The Iranian modus operandi – borrowing a leaf from the Russian playbook – relies on using local hires,” Jason says. “Instead of deploying their own intelligence operatives, they recruit low-grade agents on the ground, some of whom may not fully realise what they are involved in.”

Since the US-Israel war on Iran began, a series of UK security incidents have been linked with Iran. Earlier this month, a man and a woman were arrested after raids on homes in north London on suspicion of assisting Iran’s foreign intelligence service. In March, four Jewish community ambulances were destroyed in an arson attack – counter-terror police explored the possible involvement of Iranian proxies, though aside from a reference to a “terrorist connection”, no mention of Iran was made by prosecutors in court when four men admitted responsibility.

Similar suggestions have been made about tens of other antisemitic attacks in the UK and Europe – Iran’s embassy in the UK has denied any involvement.

In April, Jason reported that, while direct proof of Iran’s involvement in incidents on UK soil remained elusive, the consensus among security officials was the attacks look to be part of a campaign of hybrid warfare launched by Tehran. Since then, Jason says, more evidence has emerged, in part due to the prosecution of 32-year-old Iraqi national Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi in a US court. “This case laid out in extraordinary detail how he, on behalf of the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps, commissioned, organised, and executed a series of attacks in Europe, including in Britain.”

If Iran is proven to be responsible, an intended attack on this scale would represent a significant escalation. “It would be a major step up from targeting synagogues, Israeli embassies and US-owned banks,” says Jason, “given this is a piece of major military infrastructure in Britain.”

With Andy Burnham leading a new government, it’s possible there may be a recalibration of UK foreign policy. He has said he’d be willing to deviate from Trump when necessary. Burnham’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, was reportedly central to attempts made during a national security meeting to dissuade then-PM Starmer from granting the US permission to use UK bases. But this would not significantly alter the risk of attacks, Jason says. “Iran’s targets are not necessarily chosen to directly punish a country; most experts believe they are selected to sow division in societies, distract policymakers, and divert resources.”

Palliative nurse Jane Turner makes a poignant point in this column: regardless of your belief about assisted dying, every side agrees on the need to radically improve end-of-life care in the UK. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team

I devoured Jess Cartner-Morley’s interview with Celia Birtwell, in which Birtwell talks about her friendship with David Hockney and her marriage to Ossie Clark: “He was spectacular, at the beginning,” says Birtwell – even if he did leave her the day after their wedding, pregnant, to honeymoon in Barbados on his own. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

Some vital tips in this piece by Sarah Phillips on the conversations every couple should have to keep a household running safely and happily – I’ve already pencilled in my first weekly “check-in”. Charlie

All of the photographs in this gallery of the Porthcawl Elvis festival are wonderful. But my favourite has to be of Brian, AKA Smurf Elvis, who remixed his costume this year after a decade of attending the largest gathering of Elvis fans in Europe. Lucinda

Rob Draper’s look back at how Arsenal’s hiring of Arsène Wenger changed football is brilliantly reported – make sure to share it with your nearest mustachioed graphic designer friend called Sam, Ed or Harry. Charlie

Nations League | Israeli football team captain Manor Solomon has hit out at Ireland after his team’s 3-o loss in a politically charged Nations League game, saying “They hate us and we don’t like them.”

Rugby | In west Wales, fans want to know why the Scarlets and Ospreys, two teams who have won titles and turned out hundreds of Test players, are on the chopping block under the Welsh Rugby Union’s proposal to cut a club by 2028.

Football | The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, is poised to bow to demands from Uefa and Concacaf to distribute more money from its $6bn cash reserves to member associations.

The Guardian splashes on “PM unveils electricity grid plan in push for public control of utilities”. The Mail leads with “PM to vow public control of energy, water and housing” and the Mirror looks at Burnham’s energy prices pledge with “Taking back power”. The Financial Times also reports “Burnham to outline plans for social care, welfare and ‘control’ of utilities.”

The Times goes with “Labour split on prospect of ending triple lock”, the Telegraph has “Burnham signals end of triple lock”, while The i Paper says “End of UK state pension triple lock moves a step closer”. The Sun looks at the RAF terror drama, asking “Plot’s going on, PM?”

The Pussy Riot activist turned Kremlin informer

In August, Rita Flores, a Russian artist, activist and former member of the Pussy Riot collective, revealed in a video that she had been working as an informant for Russia’s FSB security service, a cooperation she only broke days after fleeing the country. Masha Alekhina, a founding member of Pussy Riot who was jailed for her support of the group and fled the country, tells Helen Pidd about why she does not feel angry at her former comrade in activism.

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Our weekly series The pet I’ll never forget is always a source of joy. And the story of scruffy little terrier Dennis is no exception.

Sophia Money-Coutts got Dennis in 2024 with her then-boyfriend, but within three months the couple had split. “I was distracted from my sadness by this small, bouncy, intensely disobedient dog,” says Money-Coutts, explaining that he raced after every squirrel, raided her bins, licked a man she was dating during an amorous moment, and “once farted on Jilly Cooper’s sofa”.

Dennis had accompanied Money-Coutts, a journalist, to an interview with the animal-loving novelist, whose response was typically indulgent. “It doesn’t matter a bit, does it darling?” she recalls Cooper crying, clutching Dennis closer to her. “He can do whatever he likes.”

Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday

And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

title: RBA interest rates: Reserve Bank hikes cash rate to 4.6%, the highest level since 2011
excerpt:
Widely expected decision is fourth increase to interest rate this year and will be blow to mortgage holders across Australia

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking n...
body_text:
Widely expected decision is fourth increase to interest rate this year and will be blow to mortgage holders across Australia

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Reserve Bank of Australia has lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, its highest level since 2011, while warning of further hikes.

The widely expected fourth increase to the cash rate this year will add to repayment costs for millions of mortgage holders across the country. Before Tuesday’s meeting, it sat at 4.35%.

In a statement accompanying the RBA’s rate setting board’s unanimous decision, it warned its fears about inflation were beginning to be realised and it was ready to lift interest rates again.

It highlighted a broadening Middle East conflict and strong AI-related demand for pushing up prices globally. Locally, inflation was higher than the RBA expected, and businesses were either lifting prices or looking to do so.

The board said higher fuel costs were affecting the prices of other goods and services, and it was possible the ongoing US war on Iran could push inflation higher and drag global economic activity further down.

The RBA had previously lifted interest rates three times this year. The board said those hikes appeared to be slowing the economy, but that another was needed to bring inflation down “in a reasonable period”.

“The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed,” the statement read.

Data to be released on Wednesday is expected to show underlying inflation rising at an annual pace of 3.6% for the third month running in August, well ahead of the RBA’s target range of 2% to 3%.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has said the US war on Iran – not government spending – was to blame for inflation.

“When you see what’s happening with global oil prices, when you see what’s happening with the re-escalation of the war in the Middle East, obviously, factually, that is one of the big drivers of that inflation,” Chalmers told Channel Seven on Tuesday morning.

Before the decision, markets were predicting a further hike by February and more than a 50% chance of another by mid-2027.

Bets on higher rates gained confidence after the decision, with the Australian dollar rising from 70.11 US cents to 70.17. Bond yields rose and the sharemarket benchmark, the S&P/ASX200, slipped from 8,697 to 8,671 points.

The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, will speak at 3.30pm AEST to explain the decision.
