title: Sen Kennedy says no living politicians should have buildings named after them after Trump's moves
excerpt: Workers begin removing Donald Trump's name from the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. following a federal appeals court ruling. The court denied a last-minute appeal to keep Trump's name on the buildi...
body_text:
Workers begin removing Donald Trump's name from the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. following a federal appeals court ruling. The court denied a last-minute appeal to keep Trump's name on the building, which had been added after a unanimous board vote in December.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Sunday that living public officials should not have buildings named after them and proposed a rule to prohibit such renaming efforts.

This comes as President Donald Trump continues to push to rename the Kennedy Center after himself. The president has also sought to rename other prominent federal buildings in Washington, D.C., after himself since returning to the White House last year.

Kennedy said public officials, including Trump, should not "spend public money on private ads for themselves."

"The White House sees it differently, but … you can’t spend public money to … promote yourself," Kennedy told host Margaret Brennan during an appearance on CBS News' "Face the Nation."

KENNEDY CENTER CEILING PARTIALLY COLLAPSES AS TRUMP-LED BOARD PUSHES FOR 2-YEAR CLOSURE

Sen. John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, speaks during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Kennedy's comments came as a new ad promoting Trump appeared on multiple networks, that was funded by the federal government.

The senator then suggested public officials should be barred from having a building named after them while they are still alive.

"I may end up with a sombrero on my head, but I also think we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him when he’s alive," he said, referring to Trump mocking Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., last year by sharing AI videos of the lawmakers wearing sombreros.

FEDERAL JUDGE ORDERS TRUMP'S NAME REMOVED FROM KENNEDY CENTER, SAYS ONLY CONGRESS CAN RENAME IT

People watch construction workers build scaffolding near the Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts sign in Washington, D.C., on June 12, 2026. The Kennedy Center board sought an emergency appeal to block a court order requiring the removal of President Trump's name, but a judge denied the request. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Trump has attempted to rename multiple buildings after himself since returning to the Oval Office, including the Kennedy Center, although federal judges blocked multiple attempts by the center's board — handpicked by Trump — to add the president’s name to the building.

Trump's name was briefly added to the building's facade but was ordered removed after courts ruled that only Congress holds the authority to change the center's name.

The State Department also added Trump’s name last year to the U.S. Institute of Peace, but former institute officials removed by the Trump administration filed a court motion earlier this month to block construction crews from putting the president’s name onto the outside of the building.

Workers affix signage adding US President Donald Trump's name on the facade of the Kennedy Center in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, Dec. 19, 2025 (Al Drago/Getty Images)

Trump also suggested he wanted New York's Penn Station and the D.C. area's Dulles Airport named after him as a condition for a funding deal earlier this year.

The president has additionally floated a project to construct a promenade connecting the back of the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River, saying that allies wanted to call it the "Trump Promenade."

"They want to call it the Trump Promenade, but I don't know if I want to do that, but it's going to be beautiful," he said at the time.

title: Victoria police apologise over death of injured man taken to cells instead of hospital
excerpt:
Inquest into 2023 death shown footage of John Makai struggling to stand after suffering serious head injury from being punched in head by son

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

G...
body_text:
Inquest into 2023 death shown footage of John Makai struggling to stand after suffering serious head injury from being punched in head by son

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victorian police have apologised to the family of a man who died after being held for five hours in a police cell without medical treatment for a significant head injury.

John Makai, a 58-year-old father of 10, died in 2023 from serious head trauma that went untreated despite him being unresponsive in a Broadmeadows cell, the Victorian coroner’s court heard on Monday.

On the first day of an inquest into his death, footage was shown in court of Makai being dragged from a divisional van into police cells, and repeatedly failing to respond when officers checked on him through the cell door.

The officers twice claimed that he had responded, despite the CCTV of the incident showing no such physical response, counsel assisting Rachel Ellyard told the court.

After the footage was shown, a lawyer for Victoria police’s chief commissioner, Mike Bush, said he apologised for the death.

Andrew Imrie, for Bush, said that Makai’s care “was not at the standard that … any member of the Victorian community is entitled to expect”.

He offered sincere condolences to Makai’s family and said it was “a situation Victoria police and all its employees work tirelessly to avoid”.

Imrie said there was a failure to complete a medical checklist when Makai arrived at the Broadmeadows station. He also said there were failures to notice his deteriorating condition, to complete a risk assessment, and to conduct adequate checks.

There had been disciplinary action taken against officers “where a basis was available”, he said.

“At this stage it is unclear whether these shortcomings would have made any difference to the tragic outcome in this case,” Imrie told the inquest.

The court heard that an ambulance was initially called – but was cancelled – after one of Makai’s sons punched him twice while the pair were drinking with another of his sons and a friend at a house in Sunbury.

Police attended the house and in footage shown to the court could be seen watching on as Makai struggled to stand and then collapsed into a bookcase while trying to sit down.

Police then had to support him to walk to the divisional van, and could be heard telling him to “get his legs up”.

When they arrived at the Broadmeadows police station about 20 minutes later, Makai could no longer stand, and had to be dragged out of the van by his legs, with his head seen striking the floor and walls of the van.

He was then placed seated on the ground, the footage showed.

Officers lifted him under the arms to drag him into a cell, where he was placed in what is known as a “coma position”, the inquest heard. He made no verbal response during this transfer, nor at any other time at the station, the court heard.

Police requested another ambulance at 1.25am, telling them that Makai had a minor facial injury and was in a very deep sleep because of his state of drunkenness, and they would like him to be checked by paramedics.

Ambulance Victoria told police they were struggling with workload but would dispatch paramedics when they were available.

“What was interpreted as deep sleep was in fact the increasing effects of traumatic brain injury and bleeding into the brain,” Ellyard said.

The court heard that because of an issue with Triple Zero Victoria, the job was not actually logged as outstanding. An ambulance was not dispatched until the same police officer again requested another five hours later.

The fresh call for an ambulance came after police entered Makai’s cell and could not get him to respond verbally.

“I’ve got a guy been in custody a number of hours, he’s breathing, trying sternum rubs, all sorts of … we can’t get any verbals out of him, we’d like an urgent check on his welfare,” the police officer said in a recording of the call.

“This request’s made since midnight, and for some reason it’s been cancelled at your end … I’m the custody sergeant, this guy’s breathing but we can’t raise any verbals from him.”

When asked about his breathing, the sergeant responds he had been snoring heavily but not responding “since he came in, since midnight”.

“Unconscious? And you haven’t had any response for six hours?” the Ambulance Victoria operator responds.

The sergeant then goes on to say his officers had been checking on him every 15 minutes, which Ellyard said was proven incorrect in a review of the footage.

When paramedics did respond, Makai was found to be showing signs of a brain injury, the court heard. He was transported via ambulance to hospital, where he was diagnosed with a non-survivable brain trauma.

The first witness, Ryan Goon, the director of operations support for Triple Zero Victoria, said that the dispatcher wrongly cancelled the police request for an ambulance.

This was because of an issue with “multiple associated events”, as the first person to call for an ambulance at the Sunbury house had later cancelled the request.

Ellyard said the scope of the inquest – expected to run for two weeks – would consider the cause and the circumstances surrounding Makai’s death, including what treatment he could have received if he was taken to hospital rather than to a police station. It will also examine any changes to policies and reviews that had been completed after his death.

The inquest before coroner Paresa Spanos continues.

title: US, China list goods recommended for tariff cuts following Trump-Xi summit
excerpt:
The United States and China have unveiled a list of goods recommended for reduced tariffs following last week’s summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

The release of the list on Sunda...
body_text:
The United States and China have unveiled a list of goods recommended for reduced tariffs following last week’s summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

The release of the list on Sunday comes after Trump and Xi agreed to work towards lowering tariffs on $60bn worth of trade.

The agreement, which covers $30bn of each side’s imports, identifies 77 Chinese goods and more than 1,600 US products to be considered for more favourable tariff treatment.

Chinese goods on the list include microwave ovens, fish hooks, artificial flowers and weighing scales.

US exports identified for lower tariffs include poultry, dairy products, noodles, eggs, peanuts, canned tomatoes, pure-breed breeding horses, and silk.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the agreement would improve market access for about 30 percent of US exports to China and also benefit US consumers.

“The Trump Administration will continue to pursue fair, balanced, and reciprocal trade with China by ensuring compliance with commitments on agricultural and energy purchases, pursuing balanced trade in non-sensitive goods, and securing market access for American farmers, manufacturers, businesses, and workers,” Greer said in a statement.

China’s Ministry of Commerce, which confirmed the list on Monday, shortly after the White House announcement, said the sides would discuss “a reciprocal tariff reduction framework of $30 billion for $30 billion, aiming to reach a consensus”.

“This arrangement will help stabilize China-US trade, create better conditions for Chinese exports of relevant products to the US, meet domestic market demand, and strengthen trade cooperation in agricultural products, energy, manufactured goods, and consumer goods,” the ministry said in a statement.

While Trump and Xi’s summit was heavy on pomp and ceremony, their talks wrapped up on Friday with few concrete announcements on the myriad divisions between the superpower rivals, which span everything from trade to artificial intelligence and Taiwan.

Trump and Xi, who have held three face-to-face summits since last October, are expected to meet again at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, and the Group of 20 gathering in Miami, Florida, in December.

Trade between the US and China, the world’s two largest economies, has declined substantially since Trump, a longtime critic of free trade policies, returned to the White House in January last year.

Two-way trade totalled $495bn in 2025, down 25 percent from the previous year, according to the US Trade Representative.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, said the latest announcement did not point to a major shift in US-China trade.

“Instead, both sides have largely listed goods that do not move the needle on overall trade flows,” Elms told Al Jazeera.

“They may reduce some prices in the US for consumers, but none is going to make a dramatic difference in inflation figures or result in meaningful sighs of relief by most US buyers,” Elms added.

“The same is broadly true with the Chinese list. Although there are many different agricultural products on the list, most are not actually exported to China or not exported in meaningful quantities.”

title: Serbia’s snap election: Can Vucic outmanoeuvre the student revolt?
excerpt:
For weeks, the streets of Serbia were teeming with young people rallying against the government. At the height of the protests in March 2025, more than 100,000 took to the streets.

The student moveme...
body_text:
For weeks, the streets of Serbia were teeming with young people rallying against the government. At the height of the protests in March 2025, more than 100,000 took to the streets.

The student movement had called for early elections for nearly two years, and President Aleksandar Vucic, who resigned on Sunday, finally heeded their call earlier this month. He announced snap parliamentary elections for October 25.

With the elections originally not due until December 2027, the early vote is seen as an attempt by governing populists to cling to power despite widespread discontent.

Vucic is vying for the prime minister’s post, a role he has held before, appearing to yield to protesters’ demands not out of goodwill but in the hopes of ushering in a result that keeps him in office, analysts say.

But experts warn that elections will hardly solve the underlying political tensions gripping the country, triggered after 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a railway station. Student protesters blamed the disaster on government negligence and alleged corruption.

The move “is essentially about reducing political risk”, Viktor Stamenkovic, a researcher at Belgrade’s Institute for Political Studies, told Al Jazeera.

“Given the circumstances, the ruling camp is choosing the electoral sequence it considers least dangerous,” he said, referring to Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

Vucic could stall no more – both the presidential and parliamentary vote would have had to be held next year.

“Vucic has, for some time, been aware that further delay is unlikely to work in his favour,” Stamenkovic said.

Vucic’s presidential term expires before the mandate of the current parliament, said Stamenkovic. Serbia’s recent political history explains the order of the elections – the parliamentary before the presidential, the analyst added.

Presidential elections can fundamentally alter the parliamentary dynamics that follow – which is how Vucic’s party came to power, Stamenkovic explained.

Vucic cannot run for a third term under Serbia’s constitution, and no other SNS figure is as popular as him.

“In 2012, the presidential victory of the SNS candidate Tomislav Nikolic changed the political momentum so dramatically that the bloc, which had previously appeared capable of forming a parliamentary majority, was ultimately unable to do so,” said Stamenkovic. “The presidential result altered the calculations of the parliamentary parties and paved the way for a government led by SNS.”

Vucic, therefore, has good reason to fear the same scenario being repeated.

Vucic has built a personalised political system centred on himself rather than his party or any successor, said Stamenkovic.

“He therefore has to find a way of transferring his own political strength from the presidency into the parliamentary arena … effectively staking his political future on the parliamentary election.”

For Milica Vojinovic, an investigative reporter at the Serbian outlet KRIK, the goal of the governing party is to stay in power at any cost.

“They [want to] continue their corruption projects, which usually means finding new ways and public procurements through which they can take money… [including from] public budgets,” Vojinovic told Al Jazeera.

She cited irregularities in past elections, such as vote buying by the SNS, documented by election observers and human rights organisations, and feared that the next elections will see an “escalation of these tactics, now that the student movement is actually threatening to win the election and take power from Vucic’s party”.

Since 2024, the governing party has lost a sense of political legitimacy, said Stamenkovic.

“Even if – and this is a big if – SNS wins another parliamentary majority, it is difficult to envisage a return to a situation in which it can govern normally and claim the kind of broad social legitimacy it once enjoyed,” he said. “Virtually all polling shows that a majority of the country believes Serbia is heading in the wrong direction and that the time has come for change.”

Mass demonstrations have not taken place in Serbia for some time, as the student movement has shifted from organising large rallies to election campaigning.

The youth movement recently submitted their election list to state election authorities after a jubilant march through the capital of Belgrade, formally entering the race.

Polls show that this vote could bring representatives of the student movement into parliament and state institutions, said the Serbia-based Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA).

“This is important for Serbia’s democracy … [They] will definitely improve the legitimacy of the parliament as the representative body,” the group said.

Transparency and anticorruption are priorities for most citizens, with the social and political reality in the country having changed in the two years since the railway station incident, the organisation added.

Vojinovic, however, predicted that if Vucic’s party continues to hold power, “we are to expect the most repressive measures seen so far against everyone who has been criticising, or in any way opposing, the government”.

Criminal cases have already been brought against some activists in the student movement, as well as a political analyst, she said.

According to Human Rights Watch, foreign agent laws, first introduced by Russia and seen being picked up by other nations, have been used to brand independent civil society, media and other dissenting voices as illegitimate and acting on behalf of foreign interests. Such a law was proposed in Serbia in 2024.

“Recent smear campaigns against my newsroom, as well as other independent media outlets and NGOs, lead us to believe that they may be a precursor to the introduction of a ‘foreign agents law’ in the near future, should Vucic’s party remain in power,” Vojinovic added.

Meanwhile, Serbia is no closer to joining the European Union, but that is not a real priority for Vucic, the experts said.

“It is widely understood that Serbia cannot make meaningful progress towards EU membership under the current system of government,” said Stamenkovic. “What matters much more to Vucic is avoiding serious political pressure and criticism from Brussels.”

Ratko Mladic’s funeral illustrates this balancing act: Serbia hosted the semi-official honouring of the former Bosnian Serb army general – who died while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1992–1995 war in Bosnia – but Vucic did not attend, he said.

“In some ways, the relationship between Vucic’s government and the EU resembles a couple trapped in a disastrous marriage who nevertheless do not divorce because both sides continue to benefit from the relationship.

“Vucic cooperates with the EU on issues that matter to Brussels, while the EU has for years been willing to overlook a great deal about the increasingly authoritarian nature of his rule,” he added.

The two are also at odds over Russia, which Serbia has ties with.

A public opinion poll in June by the CRTA and Stanford University’s Democracy Action Lab showed that among SNS voters, 15 percent wanted closer ties with the EU while 60 percent favoured relations with Russia.

“There is every reason to expect election day itself to be highly contentious,” said Stamenkovic.

title: The endangered native ponies of Eriskay in the Outer Hebrides – a photo essay
excerpt: Fewer than 400 Eriskay ponies remain. One of the rarest native breeds in the world, their plight is unique because the community living on their tiny Hebridean island are fighting for them. The ponies...
body_text:
Fewer than 400 Eriskay ponies remain. One of the rarest native breeds in the world, their plight is unique because the community living on their tiny Hebridean island are fighting for them. The ponies wander the village and townsfolk care for them together

On the slopes of Beinn Sciathan, a rocky outcrop in the Outer Hebrides, white and grey ponies roam freely. Eriskay ponies, one of the rarest native breeds in the world, are critically endangered.

They have often been mixed with the Highland pony and other breeds, giving the false impression of higher population numbers. Only about 300 to 400 true Eriskay ponies are thought to remain.

Efforts have been made to boost their numbers since the 1970s, both on their small homeland, Eriskay Island, and on the mainland. The island’s ponies have a lifestyle fascinating enough to draw tourists. They are neither wild nor kept enclosed. For half of the year, including winter, they are free to roam the island and its village. Each pony has an owner who can easily identify their own despite them looking nearly identical to the average observer.

Sandra MacInnes, the chair of Comann Each nan Eilean, the island’s pony society, married into the community caring for the ponies and her affection for them has only grown over time

About 150 people live on Eriskay, many of whom speak Gaelic. It is a close-knit community, but over time the island has become a tourist destination known for stunning beaches with clear blue water, the grounding of the SS Politician, and even a Fifa-recognised football pitch. But its history of fishing, crofting and Catholicism, and of course its ponies, are integral to its culture.

“It all makes Eriskay what it is today,” says Sandra MacInnes, the chair of Comann Each nan Eilean, the island’s pony society, who owns several of the animals.

Eriskay ponies grazing outside the community hall

In the 1850s, thousands of families in the Outer Hebrides were forced from Barra and South Uist during the Highland clearances. For many, Eriskay became a crowded refuge. MacInnes says: “[The landlords] thought it’s rubbish for grazing so they sent them here thinking they’ll never survive. They came here and made their houses … They were cleared from crofting communities and had to learn fishing, but then they thrived.”

Once the Eriskay community was established, the ponies thrived because of their role in the region’s social fabric. Originally used for crofting, they would be fitted with creels to bring peat up the hill and move seaweed as fertiliser for crops.

In the 1970s, however, their population shrunk to a low of about 20 purebreds. Mechanisation was one of the main reasons for their decline, and Comann Each nan Eilean was founded in 1972 to restore the breed.

A mare recently brought to the island works out her place in the herd

Eriskay ponies grazing on a rocky outcrop

Community members also note that the climate crisis has begun to affect their island. Recent winters have hit hard, and the beaches are starting to erode. But the ponies adapt well to harsh and fluctuating winters with their hardy coats and their ability to navigate the island to stay out of the wind.

Triona MacKinnon owns two ponies on Eriskay and a few others on South Uist. “Winters are getting longer and wetter,” she says, noting that the community is having to help more in feeding the ponies – but at the same time that milder weather encourages ticks, which affect the animals.

“This winter’s been particularly long,” she says. “You can get loads of rain. Some ponies can get rain scald, and you’re not used to seeing that.”

The ponies have shaped the town’s culture over time. Local people quote the former parish priest Father Calum MacLellan, who once said: “Without the people of Eriskay there would be no pony, but without the pony there would have been no people on Eriskay.”

Or as MacInnes says: “They both needed each other.”

The ponies’ population has increased in the last 60 years, but there is still work to do. Comann Each nan Eilean is developing a breeding programme, and it manages the herd numbers to ensure the the grazing land can sustain the animals without them overrunning the community.

Fiona Misselbrook pets her Eriskay foal at her farm in Haddington near Edinburgh

One foal was born on the island this year, and the community hopes for a few more next year. When first born, the ponies are almost black and then become lighter as they age. Most turn white, but adults have brown coats.

In the winter months, the ponies need extra food and their owners feed them with support from the island’s pony society. In the summer, the ponies are kept up on Beinn Sciathan to allow the soil on lower slopes to recover so it can be used for farming.

Owners hike up and down whenever they can to check on their ponies. Some tend to their own ponies’ hooves, but many need to pay for a farrier, as well as veterinary care when needed. The work is financially demanding and time-consuming, but many islanders see a life alongside the ponies as something beautiful and part of their heritage.

Although MacInnes married into the community caring for ponies, she has since become attached to them.

“You get to know how docile they are. They all have their own personalities, they all have names, they all have little characters,” she says. “It’s nice to see herd dynamics as families. They are families.”
