title: Strait of Hormuz tensions linger as Iran and US move further from a deal
excerpt: Tehran, Iran – Hours after US President Donald Trump rejected a diplomatic solution put forward by Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, explosions were heard in the waterway, according to Iranian medi...
body_text:
Tehran, Iran – Hours after US President Donald Trump rejected a diplomatic solution put forward by Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, explosions were heard in the waterway, according to Iranian media.

Reports of blasts near southern Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz suggested that multiple antiship missiles and drones were fired at vessels transiting the waterway against Tehran’s wishes.

While Iranian authorities did not confirm any attacks in the Strait of Hormuz that day, shipping continues to be attacked in the waters, including an Indian cargo ship last week, which killed a sailor.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) maintains that the strait is closed to any ship that does not coordinate with Iranian authorities. On Sunday afternoon, it released video of what it said was a second US underwater drone seized this month.

Tehran has issued instructions to shipping companies transiting the Strait of Hormuz to use a temporary route approved by Iranian authorities and pay relevant fees. But it has also said the strait will not fully reopen until the US blockade on Iranian ports ends.

Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority announced on Saturday that it would blacklist any shipping charterer company which orders crews to use routes it considers to be unauthorised.

It also published what it described as an apology from an unnamed shipowner blaming commercial pressure from its charterer for trying to pass through the strait.

Washington still insists that its warships are successfully guiding oil tankers out of the strait via a different route. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News on Sunday that the “running average” of crude oil in transit was nearly 13 million barrels per day.

A September 19 operational update by US Central Command claimed that its forces had helped move more than one billion barrels of crude out of the Gulf over roughly two months.

The US military also says its forces have redirected 122 commercial vessels to enforce the naval blockade of Iran’s ports, halting all Iranian crude exports.

Tehran has claimed that the US is providing false information regarding Strait of Hormuz traffic to project control over the key waterway. Shipping has been severely disrupted since the US and Israel started their war on Iran on February 28.

Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, said Iran’s strategy of launching maritime attacks has spread the economic costs of the conflict beyond its borders.

While Iran has suffered economically from war damages, the US naval blockade and sanctions, it would be a mistake “to assume that reaching that threshold produces submission”.

“The next Iranian move is therefore likely to be an attempt to increase the pain experienced by the Gulf rather than simply absorb further American pressure,” Krieg said.

“That could mean more aggressive vessel interdictions in Hormuz, attacks on energy infrastructure, greater Houthi pressure around Bab al-Mandeb and pressure from Iranian-aligned groups against alternative Saudi export routes. We are already seeing how pressure on Hormuz, the Red Sea and Saudi infrastructure can interact.”

At the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Iran projected a message of defiance while also proposing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if its seven conditions were met.

They included lifting the blockade on Iran, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to attacks on all fronts, including Israel’s assault on Lebanon. The demands mostly amounted to a return to the June memorandum of understanding between the US and Israel.

Tehran has added that reopening the strait must be undertaken through a bilateral arrangement already finalised with Oman, the only other country with territorial waters in Hormuz.

US President Donald Trump told reporters he rejected the offer, but Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday they were adamant about the conditions and would await an official response through mediators, such as Pakistan, Qatar and Oman.

Abolfazl Shekarchi, chief spokesman of the Iranian armed forces, warned that if the US further intervenes in the Strait of Hormuz, “it will get slapped”.

“The Americans have no way out other than withdrawing from the West Asia region. The sooner they leave, the fewer losses they will incur and the region will certainly become safe after that,” he said.

Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia  said conditions were deteriorating so badly for the US that it might launch another “military aggression” on Iran.

Krieg said that as the US moves to isolate Iran via sanctions, Tehran, unable to respond with mutual financial measures against Washington, will be forced to rely on continued coercion in the Strait of Hormuz.

“The most likely level remains controlled attrition rather than an immediate return to the massive air campaign of the opening months,” Krieg said.

“Over the coming weeks, I would expect further attacks or attempted attacks on tankers, US-enabled shipping and regional infrastructure, followed by limited US strikes against IRGC maritime assets, coastal missile positions, drones or vessels involved in those operations. That tit-for-tat cycle has already re-emerged around Hormuz.”

title: UK politics live: Burnham says he wants to fight next election on plan for new taxes to pay for free social care in England
excerpt:
PM appears to be anticipating criticism of reforms that he will set out on Tuesday at the Labour party conference

‘I can deliver’: Burnham pledges radical change on eve of Labour conference

Q: Will ...
body_text:
PM appears to be anticipating criticism of reforms that he will set out on Tuesday at the Labour party conference

‘I can deliver’: Burnham pledges radical change on eve of Labour conference

Q: Will you do social care reform before the next election in 2029?

Burnham said he would stick to the Labour manifesto, and its commitments on tax (which rule out rises in income tax, national insurance or VAT).

Q: But what about a special, new tax to fund social care?

double quotation markTrust is really important to me here. I don’t think you can reform this system without it, without consensus.

So I’m saying to you that I will develop a very clear plan, and I will put that plan to the public at a general election.

double quotation markThat will be where the plan gets tested. And people will then be able to decide.

And I am prepared to put myself in that position, recognising that it might be difficult or unpopular with some, but that is the way to do it, to get that endorsement and then introduce the system in the next parliament. Because the the backing of people for this really matters.

When Labour, with Andy Burnham as health secretary, proposed social care reform in 2009 funded by a tax on estates, the Tories swiftly described the proposal as “a death tax” and the idea was probably doomed even before the 2010 election campaign began. Labour deployed similar tactics in 2017, when Theresa May published plans for social care reforms that would have raised costs for wealthier pensioners. Labour said it was a “dementia tax”, and May lost her majority.

Burnham said this morning that he hoped this time there would be a more responsible debate. (See 9.35am and 9.47am.)

Three hours after his interview, there does not seem to be much evidence that anything has changed. Reform UK has already accused him of proposing a “universal death tax”.

Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson, said:

double quotation markAndy Burnham has yet again refused to rule out his universal death tax. He’s too weak to cut the sky-high benefits bill, so he’s coming for your home instead.

It is an unfair, cruel levy on the people of this country, and it would make Britain the single-worst place in the Western world to hand down money to your kids.

Reform UK will fight Burnham’s universal death tax. Money that is taxed when it is earned, saved and spent should not be taxed a fourth time as you are laid to rest.

Jenrick is assuming that Burnham will propose an extra tax on inheritance. Burnham did make it clear this morning that there would have be some form of tax rise to fund his plan, but he would not give details, and he played down the idea it would just be a re-run of his 2009 plan. (See 9.47am.)

MailOnline is already running with a “death tax” headline.

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, was also on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Responding to what Burnham said about social care, Philp said the Conservative party would not support having a new tax to fund better social care. He said:

double quotation markThis country is already taxed too highly. It’s already destroying jobs. It’s already making businesses go bankrupt. High taxes are already driving businesses and successful people overseas.

What I inferred from Andy Burnham’s interview just then is they do plan more tax rises.

And let me be categorical; the Conservative party will not support more tax rises if more money is needed, for example, for social care or indeed for defence. We would find that money through savings elsewhere, particularly in the welfare budget, which is far too high.

Darren Jones, who was chief secretary to the PM when Keir Starmer was in No 10, was a guest on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. Some of his comments about Andy Burnham’s government have not been notably supportive (particularly this one).

Asked about what Burnham said about presenting the public with a plan to raise taxes to pay for an NHS-style social care system, Jones said Burnham was being “very bold and brave”. Viewers of Yes Minister will know that “brave” is a civil service euphemism for “mad”.

But Jones sounded a bit more positive than that. He said that, if Burnham could “land” this policy in the right way, it would be “a huge achievement”.

Yesterday the Times splashed on a story saying Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, had criticised Shabana Mahmood’s plans to make foreign care workers wait up to 15 years before they can apply to permanent residency in the UK. Other news organisations have presented this as a major split, or even “civil war”.

Rayner was on Sky News this morning and she insisted she was just restating a view she has already expressed. Asked about the split, she said:

double quotation markShabana had a consultation on the transitional arrangements, and she’s been really clear that we’ve got to have a fair system that is fair for people that contribute today, and those that come to this country to contribute.

I have absolute support for Shabana in that, and I’m sure she’ll come to a good conclusion on that.

I contributed to that consultation, and I’m on the record for that.

We’re all united. We’ve seen on illegal migration, those figures coming down, so I think that she’s doing a fantastic job. So there’s no split story there, unfortunately.

In fact, there is a clear division between what Rayner wants and what Mahmood proposed when the plans were first published last year. But it is probably misleading to present this as a bitter row – because Andy Burnham has also expressed clear views on this, and he broadly sides with Rayner. In evidence to the home affairs committee earlier this month, Mahmood strongly hinted that she is going to accommodate the views of her boss and there will be a compromise.

At the Labour conference, Steve Rotheram, the Labour mayor of Liverpool city region, is giving a speech opening the proceedings in the main hall. He is a close friend of Andy Burnham and he says it is great to have an Evertonian PM. He also says the last prime minister to come from Liverpool was Gladstone, who served four terms. So no pressure on Burnham, then, he jokes.

Q: What do you say to people who argue you should have banned the Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road today?

Burnham said that a decision like that would have had to have been made on the advice of the chief constable of the Police Service of Northern Ireland. And the chief constable did not recommend that, he says.

But he says he has spoken to Chris Bryant, the Nothern Ireland secretary, this morning. He says they are appealing for calm.

That was the final question in Burnham’s interview with Laura Kuenssberg.

Frances Mao has further coverage of the march on a seperate live blog.

Q: Would you consider more radical policies, such as sending asylum seekers to a country like Albania to have their claims processed there?

Burnham avoided the question, but stressed there was some evidence that “things are going in the right direction.”

He said he would be “relentless” in addressing this issue.

And he praised what Shabama Mahmood, the home secretary, is doing on this.

double quotation markShe’s got a strong grip on this issue. What we have been doing is working, but more is needed and more will be done.

Q: What would you say to the women of Piddington concerned about having a camp for asylum seeker near their village, or women in other villages with similar concerns?

double quotation markThose concerns are understandable and they have to be addressed in whatever solution is finally agreed.

There were also concerns expressed about the use of hotels and the reason why the nature of accommodation is changing across the country is because a commitment was given to end the use of hotels, and that was what many people were calling for a few years ago.

Asked if he regarded the far-right activist Daniel Thomas, who has organised the masked protests and who is known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, as racist, Burnham replied:

double quotation markWell, it’s hard to conclude that he’s anything other than someone who has racist views.

I hesitate always … I’ve not read everything that he said, I’ve not followed everything that he’s done … so I’m just going to say that because I don’t just throw labels on people.

But given everything and the way he’s behaving and what he’s seeking to whip up, I mean this is the worst kind of hateful behaviour.

Asked about the masked men on the streets how have protesting about migrants in towns in the south of England recently, Burnham said this was “unacceptable”.

double quotation markUnacceptable. Creating fear and intimidation on British streets – this is not something we’ve seen in this country before and it’s not something we want to see.

Burnham said there were “real worries” about immigration. But he went on:

But let’s look at the facts. Net migration is down 80% on what it was in the Boris Johnson era.

Boat crossings are down 50% this year on what they were in the early 2020s.

So I understand people’s concerns and I will be relentless in addressing their concerns.

But people also have to look at the facts, and they also have to see when people are playing the worst kind of politics with this issue. That is leading to people feeling afraid in their own communities.

title: Legendary agent warns NFL teams about making key quarterback mistake that could derail season
excerpt:
Leigh Steinberg tells OutKick that the New York Giants quarterback must focus on the long term after his brutal knee injury.

Amid a rash of quarterback injuries, legendary sports agent Leigh Steinber...
body_text:
Leigh Steinberg tells OutKick that the New York Giants quarterback must focus on the long term after his brutal knee injury.

Amid a rash of quarterback injuries, legendary sports agent Leigh Steinberg thinks NFL teams that don’t have multiple backup options are putting their seasons and Super Bowl hopes in jeopardy.

Going into Week 3, five starting quarterbacks have already been injured, with New York Giants star Jaxson Dart out for the regular season. With the rash of injuries at the most important position in sports, Steinberg said it’s paramount that teams have multiple options.

"It's a real problem, which is why I always think that teams that don't keep three quarterbacks are making a mistake, because the likelihood is that the starting quarterback will be hurt at some point," Steinberg told OutKick in a recent interview.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Jayden Daniels of the Washington Commanders looks on before being carted off the field after sustaining an injury against the Dallas Cowboys in the second quarter at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas, on Sept. 20, 2026. (Stacy Revere/Getty Images)

The famed agent said that teams that have only two quarterbacks on the roster, like the Giants did with Dart and backup Jameis Winston, leave themselves exposed. If Winston had gotten hurt after Dart did on Monday night, the Giants would not have had another quarterback on the active roster and would have been in further trouble.

Now that Dart is hurt, the Giants are left scrambling to find a quality option behind Winston in the event the former Florida State star goes down while replacing Dart.

Steinberg noted that with the salary cap, it’s harder for teams to invest heavily in the backup quarterback position because starting quarterback salaries are ballooning. While it may be difficult to have multiple quality backups, Steinberg warned that teams that don’t have them leave themselves in a dangerous position.

"You have bigger, stronger defensive players on the line who can inflict all sorts of harm on the quarterback. The position starts with that player, so all the action coalesces around him, and there's just more opportunity to get hit and hurt," Steinberg said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart walks off the field with an injury during the first half of an NFL game against the Los Angeles Rams in Inglewood, Calif., on Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Caroline Brehman)

Despite rules that have been put in place to keep quarterbacks healthy, most notably in 2018 when the NFL restricted defenders from landing on quarterbacks with their full body weight, Steinberg said quarterbacks are vulnerable by the nature of the position.

Steinberg also noted that while an injury to a franchise quarterback is devastating to a team’s season, it’s also detrimental to the NFL. He noted how quarterbacks have become like movie stars in American culture and are the sport’s highest-profile celebrities, and injuries to them could cause viewership to decline.

However, Steinberg said that as much as the NFL has tried to protect quarterbacks with more "vigor," fans don’t notice the added measures because quarterbacks are still getting hurt.

Leigh Steinberg attends the 39th Annual Leigh Steinberg Super Bowl Party at Storek on Feb. 7, 2026 in San Francisco, California. (Jesse Grant/Getty Images)

"I want you to remember that every time they put in more protective rules and procedures. There's a hue and cry from football purists that they're taking the toughness out of the game," Steinberg said.

"I'm all for the most vigorous protections while retaining the competitive aspect of the game."

Steinberg, who was inducted into the California Sports Hall of Fame in 2017, has had many high-profile clients throughout his impressive career. Across football and baseball, Steinberg’s clients include Steve Bartkowski, Steve Young, Troy Aikman, Warren Moon, Bruce Smith, Thurman Thomas, Kordell Stewart, Jeff George, Ben Roethlisberger, Myron Rolle, Matt Leinart, Mark Brunell, Ricky Williams, Howie Long, Eric Karros and Dusty Baker, among others.
