title: ‘No role for UNRWA in Gaza’: Does the Board of Peace toe Israeli lines?
excerpt: The United States-led Board of Peace (BoP) has said the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) will have no role in Gaza – echoing a longstanding Israeli demand to sideline the organis...
body_text:
The United States-led Board of Peace (BoP) has said the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) will have no role in Gaza – echoing a longstanding Israeli demand to sideline the organisation considered a lifeline for millions of Palestinians.

The board, which has been tasked with overseeing the “ceasefire” and Gaza’s reconstruction, said on Friday it would work only with partners it deems reliable and who it believes can meet the needs of Gaza’s population – a standard it says UNRWA does not meet.

The move comes as the BoP unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan on Wednesday aimed at beginning Gaza’s reconstruction, nearly a year after a so-called “ceasefire” came into effect in the devastated Palestinian territory.

The plan, presented on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly (UNGA), comes as key elements of the “ceasefire” remain stalled, including the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hamas.

UNRWA was established in 1949 to cater to tens of thousands of Palestinians displaced from their homes by Jewish militias from areas that currently form part of Israel.

BoP’s stance on UNRWA comes as Israel’s genocide in the coastal enclave continues, with Palestinians facing nonstop attacks, severe restrictions on humanitarian aid and stalled reconstruction plans.

So what has BoP said about UNRWA, and does it keep toeing the Israeli line on the future of Gaza?

The BoP unveiled a 66-project reconstruction blueprint on the sidelines of the UNGA, with $2.4bn proposed for projects aimed at beginning Gaza’s recovery.

UNRWA was left off the list of UN agencies the board identified as partners.

“The Board of Peace’s policy as it relates to UNRWA’s involvement in Gaza is unchanged,” the BoP said in a post on X on Friday.

“We will only work with trusted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a deradicalised Strip. UNRWA fails on those litmus tests.”

However, a BoP official, speaking to The Associated Press news agency on condition of anonymity, confirmed that board members had met UNRWA officials several times.

The official said the agency’s programmes could continue if they served Gaza’s residents well, but maintained that “UNRWA’s days are over”.

The BoP, which US President Donald Trump launched earlier this year, was conceived to oversee the rebuilding of Gaza after nearly three years of Israel’s genocidal war on the Strip.

In an indirect response, UNRWA acting Commissioner-General Christian Saunders said on Friday in Gaza, “UNRWA remains an institution of considerable humanitarian and strategic value, with capabilities and expertise that are difficult to replicate today.”

“To disregard these capabilities at a moment of such profound need is neither logical nor responsible,” Saunders said in a statement.

Former UNRWA chief Philippe Lazzarini on Thursday warned that removing the agency would have a “devastating” effect on Palestinians.

“They want to get rid of the agency, but on the other hand they know that if you get completely rid of the agency today, it might have a further … devastating impact on the population,” Lazzarini told AP on Friday.

In a separate statement on X, Lazzarini said, “grandiose plans are what the Board of Peace does best”, noting widespread suffering across Gaza amid Israel’s ongoing genocide.

The agency has about 11,000 Palestinian employees in Gaza and remains heavily involved in healthcare, education, water and sanitation services. Its exclusion is particularly significant given the scale of displacement and the continuing restrictions on aid entering Gaza.

UNRWA has for decades provided aid and education services to Palestinians in Gaza, occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank as well as Jordan, Syria and Lebanon – the neighbouring countries where the Palestinian refugees have been living.

Palestinians see the agency as safeguarding their right of return to their homeland, while Israel wants it dismantled.

Hamas accused the BoP of adopting Israel’s position.

Spokesperson Hazem Qassem on Saturday called the decision to exclude UNRWA “a complete alignment with the Zionist [Israeli] position”, saying it was aimed at ending the agency’s operations, preventing it from delivering aid and undermining Palestinian refugees’ right of return.

Qassem said it was “strange for the peace council to adopt this hostile stance towards UNRWA while simultaneously failing to provide aid to Gaza or compel the occupation to abide by the ceasefire agreement and halt the daily killings of Palestinians in the Strip”.

Experts say the workings and demands of the BoP align closely with Israel’s vision of the Gaza Strip and the Palestinians.

Israel has for years sought to remove UNRWA from Gaza, accusing the agency of being infiltrated by Hamas.

The International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion in October, said allegations that “a significant part of UNRWA’s employees are ‘members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions'” had not been substantiated.

The BoP’s position strengthens the Israeli efforts to dismantle the UN agency.

Hamas and other Palestinian factions agreed in July to a roadmap under which weapons would be surrendered in stages as Israeli forces gradually withdrew. The two processes were explicitly linked.

But following an August meeting between Nickolay Mladenov, the BoP’s director-general, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the board said Israeli forces would not withdraw beyond the “Yellow Line” until Hamas’s decommissioning was complete, including “light weapons, heavy weapons, and the tunnels alike”.

Hamas maintains that it will not implement its obligations unless Israel fulfils its own.

Israel currently occupies more than 60 percent of Gaza while most of the territory’s 2.3 million people remain displaced.

Article 17 of the BoP plan calls for “temporary reconstruction” beginning in areas designated free of Hamas control, including humanitarian compounds for unarmed civilians.

The proposed system would direct reconstruction, aid and shelter towards areas outside Hamas’s control while Israeli forces remain behind the so-called “Yellow Line”.

However, Israel has refused to allow the Palestinian technocratic committee into Gaza, open crossings or begin reconstruction until Hamas is completely disarmed.

After unveiling the reconstruction plan on the sidelines of the UNGA, BoP high representative Mladenov said once again the proposed plan depends on Hamas’s disarmament.

Almost a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, reconstruction has yet to begin on any meaningful scale and Israeli forces continue to occupy large parts of the Strip.

At least 1,451 Palestinians have been killed and 4,953 wounded in Israeli attacks since the “ceasefire” began in October 2025, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

The healthcare system is on the verge of “total collapse”, the ministry said last week, while shortages of fuel, medical supplies and spare parts have disrupted hospitals, water and sanitation services.

The scale of destruction is also immense. More than half of Gaza’s hospitals and clinics remain nonfunctional, less than 1.5 percent of cropland is accessible and undamaged, and reconstruction needs have reached an estimated $71.5bn.

Nearly 84 percent of Gaza’s population – more than 1.76 million people – are living in displacement sites or damaged and inadequate shelters, the UN has said.

title: Counter-terrorism police investigate ‘major incident’ near RAF Fairford
excerpt:
People evacuated from village after men are arrested on suspicion of explosives offences near Gloucestershire airbase used by US forces

Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation in which...
body_text:
People evacuated from village after men are arrested on suspicion of explosives offences near Gloucestershire airbase used by US forces

Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation in which several men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences near an RAF base.

After the declaration of a major incident at RAF Fairford, a bomb squad was sent to the village of Whelford with extra security measures, including the fortification of entrances to the base, put in place. Roadblocks and armed police have also been seen in the area over the weekend.

The operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting that investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance.

Homes were evacuated and the army was also inspecting a number of vehicles as security was stepped up at the Gloucestershire airbase, which is used by US forces. Evacuated residents were being taken to a nearby leisure centre.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, was being updated on the matter from Liverpool, where the Labour party conference is taking place. He cancelled plans to take part in a journalists versus politicians football match in order to take calls about the matter.

A government spokesperson said: “The prime minister is being kept updated on the incident in Gloucestershire. We are grateful to the emergency services, who have acted quickly to detain several suspects and put measures in place to keep the community safe. It would be inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing.”

RAF Fairford has been at the centre of protests in recent months over the British government’s decision to allow the US to use the base to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards told Britain in July not to allow US bombers to fly from the base. At the time, a government spokesperson said: “Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it’s on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself.”

Gloucestershire police said: “A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident.

“It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act.

“We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place.”

A police spokesperson added that the situation was contained and said local people need not be alarmed.

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said: “I would like to thank all those emergency and specialist teams who have acted so swiftly regarding the incident in Gloucestershire. We can be reassured that this is being dealt with, and it is exactly why our emergency response teams and armed forces are on standby 24/7.”

Armed police have been seen blocking access to the main gate of the base, and many emergency vehicles including police cars, ambulances and fire engines were visible on Sunday morning in Fairford, the town near the base.

A ‌spokesperson for the US air force said they would not discuss specific force protection measures.

“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow ​UK-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors and their families,” the spokesperson said.

“We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect ⁠our installations, our people and their families.”

The MP for South Cotswolds, Roz Savage, described the situation as “worrying” but said it was believed to be “contained”. She added: “I have contacted the police for further updates and I’ve been told that it is believed the incident is contained. I would like to thank them for the work they are currently doing.”

In May, the Royal International Air Tattoo, which is usually held at the base, was cancelled due to the escalating geopolitical situation in the Middle East.

title: Lee Gilley’s Texas attorney ‘never had one like this’ as accused wife killer clings to Italian lifeline
excerpt:
Lee Gilley’s attorney, Dick DeGuerin, discusses the extradition battle in Italy and the unusual legal hurdles delaying his client’s return to Texas, where Gilley is charged with murdering his wife.

T...
body_text:
Lee Gilley’s attorney, Dick DeGuerin, discusses the extradition battle in Italy and the unusual legal hurdles delaying his client’s return to Texas, where Gilley is charged with murdering his wife.

Texas criminal attorney Dick DeGuerin has been practicing law for six decades; he is currently representing Lee Gilley.

Gilley, 39, is the Houston husband accused of murdering his pregnant wife Christa Bauer Gilley, 38, inside the family's home in October 2024.

Prosecutors allege Lee Mongerson Gilley killed his wife, Christa Bauer Gilley, who was nine months pregnant, in Houston in 2024. (Christa Bauer Gilley/Facebook)

TEXAS MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PREGNANT WIFE ALLEGEDLY CUTS OFF ANKLE MONITOR AND FLEES TO ITALY

Investigators say the murder suspect cut off his ankle monitor and fled from the U.S. to Italy in May, weeks before his trial was supposed to start.

"I've been a criminal defense lawyer for 60 years," DeGuerin said. "In that time, I've had other clients who have skipped bond, not often, very infrequently – I've never had one like this."

LEE GILLEY BEGS FOR ITALIAN PROTECTION AS ALLEGED SQUATTER TARGETS HOME WHERE PREGNANT WIFE WAS KILLED

He said Gilley was taken into custody by Italian authorities following his arrival – he's been sitting in an Italian jail cell in Turin ever since.

Lee Gilley has been housed inside a jail cell in Turin, Italy following his arrest by Italian officials. (Getty Images: FilippoBacci)

Over the summer, the U.S. government initially tried to extradite Gilley back to the country to face his alleged crimes – but that came to a halt when the Italian courts blocked it.

TEXAS LAWMAKER WARNS ACCUSED WIFE-KILLER'S ITALY ESCAPE COULD OPEN 'PANDORA'S BOX' FOR FUTURE SUSPECTS

"The Italian courts will not extradite if the death penalty is on the table, and the charge against Mr. Gilley is capital murder. In Texas, there are only two punishments for capital murder, death or life without the possibility of parole," DeGuerin said.

On Sept. 18, Harris County prosecutors dropped the death penalty after Italian judges demanded written guarantees before extradition.

NICK REINER WON'T FACE DEATH PENALTY IN ROB, MICHELE REINER MURDER CASE

Lee Mongerson Gilley and his defense attorney, Ed McClees, right, are shown in the 497th District Court at the Harris County Justice Center, 1201 Franklin, Thursday, Oct. 17, 2024, in Houston. He is charged with capital murder in the death of his wife, Christa Gilley. (Melissa Phillip/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)

"Italy is asking that they commit fully that the death penalty is off the table," DeGuerin said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

He went on to say, "We never thought that was on the table anyway, but Italy has required that."

EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY'

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Defense attorney Ed McClees and his client, Lee Mongerson Gilley, appear in the 497th District Court at the Harris County Justice Center in Houston on Oct. 17, 2024. Gilley is charged with capital murder in the death of his wife, Christa Gilley. (Melissa Phillip/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)

DeGuerin said Italian courts are concerned a judge could have the power to overrule that and assess the death penalty.

TATE BROTHERS TO REMAIN BEHIND BARS FOR NOW AS UK SEEKS EXTRADITION ON RAPE, TRAFFICKING CHARGES

"The answer to that clearly is no. Only a jury can do that," he said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Gilley's attorney also told Fox News Digital that Italy can refuse Gilley's extradition if there is a possibility he could could be sentenced to life without the possibility of parole, if convicted.

IRISH AUTHORITIES SEEK EXTRADITION WARRANT FOR SUSPECT IN MURDER OF AMERICAN MOM JAMEY CARNEY: REPORT

Lee Mongerson Gilley, 39, is accused of murdering his wife, Christa Bauer Gilley, and their unborn child in Houston in 2024. (Christa Bauer Gilley/Facebook; Melissa Phillip/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)

The U.S. has until Sept. 30 to respond to Italy's requests for clarification. After that happens, there will be a status conference on where Italy stands in the extradition process.

"We've maintained from the very beginning that he is not guilty and he did not kill his wife," DeGuerin said. Gilley's status conference is set for Oct. 7.

title: GOP is running 2026 like it’s 2006, repeating George W. Bush’s Iraq War election failure
excerpt:
Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter highlights concerns over election security and the enforcement of federal voting laws on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

The 2026 midterm election is bearing down ...
body_text:
Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter highlights concerns over election security and the enforcement of federal voting laws on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

The 2026 midterm election is bearing down on Republicans. How it will turn out will be determined, in part, by whom history says controlled the narrative. Sadly, Republicans are losing that battle just as they did in 2006 when the Iraq War became the decisive issue.

After the 2004 presidential election, Republicans had a House majority of 232 seats to 202 seats held by the Democrats. After the 2006 election, that was reversed, with Democrats holding 233 seats to 202 for Republicans, with Democrats even picking up the one independent seat.

What might be surprising about that loss is that the 2006 economy was growing at 3% and there were 1.8 million new jobs added in 2006.

MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE

So, how did Republicans lose the House in that dramatic fashion in 2006? Two ways: by not controlling the narrative and failing to offer the voters a plan for the years ahead.

President George W. Bush went from being very popular after 9/11 to being in charge when the GOP lost the 2006 midterms. (Brooks Kraft/CORBIS/ via Getty ImageCorbis via Getty Images)

The dominant issue of the 2006 campaign was not the economy, it was the Iraq War. The public was weary of it and exit polls showed that 56% of Americans disapproved of it. President George W. Bush’s approval ratings were tied to that war, and he had a similar disapproval rating.

REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY.

There was also the late-breaking Mark Foley scandal, a Republican congressman.

In the process, independent voters voted decisively for Democrats 57% to 39% in those midterms in contrast to voting slightly in favor of Republicans in 2004.

Keep in mind that the Iraq War did not result in substantial hardships for Americans as compared to prior wars such as Vietnam, Korea or the world wars.

Obviously, the Iraq War was a Middle East War far from the American homeland. Yes, gas prices did rise (sound familiar?). But they were significantly dropping by the time of the election.

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

As for the Iraq War itself, nearly 20 times as many Americans had died in the Vietnam War than had in the Iraq War by the 2006 midterms. While all troop deaths are always tragedies, that comparison is made to give context between two major wars and public perception about their gravity and losses.

To a large degree, the controlling dynamic of the 2006 election was the public’s view of the Iraq War, the Foley scandal and the lack of a Republican narrative.

REPUBLICANS NEED A REAGAN-STYLE VISION TO WIN THE BATTLE OVER AMERICA'S FUTURE

Elections, however, should never be analyzed just for what happened. They also should be analyzed for what didn’t happen. What didn’t happen in the 2006 midterms was the voters getting a forward-looking reason to vote for Republicans.

The dominant issue of the 2006 campaign was not the economy, it was the Iraq War. The public was weary of it and exit polls showed that 56% of Americans disapproved of it.

Elections are always about the future – regardless of what you have done in the past. However, in keeping with almost every midterm election in the past, the party in the White House did not present voters with a plan going forward. Republicans had no three-point plan that they promised voters they would implement if elected to take control of the House.

REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE

Instead, they placed their hopes on a money advantage, past laurels and a sophisticated get-out-the-vote plan. In plain terms, that did not and could not result in Republicans controlling the narrative of the 2006 midterms. As a result, Republicans were defined by events and the Democrats.

Fast-forward to today, and the comparisons between 2006 and 2026 should be manifest. Today as then, Americans are in a Middle East war. Both times, Americans had grown weary of the war – although the Iraq War had been waged for nearly three years compared to just six months in 2026. Both times gas prices had risen.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG?

Today, the economy has many very bright spots, including record-low poverty rates, a manufacturing boom and strong consumer spending. Wages are outpacing inflation (unlike the Biden years) and the stock market is booming.

A good deal of the country, however, would never know it given the Divided Media Era in which we live. Worse yet, Republicans have not told voters their plan for 2027.

LIZ PEEK: AI ALARM BELLS ARE RINGING AND TRUMP NEEDS TO TAKE THEM SERIOUSLY

They have called out the Democrats and their socialist ways. However, saying the other side is bad, isn’t a forward-looking plan. Indeed, Republicans have yet to say, "Elect us to control of the House and we will do one, two and three."

As a result, Republicans have failed to control the narrative just as they did in 2006. While their losses likely won’t be as large as 2006 because of gerrymandering, Republicans should have learned from their past mistakes.

Fortunately, there is still time and there three-point plan should be:

The old saying goes, "You can’t be something with nothing." If the Republicans want to win in 2026, they need to offer something, and they need to do it now.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM TOM DEL BECARRO

Thomas G. Del Beccaro is the author of "The Lessons of the American Civilization" and "The Divided Era." He ran against Kamala Harris in the 2016 U.S. Senate race in California.

title: DEPROGRAMMED: Three abortions and eight decades later, this woman says feminism 'failed' her
excerpt: After three abortions, 'Feminine, Not Feminist' author Candy Thompson says the ideology she embraced 'pitted' women against men. Now, she's reclaiming the memory of her lost children and urging women ...
body_text:
After three abortions, 'Feminine, Not Feminist' author Candy Thompson says the ideology she embraced 'pitted' women against men. Now, she's reclaiming the memory of her lost children and urging women to question the beliefs she once held.

Octogenarian Candy Thompson, who says she left her Christian faith after embracing feminism and later had three abortions during her first marriage, eventually returned to Christianity and said feminism "failed" her.

"The feminists pitted [women] against men, they pitted us against having children … It belittled who we were in the home and [as] mothers, and it belittled who we were as just women in a marriage," Thompson told Fox News Digital.

"When it pitted us against God even … then that's what really led to what happened to me," she continued.

DEPROGRAMMED: THE 'RADICAL PERSPECTIVE CHANGE' THAT LED THIS TRANSGENDER ATHEIST TO JESUS

Candy Thompson and her second husband on their wedding day, left, and today after decades of marriage, right. (Candy Thompson)

Thompson, who attended the University of North Carolina in the 1960s, said learning about feminism while in college helped lead her away from her Christian values.

"[Those values] didn't seem to answer the questions that I was asking. And then I heard about feminism, and that was in the culture … It sounded good because it was about equality," she added.

"I had a really, really traumatic experience between my junior and senior year. I had a miscarriage in the college dorm … Instead of going to my parents, instead of going back to God … I just went right on with what I had been doing. I look back at that and see that was when my life began to go really downhill from there," Thompson continued.

EX-DEMOCRAT SHARES ABORTION PILL EXPERIENCE THAT LEFT HER 'HEMORRHAGING IN THE BATH'

Candy Thompson said she had three abortions and experienced a miscarriage. Decades later, the octogenarian is recognizing the lives of the children she lost with acknowledgment-of-life certificates. (Candy Thompson)

After a miscarriage, Thompson said she married the first man she dated. The marriage ended in divorce, and Thompson said she had three abortions during the relationship. She now recognizes those pregnancies with acknowledgment-of-life certificates.

"There were lots of effects like anger. I did not understand as a young woman what my actual created purpose was … Those things were not really clear until I returned to my former faith," she said.

RED STATE HEARTLANDS PUT A RING ON YOUNG LOVE WHILE PROGRESSIVE BLUE CITIES LAG ON EARLY MARRIAGE

Candy Thompson said feminism pitted women against men, children and God, and linked her embrace of feminism to decisions she made before returning to her Christian faith. (Candy Thompson)

"We have young people from the colleges into our homes and they're hungry. They are hungry to know who they really are and they want to be married," Thompson continued. "They want to have this love, but they don't trust men … and having their hearts broken and hurt because we're made in that way of wanting to have that relationship that is a lifetime relationship."

"They're wanting this in their spirits, but they don't know how to get it because nobody's telling them. These women are lost," she added.

Alba Cuebas-Fantauzzi is an Associate Producer at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
excerpt:
Supplies cut off from Ukrainian city where bodies are being left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones

The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter of fac...
body_text:
Supplies cut off from Ukrainian city where bodies are being left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones

The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter of fact: food for the 2,000 or so civilians still remaining in the city and its surrounding villages had finally run out.

“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message, from a woman in the besieged city, who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.

Before the war, she weighed 110kg (17 stone); now she weighs just 67, she wrote.

“At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”

Oleshky, across Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.

Accounts of the dire conditions in the city emerged as the Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.

In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.

“Russia is deliberately making life there impossible,” Sybiha said in an address during the general assembly. “They are starving them to death.”

The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.

Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000.

But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.

Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has also caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops – who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.

In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.

“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”

On 1 September a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.

Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.

According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, issues began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.

“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.

“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning.

“People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson City. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”

Hasanenko described another reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.

“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.

Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.

“The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields,” said Hasanenko.

“It’s an old city,” adds Hasanenko. “It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”

In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”

“A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.

“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”

title: Iran ‘miscalculating’ by betting on midterms after 3-hour talks, Trump officials warn
excerpt:
State Department Principal Deputy Spokesperson Tommy Pigott tells Fox News Digital the United States is pushing the United Nations to "get back to basics" as future funding remains tied to reforms.

N...
body_text:
State Department Principal Deputy Spokesperson Tommy Pigott tells Fox News Digital the United States is pushing the United Nations to "get back to basics" as future funding remains tied to reforms.

NEW YORK — Trump officials say Iran is miscalculating if it believes rising prices and the midterm elections will weaken President Donald Trump's hand in negotiations to end the nearly seven-month conflict.

The administration is projecting confidence that mounting economic pressure will push Tehran toward a deal, even after three hours of talks this week ended without an announced breakthrough.

"The president holds all of the cards here," State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

Americans, meanwhile, are facing a mounting cost at home. The national average for regular gasoline reached $4.49 per gallon Friday, according to AAA, up from $3.16 a year ago. AAA said volatility in the Strait of Hormuz and high crude oil prices have driven the national average to its highest level ever recorded for this time of year.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged those costs Wednesday while arguing that allowing Iran to eventually obtain a nuclear weapon would carry a far greater price.

THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES

President Donald Trump delivers remarks to the United Nations General Assembly at the UN headquarters in New York City on Sept. 23, 2025. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

"It comes at a price and at a cost, there's no doubt about it," Rubio told reporters. "But the cost of not doing something about it is substantially higher, especially for future generations."

Trump himself laid out the stakes in stark terms during his address to the U.N. General Assembly Tuesday, presenting Tehran with a choice between reaching a deal that would allow Iran to rebuild or facing potentially devastating further U.S. action.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said. "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"

But Trump predicted Tehran would ultimately choose a deal, arguing that Iranian leaders are waiting to see whether the November midterm elections weaken his position.

"They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," Trump said. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running."

"I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran," Trump added. "It doesn't even enter my mind."

A U.S. official told Fox News Digital Friday that discussions through mediators remained "positive and constructive," but said the administration was in no hurry to reach an agreement.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush," the official said, adding that nearly 40 million barrels of oil had transited the strait over the previous 48 hours. The official predicted oil and gas prices would fall back to pre-conflict levels as the U.S. continues to maintain control of the strait.

Trump said U.S. officials held a "very good" three-hour meeting with Iranian officials Tuesday as part of a renewed diplomatic push to end the conflict. But Rubio cautioned Wednesday against characterizing the talks as a "major breakthrough," saying they were largely a continuation of previous conversations.

"I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation," Rubio said.

Rubio also said the administration would make public any "good outcomes or things to announce jointly" stemming from its diplomatic engagements. No such announcement immediately followed the Iran meeting.

Iran has since put forward a proposal of its own. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran presented U.S. mediators with a seven-day plan this week that would restore passage through the Strait of Hormuz at the end of the seven days if certain conditions are met, followed by renewed negotiations toward a broader agreement.

The proposal draws from the memorandum of understanding Trump and Iran reached in June. A mediator told CBS News the latest discussions were positive but remained in their early stages.

The stakes in Hormuz remain high. Commercial traffic through the critical oil chokepoint has been sharply disrupted during the conflict, although U.S. officials say the amount of oil moving through the strait is increasing.

TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

"The diplomatic door is always open. The president is a deal maker," Pigott said. "But he's going to see the fundamental principle that they cannot have a nuclear weapon accomplished one way or another."

Pigott pointed to growing oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the economic pressure Washington has imposed on Tehran as evidence that the balance remains in Trump's favor.

"We are seeing oil move [through] the Strait of Hormuz, increasing every single day," Pigott said. "We're seeing the devastating effects on the Iranian regime from economic [actions]. Hundreds of millions of dollars are being denied to the regime through this blockade that we're seeing."

Rubio offered a similar assessment Wednesday when asked about Trump's assertion that Iran may be waiting for the outcome of the midterm elections before making a deal.

"I think the Iranians misread our system," Rubio said. "I think the Iranians are under this illusion that Democrats are going to win in November, and the president will no longer be able to do things against them."

Rubio said Congress remains an important branch of government but argued Tehran misunderstands the limits of congressional power over sanctions and military action.

"The president has extraordinary powers. Every president does," Rubio said. "He's the commander in chief, both constitutional and otherwise, to be able to carry out those functions."

"So I think that the Iranians are fundamentally misreading our political system," Rubio continued.

Soldiers from Iran's land, navy, air force and special forces parade during National Army Day on April 18, 2025, in Tehran, Iran. The country held its annual Army Day parade, which included an address by President Masoud Pezeshkian. (Getty Images)

The administration is also confronting threats to energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have targeted Saudi Arabia as the conflict has expanded, adding another source of uncertainty for global energy markets.

Rubio said Wednesday that the restart of a Saudi pipeline following attacks was "critical for their economy" and "critical for the global economy." He said energy infrastructure had been targeted by the Houthis as well as Shiite militias in Iraq that the U.S. says are backed by Iran.

"Every time you guys ask me a question about the Middle East, it goes back to someone who's supported by Iran," Rubio said.

Rubio said the U.S. would continue honoring its defense commitments to Saudi Arabia while declining to discuss what additional military options Trump could consider.

"They are a strategic defense partner," Rubio said. "The U.S. made commitments to them. We will live up to those commitments. We are living up to those commitments now."

title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
excerpt:
Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer

Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon ...
body_text:
Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer

Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.

“It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.

Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.

“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”

Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”

The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.

In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.

Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.

However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.

Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.

Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.

“No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.

“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI
excerpt:
‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’

The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by ...
body_text:
‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’

The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a Silicon Valley mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “System Error: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”.

When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”

The technos were onto something. Silicon Valley’s power players have just been blindsided by democracy, which has slammed into their program to transform the world with artificial intelligence. A cabal that never doubted the greatness of their ambitions unexpectedly finds their project in the hot seat, forcing them into the unusual position of having to persuade the great unwashed of the merits of their endeavor. So far, the public is not buying. And for all their blindingly high IQs and their massively endowed wallets, Silicon Valley’s greats don’t quite know what to do.

Everyday Americans are up in arms against the AI datacenters sprouting across their communities. Villages, counties, cities and states are imposing moratoria and bans on further development. While the backlash has largely focused on stopping the proliferation of sprawling sites packed with energy-guzzling computer servers, the revolt is not merely nimby opposition to local development.

Public opinion has also turned decidedly sour on the AI project that has called these datacenters into being. Some 73% of Americans think the costs of datacenters outweigh the benefits, according to a survey by the Marquette University Law School. The same survey found that 70% of Americans think that AI is bad for society.

Americans were not always this down on the tech. In 2021, only 37% declared themselves more concerned than excited about the technology, according to surveys by the Pew Research Center. But the share has climbed to 52%. Even 55% of young adults – usually the most excited cohort – have soured on it. And this is not a partisan fear. Democrats and Republicans alike are vastly more concerned than excited. Interestingly, Americans are generally more mistrustful of the technology than people in other countries.

This surely has something to do with the terrifying announcements that have come out of Silicon Valley recently. A widely shared belief that there’s at least a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction has, rightly, scared the bejesus out of many and follows repeated statements that artificial intelligence will end all jobs as we know them. Assuming we do avoid an AI apocalypse, vague promises of an AI cure for cancer and a universal basic income or some such to replace wages across the economy sound hollow coming from a clutch of out-of-touch billionaires with questionable moral codes in a country with huge holes in its social safety net.

The political backlash is built on a deeper discomfort, though, beyond fear of the dystopia threatened by the masters of the valley. A fear built in the here and now and fueled by a brooding mistrust in US democracy itself, distrust of a political system that allowed a clutch of weird, sci-fi addled plutocrats to pursue a civilization-threatening project behind people’s backs. As noted Henry Farrell, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, “the push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives.”

People are not wrong about this. As AI ethicist Rumman Chowdhury points out, the dominant narrative out of Silicon Valley, that AI systems are becoming so powerful that nobody – including the companies that developed them – can stop them, is a stratagem to avoid responsibility for whatever harm their products may cause, depriving meat-and-bones humans of any recourse to law.

The popular backlash is unlikely to stop the buildout of datacenters. Donald Trump remains steadfastly on the side of the moguls hoping to build an AI future. In response to the popular backlash, the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to nix the rule that requires states to solicit public input on applications for air pollution permits for industrial facilities like datacenters and the power plants that feed them, which could keep locals in the dark until construction starts.

The sorry truth is that tech’s power does insulate it from small democratic pressure. “If there is one sector in the US that is still globally dominant and profitable, it is tech,” Boston University historian Quinn Slobodian said. “They can be confident that even if there is a change of leadership, the next person will have to dance with them anyway.”

Critically, there is a bipartisan consensus that ensuring the US’s capabilities in artificial intelligence remain ahead of China’s is of paramount importance. Fear of Chinese catch-up is likely to keep driving policy, overriding voters’ concerns about the risks embodied in this new technology.

And yet voters’ rejection of datacenters, the most immediate, concrete expression of the AI project, raises a question about how the technological revolution of our time will deal with intense popular skepticism and navigate democratic governance. It poses a challenge to a technological elite which exhibits nothing but contempt toward democratic rule.

This is not, of course, the first time that some technological revolution brings about societal upheaval without asking for democratic buy-in. The people that brought about America’s transformation from an agricultural society to an industrial powerhouse did not survey farmers about what mechanization would do to their farms. The Luddites of 19th century England would have loved the chance to put approval of the steam-powered loom to a referendum.

But technological change over the last few decades has not delivered the kind of uplift to everyday workers that their ancestors enjoyed as they were displaced from agriculture to join a highly productive industrial labor force. Automation, instead, has flushed workers without a college degree into a low productivity economy where hotel and restaurant workers, nursing home caretakers, janitors and 7-11 cashiers eke out a living on little more than the minimum wage. Americans have earned their skepticism about the wonders of AI.

One must wonder how such a transformative project as the mass deployment of artificial intelligence across society and the economy will navigate today’s democratic political systems. The technological elite’s contempt for the people’s concerns suggests that they hope to somehow bypass popular concerns in pursuit of the AI program. It seems unlikely that a crew of billionaires who dream of building enclaves at sea, outside the legal jurisdiction of any state, will simply accept democratic constraints. The question is what they will do to overcome them.

Until China became a hi-tech powerhouse and proved them wrong, the political class across the liberal market democracies of the West was convinced that capitalism needed democracy to thrive. But the neoliberal project that guided policy across much of the 20th century was largely about putting capitalism beyond democracy’s reach.

The emergence of independent central banks like the Federal Reserve, which is supposed to set interest rates free from political pressure, is perhaps the prime example of this process. The agreements that led to the creation of the World Trade Organization were largely about putting trade policy beyond the reach of domestic politics. Myriad international treaties were similarly designed to protect economic intercourse from democratic challenges, to provide businesses insulation from political agendas and guarantee the political stability they required to invest.

But the neoliberal project was not driven by “a foundational belief that democracy needs to be snuffed out entirely,” noted Slobodian, author of “Globalists” which traces the history of neoliberalism, as well as an explanatory tome on Elon Musk, “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.” It “acknowledged at some basic level the legitimacy of democracy, which needs to be counterbalanced.”

The barons of Silicon Valley are not so forgiving. “The Silicon Valley leadership class has a programmers’ mentality,” said Slobodian. “For them, the messiness of democracy has no function or utility. It is only bad code.”

Peter Thiel, the weirdest of the Silicon Valley billionaires, who can’t but bring up the Antichrist in every conversation, has argued that democracy and liberty are incompatible. Similar strains of thought are also popular with the less idiosyncratic billionaires in the Valley ecosystem. OpenAI’s Sam Altman salivates about an “awesome” future in which human presidents are replaced with an AI that “can go around and talk to every person on Earth, understand their exact preferences at a very deep level, you know, how they think about this issue and that one and how they balance the trade-offs and what they want and then understand all of that and like collectively optimize for the collective preferences of humanity or of citizens of the US.”

The technos’ conflict is not exclusively with democracy. It is with any institution that dares impose constraints on whatever Grand Project they plan to unleash on the world. This could be reconfiguring human interactions by plugging everybody into social media, inventing a new form of money that can evade government control, civilizing space or bringing about a superintelligent Golem.

Musk has no patience for corporate governance tools that may limit what he can do at the helm of his empire. He aspires to be answerable to no one and will organize his companies to that effect. Thiel can’t even countenance competition. It “means no profits for anybody, no meaningful differentiation, and a struggle for survival,” he has fumed. Across the Valley, these thoughts draw from an unshakeable faith in the civilizational, transformative greatness of their endeavor. Technology will solve the world. They will provide the technology. Everybody else, please get out of the way.

There is, however, a historical discontinuity to the story of these masters of the universe: They used to think of themselves as the Good Guys in the liberal democratic fold. Most of them were aligned with the Democratic Party, culturally liberal, empathetic, and willing to accept some modicum of taxation to finance redistribution. Emerging after the collapse of the Soviet block and the end of the Cold War, they saw themselves and their companies as agents of the End of History in Francis Fukuyama’s sense of the word.

Social media–Silicon Valley’s original Grand Project– would overcome the censorship and limits to expression that underpin authoritarian rule, unshackling freedom of expression and opening the floodgates for liberty and democracy. The project sounded so good that the masters of the Valley managed to convince Congress in 1996 to give them a free pass: section 230 of the Telecommunications Act, which said social media companies were not responsible for anything posted on their platforms, based on the dubious argument that they just provided the blackboard but had no say over what was written on it.

Then, the tech moguls’ love affair with democracy went sour. For it turned out that social media could also do a lot of damage. Reports of teen suicides and online bullying bred unease about social media, which built into open mistrust as it became evident that the billionaires at the helm of these technologies knew about the potential perils of their products and yet kept adding features designed to hook users to their screens.

When social media platforms emerged as vectors of misinformation and political manipulation during the 2016 election, the romance between the tech bros and society fractured irretrievably. Founders and their funders who were used to being revered as purveyors of rainbows and puppies, found themselves under harshly unsympathetic scrutiny.

By the time Covid hit in 2020, the former paragons of liberal democracy had found a new role as magnifiers of conspiracy theories, enemies of “woke”, partisans in a libertarian revolt against “government control”. Joe Biden’s attempts to use antitrust law and other regulations against the techno-plutocrats’ empires pushed them to the dark side, where Trump and his angry Maga movement awaited their embrace.

How long will the honeymoon last? Mark Zuckerberg seems excited about the gold chains, the new hairdo and the mixed martial arts. Perhaps his embrace of the Maga-friendly manosphere is genuine. Musk, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Altman all seem comfy in Trump’s squishy embrace. And Trump’s Washington keeps giving Silicon Valley what it wants. The administration is promising to punish European countries who dare fine the US’s hi-tech behemoths. The president has called the power plants built to feed AI datacenters “beautiful”. And he will never do anything to hinder crypto, which is proving so lucrative for him and his family.

Still, the furious backlash against datacenters suggests that Silicon Valley’s Maga-friendly strategy may run out of runway. Their allegiance with Trump, whose popularity ratings are plummeting, may start feeling like an anvil around their neck.

Abdul El-Sayed, the democratic socialist running for the Senate in Michigan, put it this way in a conversation with Jasmine Sun: “This entire industry feels misplaced, and it’s being driven by the interaction between all the worst players. Number one, tech billionaires who are already billionaires, who don’t really need more money but want power. And then VC firms who want to make more money. And then big corporations who want to automate your job. So who wins here? Definitely not the people who live there.”

Silicon Valley may have oodles of money to change the conversation. But it is right to be terrified that this argument may win the day. As Slobodian put it, “the tech barons may not care about democracy, but democracy cares about them.”

Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Fake ChatGPT billing emails can steal your login
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you pay for ChatGPT, an email saying there is a problem with your subscription could easily get your attention. May...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you pay for ChatGPT, an email saying there is a problem with your subscription could easily get your attention. Maybe your card expired. Maybe the payment failed. Either way, you probably want to fix it before anything happens to your account. Cybercriminals are counting on that reaction.

Security researchers at Cofense uncovered a phishing campaign that impersonates OpenAI and ChatGPT. The fake email looks like a routine subscription notice. However, the button inside can lead to a convincing copy of the ChatGPT login page. Cofense says the campaign targets account credentials and payment information.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Get Better Healthcare With AI replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay now at CyberGuyLive.com

A fake ChatGPT billing email claims a subscription payment was declined and urges the recipient to update payment information. (Cofense)

The scam starts with an email that looks polished enough to make you pause. According to the Cofense Phishing Defense Center, it uses the real ChatGPT logo and claims your subscription payment needs attention. Then comes the pressure. The message prominently displays "Subscription Payment Required." It also warns that you have 48 hours to act. A large "Update Payment Information" button gives you an obvious way to supposedly fix the problem. Finally, the message signs off as "The OpenAI Team." If you are checking email between meetings or quickly scrolling on your phone, all of that can feel believable. Cofense says the attackers combine familiar images, bold wording and urgency to push people into acting quickly.

The sender's email address is one of the biggest red flags. Cofense found that the phishing message came from support@9527db6e1a[.]nxcli[.]io. That domain has nothing to do with OpenAI. OpenAI currently lists several domains that it uses for legitimate customer emails. They include @openai.com, @mail.openai.com and @email.openai.com, along with other official OpenAI domains used for specific communications. That makes the full sender address worth checking. Do not rely on the name that appears in your inbox. A scammer can make the display name look reassuring while using a completely unrelated address behind it.

FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER

The phishing link leads to a fake ChatGPT login page on an unrelated domain designed to capture account credentials. (Cofense)

The button inside this phishing email adds another layer of deception. Cofense found that clicking "Update Payment Information" first sent users through a Google API redirect. The link then forwarded them to the attacker's malicious site. That can make a suspicious link look more convincing at first glance because Google appears along the way. We have seen criminals abuse trusted services in similar attacks before. CyberGuy previously covered how hackers used legitimate Google Cloud tools to send phishing messages that looked like authentic Google notifications. So, seeing Google somewhere in a link does not tell you where you will eventually land. On a computer, hovering over a button can sometimes reveal the destination before you click. Still, redirects can make that check less useful. The safer option is to skip the email link entirely.

Once someone clicks through, the scam gets harder to spot. Cofense says the phishing page closely copies the ChatGPT login experience, complete with familiar logos, text and icons. However, the domain in the browser does not match the legitimate ChatGPT login domain identified by Cofense. If a victim enters login information, the fake site captures it and sends it to the attacker. The page then sends the victim to an error screen, which could easily look like a temporary login problem. By then, the attacker may already have the credentials. That is why it is worth checking the address bar before you enter a password. Scammers can copy the look of a login page. They cannot make an unrelated domain belong to OpenAI.

We reached out to OpenAI for comment but did not hear back before our deadline.

ChatGPT’s familiar login experience gives scammers a recognizable look to copy in convincing phishing attacks. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

If an email says there is a payment problem, skip the button. Go directly to ChatGPT.com or open the official app and sign in yourself. For web subscriptions, OpenAI says to check Settings → Billing . Some accounts may show Settings → Account → Payment → Manage instead. If you subscribed through Apple or Google Play, manage your subscription through that store.

Expand the sender information and look at the actual email address. In this campaign, the sender used an nxcli.io domain. OpenAI publishes the domains it uses for legitimate communications, which gives you something concrete to compare against.

Check the browser address bar before entering a password or payment information. If the domain looks unfamiliar, close the page. Then open the service yourself through its official app or website. This same habit can protect you from fake banking sites. We recently covered criminals who bought sponsored search ads that sent victims to lookalike bank login pages.

Never reuse your ChatGPT password on other accounts. We recommend using a unique password and suggest a password manager to generate and store it. That way, one stolen password cannot easily unlock several of your accounts.

OpenAI supports two-factor authentication, or 2FA. You can enable it from the Security section of your ChatGPT settings. Depending on your account, available verification methods may include an authenticator app, push notification, text message or passkey. 2FA adds another hurdle if someone gets your password. However, enabling 2FA does not automatically end sessions that are already logged in.

Strong antivirus software can help warn you about malicious links and phishing websites. It can also block other threats that may arrive through scam emails. Keep that protection updated on every device where you check email or sign in to important accounts. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Change your password immediately if you entered it on a suspicious site. Then open ChatGPT and go to Settings → Security → Active sessions . Review the listed devices and sessions. If you see something you do not recognize, log it out.

OpenAI also lets you go to Settings → Security → Active sessions and choose Log out of all session s. The company says signing out across every device can take up to 30 minutes. If you use Google, Microsoft or Apple to sign in to ChatGPT, secure that account as well.

If you gave a suspicious site your card information, call the number on the back of the card. Tell the issuer that your payment information may have been compromised. Then review recent transactions for anything you do not recognize. Your card issuer may recommend replacing the card. Follow its instructions rather than waiting for a fraudulent charge to appear.

Cofense says the phishing campaign targeted people using ChatGPT through personal and work accounts. If you entered work credentials or used a company-managed account, contact your IT or security team. They can review account activity and take additional steps if necessary.

This scam works because the email looks like something you might actually expect to receive. A payment problem feels routine, and that can make people lower their guard. If you get a billing warning from ChatGPT, do not use the link in the message. Open ChatGPT yourself and check your account there. If you already entered your password on a suspicious page, change it right away and review your active sessions. If you shared payment information, contact your card issuer.

Have you ever received a subscription warning that looked completely legitimate, and what tipped you off before you clicked? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
